This limits the sector\'s growth potential significantly.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-mediofisico&#95;11-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mediofisico-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-agronegocios&#95;50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-agronegocios-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Due to lack of investment only 11% of the state\'s arable land is irrigated. Seventy two percent of farmland is privately own with the rest belonging to <a href="/wiki/Ejido" title="Ejido">ejidos</a> or other types of communal ownership. The municipalities with the most cultivated land are <a href="/wiki/Chignahuapan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chignahuapan (municipality)">Chignahuapan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chalchicomula_de_Sesma_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chalchicomula de Sesma (municipality)">Chalchicomula de Sesma</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tlachichuca_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tlachichuca (municipality)">Tlachichuca</a> and <a href="/wiki/Zacapoaxtla_(municipality)" title="Zacapoaxtla (municipality)">Zacapoaxtla</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The most important activities include production of domestic fowl (eggs and meat), which accounts for 37%, cattle (dairy and meat) at 12%, grains (90% corn) and pork at 10% each, vegetables (<a href="/wiki/Tomatillo" title="Tomatillo">tomatillos</a>, onions, carrots, tomatoes, and squash) at 8% and fruit (oranges, limes, <a href="/wiki/Cactus_pear" class="mw-redirect" title="Cactus pear">cactus pear</a>, apples, <a href="/wiki/Avocado" title="Avocado">avocados</a> and peaches) at 4%.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-agronegocios&#95;50-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-agronegocios-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Other important crops include beans, animal feed, <a href="/wiki/Alfalfa" title="Alfalfa">alfalfa</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sugar_cane" class="mw-redirect" title="Sugar cane">sugar cane</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Most crops are grown in the municipalities of <a href="/wiki/Hueytamalco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Hueytamalco (municipality)">Hueytamalco</a>, <a href="/wiki/Francisco_Z._Mena_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Francisco Z. Mena (municipality)">Francisco Z. Mena</a>, <a href="/wiki/Venustiano_Carranza_Municipality,_Puebla" title="Venustiano Carranza Municipality, Puebla">Venustiano Carranza</a>, <a href="/wiki/Xicotepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Xicotepec (municipality)">Xicotepec</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jalpan,_Puebla" title="Jalpan, Puebla">Jalpan</a>. Most crops, especially corn, are grown on relatively small farms, communal fields and family plots, but perennial crops such as rubber trees, coffee and citrus from are mostly grown on large plantations.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-mediofisico&#95;11-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mediofisico-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The most important livestock in the state are cattle, pigs and domestic fowl. Cattle are prevalent in the municipalities of Francisco Z. Mena, Venustiano Carranza, Jalpan, Hueytamalco and <a href="/w/index.php?title=Chiautla_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Chiautla (municipality) (page does not exist)">Chiautla de Tapia</a>. Pigs are mostly found in Tehuacán, <a href="/wiki/Ajalpan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ajalpan (municipality)">Ajalpan</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tepanco_de_L%C3%B3pez_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tepanco de López (municipality) (page does not exist)">Tepanco de López</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tecamachalco_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tecamachalco (municipality) (page does not exist)">Tecamachalco</a> and <a href="/wiki/Yehualtepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Yehualtepec (municipality)">Yehualtepec</a>. The entire state ranks first in the production of domestic fowl with most being produced in the municipalities of Ajalpan, Tehuacán, Tecamachalco, Tepanco de López and <a href="/wiki/Tochtepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tochtepec (municipality)">Tochtepec</a>. Other livestock raised include goats, sheep and horses.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Other production of primary materials includes forest products and fish. Over 93% of the tree species exploited in the state are conifers mostly cut for wood production. In 2007, the annual production of wood products had risen to 244,803 cubic metres (8,645,136&#160;cu&#160;ft). Most forestry occurs in the municipalities of Chignahuapan, <a href="/wiki/Tetela_de_Ocampo" title="Tetela de Ocampo">Tetela de Ocampo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Vicente_Guerrero_Municipality,_Durango" title="Vicente Guerrero Municipality, Durango">Vicente Guerrero</a>, Zacatlán and Huauchinango. Fish are both caught wild and farmed and mostly concentrate on species such as <a href="/wiki/Carp" title="Carp">carp</a>, <a href="/wiki/Trout" title="Trout">trout</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mojarra" title="Mojarra">mojarra</a>. Most are harvested in the state\'s dams and lakes, which cover a surface area of 6,500 hectares.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Industry_and_mining">Industry and mining</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=18" title="Edit section: Industry and mining"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>The state has been an important industrial center since colonial times, mostly known for the production of textiles and pottery, both of which continue to be made.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-angelopolis&#95;21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-angelopolis-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Today, industries of various types, along with mining and construction employ about twenty five percent of the state\'s population.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> More than 150,000 small and medium-sized factories operate in the state, providing 60% of the state\'s GDP.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Most industry in the state in concentrated in and around the capital. The most important industries are in metals, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, electronic items and textiles.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Textiles produced in the state mostly involve thread, machinery, knitted items and woven fabrics.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-textilesgob&#95;51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-textilesgob-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Moreover, the first and one of the biggest textile factory in Mexico and in <a href="/wiki/Latinamerica" class="mw-redirect" title="Latinamerica">Latinamerica</a>, The "<a href="/wiki/La_Constancia_Mexicana" title="La Constancia Mexicana">La Constancia Mexicana</a> Factory", was built in capital of Puebla. Two important employers are Hylsa and the Volkswagen plant, both in the Puebla area.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Two important industries are automotive and agribusiness. The automotive sector is important for the state as a leading manufacturer of both automobiles and automobile parts. Some of the businesses located in the state include Denso México, Arvin Meritor de México, Mabe, Leoni, Hyundai-Kia Motors, Coramex Company and Forteq.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-automotriz&#95;52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-automotriz-52"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Industry related to agriculture consists of both producing products needed by farmers and processing agricultural produce. Some of these companies include Nestle de México, Pasan, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Chocolatera_Moctezuma&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Chocolatera Moctezuma (page does not exist)">Chocolatera Moctezuma</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Sabormex&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Sabormex (page does not exist)">Sabormex</a>, <a href="/wiki/Big_Cola" class="mw-redirect" title="Big Cola">Big Cola</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Bomba_Energy&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Bomba Energy (page does not exist)">Bomba Energy</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Ochoa_Comercial&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Ochoa Comercial (page does not exist)">Ochoa Comercial</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Grupo_Pepsico&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Grupo Pepsico (page does not exist)">Grupo Pepsico</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Compa%C3%B1%C3%ADa_Topo_Chico&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Compañía Topo Chico (page does not exist)">Compañía Topo Chico</a>, <a href="/wiki/Red_Bull" title="Red Bull">Red Bull</a>, <a href="/wiki/Grupo_Bimbo" title="Grupo Bimbo">Grupo Bimbo</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Unifoods&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Unifoods (page does not exist)">Unifoods</a>, <a href="/wiki/Novamex" class="mw-redirect" title="Novamex">Novamex</a>, <a href="/wiki/Coca-Cola" title="Coca-Cola">The Coca-Cola Company</a>, <a href="/wiki/Supermercados_Gigante" title="Supermercados Gigante">Supermercados Gigante</a>, <a href="/wiki/Soriana" title="Soriana">Soriana</a>, <a href="/wiki/La_Coste%C3%B1a_(food_company)" title="La Costeña (food company)">La Costeña</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jugos_del_Valle" title="Jugos del Valle">Jugos del Valle</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-agroindustrial&#95;53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-agroindustrial-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>There are nine state and four federal programs targeting small and medium-sized producers, which provide training, consulting, trademarks and other services. Some programs target specific industries such as software. One focus of the state is to promote technology based industries which produced high-value products. There are eleven industrial parks and other special industry zones for this purpose. Another area identified for improvement is higher education, to produce graduates to work in these kinds of industries.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Commercial events include the Exintex International Exhibition, which is held in the state each year and attracts textile manufacturers from states such as <a href="/wiki/Morelos" title="Morelos">Morelos</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tlaxcala" title="Tlaxcala">Tlaxcala</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tamaulipas" title="Tamaulipas">Tamaulipas</a>, <a href="/wiki/Guanajuato" title="Guanajuato">Guanajuato</a>, <a href="/wiki/Quer%C3%A9taro" title="Querétaro">Querétaro</a> and <a href="/wiki/Aguascalientes" title="Aguascalientes">Aguascalientes</a> as well as the cities of <a href="/wiki/Guadalajara,_Mexico" class="mw-redirect" title="Guadalajara, Mexico">Guadalajara</a> and Mexico City.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-textilesgob&#95;51-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-textilesgob-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Mining produces <a href="/wiki/Calcite" title="Calcite">calcite</a>, <a href="/wiki/Marble" title="Marble">marble</a>, <a href="/wiki/Calcium_oxide" title="Calcium oxide">calcium oxide</a>, <a href="/wiki/Onyx" title="Onyx">onyx</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Lime_(material)" title="Lime (material)">lime</a>. The most important mining processing concerns are <a href="/w/index.php?title=Calera_Santa_Ma._S.A&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Calera Santa Ma. S.A (page does not exist)">Calera Santa Ma. S.A</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Marmiparquet_S.A&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Marmiparquet S.A (page does not exist)">Marmiparquet S.A</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Qu%C3%ADmica_Sumex_S.A_de_C.V&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Química Sumex S.A de C.V (page does not exist)">Química Sumex S.A de C.V</a> and <a href="/w/index.php?title=Yacimientos_de_Travertino_S.A.&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Yacimientos de Travertino S.A. (page does not exist)">Yacimientos de Travertino S.A.</a>, and the sector employs about 270,000 workers.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Handicrafts">Handicrafts</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=19" title="Edit section: Handicrafts"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:FacadeUriartePuebla.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/FacadeUriartePuebla.JPG/250px-FacadeUriartePuebla.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="194" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/FacadeUriartePuebla.JPG/500px-FacadeUriartePuebla.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="3346" data-file-height="2592" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Uriarte_Talavera" title="Uriarte Talavera">Uriarte Talavera</a> pottery workshop in Puebla, Mexico</figcaption></figure>\n<p><a href="/wiki/Talavera_(pottery)" class="mw-redirect" title="Talavera (pottery)">Talavera pottery</a> is the state\'s best known craft. This pottery is a type of <a href="/wiki/Maiolica" title="Maiolica">maiolica</a>, which was introduced into Spain by the <a href="/wiki/Arab" class="mw-redirect" title="Arab">Arabs</a>, and into Mexico by the Spanish. Talavera is considered to be the finest of Mexico\'s pottery traditions, which is still made with the same techniques as in the colonial period.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artesaniasgob&#95;54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artesaniasgob-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Talavera pottery began in the city of Puebla when the Spaniards brought over from Europe the techniques of making maiolica pottery, itself brought from China via the Arabs. The techniques and designs were based on the pottery made in <a href="/wiki/Talavera_la_Real" title="Talavera la Real">Talavera, Spain</a>. The high-quality clay and the formation of <a href="/wiki/Guild" title="Guild">guilds</a> to ensure quality soon made pottery made in Puebla a near-luxury item. The craft waned after <a href="/wiki/Mexican_War_of_Independence" title="Mexican War of Independence">Independence</a>, but made a comeback in the latter 20th century. Today certified Talavera pottery in made only in a handful of workshops in the capital and other nearby communities. To be certified as genuine the same methods as used in the 16th century must be applied. True Talavera pottery is expensive and considered to be collector\'s items.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones44&#95;55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones44-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Other types of pottery in the state exist. One is the black clay figures made in <a href="/wiki/Acatl%C3%A1n_de_Osorio,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Acatlán de Osorio, Puebla">Acatlán de Osorio</a>. Most of these figures are animals and are almost always painted with white designs. Black clay is also used to make cups, plates and other utilitarian items in other communities. Another important clay craft are the <a href="/wiki/Tree_of_Life_(craft)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tree of Life (craft)">Trees of Life</a>, mostly made in the community of <a href="/wiki/Iz%C3%BAcar_de_Matamoros" title="Izúcar de Matamoros">Izúcar de Matamoros</a> and Acatlán de Osorio. Traditionally, these are sculptures depicting <a href="/wiki/Adam" title="Adam">Adam</a> and <a href="/wiki/Eve" title="Eve">Eve</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Garden_of_Eden" title="Garden of Eden">Garden of Eden</a>, but the craft has evolved to include other themes as well.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones45&#95;56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones45-56"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The making of textiles and embroidery dates back to pre-Hispanic times. Traditional clothing such as <a href="/wiki/Rebozo" title="Rebozo">rebozos</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sarape" class="mw-redirect" title="Sarape">sarapes</a>, shirts and pants are still made in various parts of the state and reflect the different indigenous communities which are found here. <a href="/wiki/Hueyapan_(municipality)" title="Hueyapan (municipality)">Hueyapan</a> is one of the better known artisanal textile producers, with clothing items and others richly and colorfully embroidered. Both the thread used to weave the cloth and embroider it are <a href="/wiki/Dyeing" title="Dyeing">dyed</a> with <a href="/wiki/Natural_dye" title="Natural dye">natural dyes</a> such as those obtained from the <a href="/wiki/Cochineal" title="Cochineal">cochineal</a> insect. Another area known for its textiles is <a href="/wiki/Zacapoaxtla_(municipality)" title="Zacapoaxtla (municipality)">Zacapoaxtla</a> in the north of the state.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones46&#95;57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones46-57"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The town of <a href="/wiki/Amozoc_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Amozoc (municipality)">Amozoc</a> is known for its silverwork. This tradition began when a number of metalworkers of various types settled here after the <a href="/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire" title="Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire">Conquest</a> in the 16th century. These smiths made a variety of objects from the everyday such as knives, swords, stirrups and more, eventually branching into finer metals such as silver and gold, mother-of-pearl, ivory and more. However, it is silver smithing which has best survived to the present day.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artesaniasgob&#95;54-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artesaniasgob-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>There are two widely practice paper crafts in Puebla. The making of bark paper or <a href="/wiki/Amatl" class="mw-redirect" title="Amatl">amate</a> was known in pre-Hispanic times when such was reserved for special ceremonies and the recording of important information. It had an almost magical quality to it and was used for spells, clothing of idols and other ceremonial purposes. Today, the paper is still made as an art form and often painted with elaborate designs.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones48&#95;58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones48-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In Puebla, the paper is still made by hand and often it is hand-painted with pre-Hispanic designs.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artesaniasgob&#95;54-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artesaniasgob-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> One area noted for this craft is <a href="/wiki/San_Salvador_Huixcolotla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="San Salvador Huixcolotla (municipality)">San Salvador Huixcolotla</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones48&#95;58-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones48-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Another is <a href="/wiki/Pahuatl%C3%A1n_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Pahuatlán (municipality)">San Pablito Pahuatlán</a> in the Sierra Norte.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artesaniasgob&#95;54-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artesaniasgob-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> One notable amate paper artist is <a href="/wiki/Curandero" title="Curandero">curandero</a> Alfonso García Téllez, who narrates stories and ceremonies in his works.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artesaniasgob&#95;54-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artesaniasgob-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Another paper craft is <a href="/wiki/Papel_picado" title="Papel picado">papel picado</a>, or "chopped paper." This craft began with the introduction of <a href="/wiki/Crepe_paper" class="mw-redirect" title="Crepe paper">crepe paper</a> from Asia. This paper is elaborately cut to form figures and scenes which are then hung for decorative purposes for holidays such as <a href="/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead" title="Day of the Dead">Day of the Dead</a>. This most traditional of these are laborious cut by hand, but most are done today by machine. Those native to Puebla feature a large figure with a detailed background and are considered to be part of the state\'s cultural heritage (Patrimonio Cultural del Estado de Puebla).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones48&#95;58-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones48-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>A relatively recent craft is the making of blown glass Christmas ornaments in <a href="/wiki/Chignahuapan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chignahuapan (municipality)">Chignahuapan</a>. This municipality has about 200 workshops which employ about 1,500 workers, which makes the spherical ornaments individually and many are shipped internationally to the United States and Latin America. This craft is still growing and represents one of the more stable small scale manufacturing endeavors in Puebla.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones47&#95;59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones47-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>For many rural communities, the making of handcrafted furniture, both fine and rustic, is an important economic activity. One such community is <a href="/wiki/Chalchicomula_de_Sesma_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chalchicomula de Sesma (municipality)">Ciudad Serdán</a>, which makes wooden utensils, decorative figures and banister work in addition to furniture. It has a strong reputation along with Chignahuapan. Areas outside of Ciudad Serdán are known for specializing in reproductions of <a href="/wiki/Louis_XV_style" title="Louis XV style">Louis XV</a> and <a href="/wiki/Louis_XVI_style" title="Louis XVI style">Louis XVI</a> furniture. The community of <a href="/w/index.php?title=Trinidad_Alonso_B%C3%A1ez&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Trinidad Alonso Báez (page does not exist)">Trinidad Alonso Báez</a> is known as the only place in Latin American where pianos are made purely by hand. They are also known for the repairing of musical instrument with many of the state\'s antique church organs fixed by craftsmen from here.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones47&#95;59-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones47-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Onyx is a plentiful stone in the state and it is worked into figures and other items in various parts of the state. The most important deposit of the stone is in <a href="/wiki/Tecali_de_Herrera_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tecali de Herrera (municipality)">Tecali</a> and many workshops fill the streets of this town. Most of the pieces made are decorative in nature but small utilitarian items such as plates and ashtrays are also made.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones48&#95;58-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones48-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Amozoc has been known for silver smithing since colonial times, when European techniques were brought over by the Spanish. As back then, they still make items such as jewelry, silverware, and items for church rituals. These smiths’ work is considered to be quality, with the finest pieces encrusted with precious and semi-precious gems, gold, and ivory.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones4849&#95;60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones4849-60"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The first glass workshop in <a href="/wiki/New_Spain" title="New Spain">New Spain</a> was established in Puebla by Spaniard Rodrigo Espinoza in 1542. It remained the only one in Spain\'s colonies for decades, exporting glass items to places such as <a href="/wiki/Peru" title="Peru">Peru</a> and <a href="/wiki/Guatemala" title="Guatemala">Guatemala</a>. In the 18th century, Pedro Antonio revitalized the craft with a new factory. This factory was the main producer until the establishment of the Compañia Empresarial para la Fabricacion del Vidrio Plano y Cristal in 1838. This company introduced French designs and techniques to Mexico. The next major glassmaker was Victor Martinez Filoteo, who established the Fabrica La Luz in 1935. This company is still the major producer of glass items in the state. Small workshops are prevalent in <a href="/wiki/Huaquechula_(municipality)" title="Huaquechula (municipality)">Huaquechula</a>, where they specialize items made with black and smoke-colored glass.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones49&#95;61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones49-61"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Commerce_and_transportation">Commerce and transportation</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=20" title="Edit section: Commerce and transportation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Thirty five percent are employed in commerce, tourism and transportation.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-actecon&#95;49-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-actecon-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The state has 8,995&#160;km (5,589&#160;mi) of highways and 1,024&#160;km (636&#160;mi) of rail line, as well as twenty three major malls.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Outlet Puebla was opened in 2001 on the highway between Mexico City and the city of Puebla where it intersects with the Periferico Ecologico. It contains more than 80 outlet stores with major national and international brands such as <a href="/wiki/Reebok" title="Reebok">Reebok</a>, <a href="/wiki/Guess_(clothing)" class="mw-redirect" title="Guess (clothing)">Guess</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pepe_Jeans" title="Pepe Jeans">Pepe Jeans</a>, located on a site of over 30,000m2. The enterprise is run by Asesores en Exposiciones y Calpro, S. A. de C. V. The mall targets traveling customers from the states of Puebla, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Tlaxcala as well as Mexico City.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-apertura&#95;62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-apertura-62"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The international airport in <a href="/wiki/Huejotzingo_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Huejotzingo (municipality)">Huejotzingo</a> is linked to the Mexico City airport by land transport.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Efforts have been made to expand the airport in Huejotzingo to be an auxiliary to the overcrowded <a href="/wiki/Mexico_City_International_Airport" title="Mexico City International Airport">Mexico City airport</a>. The airport has been chosen due to its relatively quiet airspace and proximity to the nation\'s capital. As of 2010<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, the airport handles sixty operations per day, 40 of which are commercial flights serving 2.5 million passengers per year.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-pidemano&#95;63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-pidemano-63"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Tourism">Tourism</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=21" title="Edit section: Tourism"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg/250px-Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="253" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg/330px-Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg/500px-Vista_de_la_Fachada_del_Templo_de_San_Francisco_Acatepec_9.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="4000" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Church_of_San_Francisco_Acatepec" title="Church of San Francisco Acatepec">Church of San Francisco Acatepec</a></figcaption></figure>\n<p>The state has 2,600 historic buildings, antiques, bars and pottery workshops.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-paravisitar&#95;64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-paravisitar-64"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The downtown of the capital is filled with churches, government buildings and large homes, built by indigenous hands for their Spanish overlords. This downtown was declared a <a href="/wiki/World_Heritage_Site" title="World Heritage Site">World Heritage Site</a> in 1987.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-angelopolis&#95;21-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-angelopolis-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The state promotes twelve tourist routes, seven in the city of Puebla and five in the rest of the state. These routes cover the most representative buildings of the history of the state up to modern attractions such as the <a href="/wiki/Africam_Safari" title="Africam Safari">Africam Safari</a> zoo.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-paravisitar&#95;64-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-paravisitar-64"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The first tourist route in the city of Puebla passes by the Cathedral, the <a href="/wiki/Palafoxiana_Library" class="mw-redirect" title="Palafoxiana Library">Palafoxiana Library</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_Santo_Domingo_(Puebla)" class="mw-redirect" title="Church of Santo Domingo (Puebla)">Capilla del Rosario</a>, Calle de Santa Clara, Palacio Municipal, Casa de los Muñecos and the Museo Amparo. The second route passes by the Casa del Alfeñique, the Mercado de Artesanias, the Barrio del Artista, the Teatro Principal and the San Francisco Church. The third route contains the Railroad Museum, the Museo y Pinacoteca Ex-Convento de Santa Monica, the Ex-Convento de Santa Rosa, the Museo de la No-Intervencion Fuerte de Guadalupe and the Mercado de Antiguedades. The fourth route contains the San Francisco Acatepec Church, the Santa Maria Tonatzintla Church, the Capilla Real, the Cholula archeological site, the Los Remedios Church and Huejotzingo. The fifth route includes <a href="/w/index.php?title=Cuauhtinchan&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Cuauhtinchan (page does not exist)">Cuauhtinchan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tecali_de_Herrera_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tecali de Herrera (municipality)">Tecali</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Africam_Safari" title="Africam Safari">Africam Safari</a> Zoo.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-angelopolis&#95;21-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-angelopolis-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Outside of the Puebla metropolitan area, the state promotes natural attractions such as the cacti of <a href="/wiki/Zapotitl%C3%A1n_Municipality,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Zapotitlán Municipality, Puebla">Zapotitlán</a>, the 100-million-year-old fossils of Cantera Tlayùa in <a href="/wiki/Tepexi_de_Rodr%C3%ADguez_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tepexi de Rodríguez (municipality)">Tepexi de Rodríguez</a> and smaller ones such as waterfalls, churches, caverns, archeological zones, former monasteries, <a href="/wiki/Traditional_fixed_markets_in_Mexico" class="mw-redirect" title="Traditional fixed markets in Mexico">traditional markets</a>, fresh water springs, lakes and more.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-smixteca&#95;65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-smixteca-65"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The tourist routes outside of the Puebla metro area are divided into the Sierra Mixteca area in the south and the Sierra Norte in the north. The Sierra Mixteca area includes the Ruta de Aguacate (Avocado Route), the Ruta del Ónix (Onyx Route), the Ruta del Maiz (Corn Route) and the Ruta Paleontológica (Palaeontology Route). The Avocado Route includes the municipalities of <a href="/wiki/Atlixco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Atlixco (municipality)">Atlixco</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tianguismanalco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tianguismanalco (municipality)">Tianguismanalco</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tochimilco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tochimilco (municipality)">Tochimilco</a>, <a href="/wiki/Huaquechula_(municipality)" title="Huaquechula (municipality)">Huaquechula</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tlapanal%C3%A1_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tlapanalá (municipality)">Tlapanalá</a>, <a href="/wiki/Iz%C3%BAcar_de_Matamoros" title="Izúcar de Matamoros">Izúcar de Matamoros</a>, <a href="/wiki/Epatl%C3%A1n_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Epatlán (municipality)">San Juan Epatlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chietla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chietla (municipality)">Chietla</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Chiautla_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Chiautla (municipality) (page does not exist)">Chiautla de Tapia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Acatl%C3%A1n_de_Osorio,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Acatlán de Osorio, Puebla">Acatlán de Osorio</a>. The Onyx Route includes the Africam Safari Zoo, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Cuauhtinchan&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Cuauhtinchan (page does not exist)">Cuauhtinchan</a>, <a href="/wiki/San_Salvador_Huixcolotla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="San Salvador Huixcolotla (municipality)">San Salvador Huixcolotla</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tecali_de_Herrera_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tecali de Herrera (municipality)">Tecali de Herrera</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tecamachalco_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tecamachalco (municipality) (page does not exist)">Tecamachalco</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tepeaca" title="Tepeaca">Tepeaca</a>. The Corn Route includes <a href="/wiki/Tehuac%C3%A1n,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Tehuacán, Puebla">Tehuacán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Santa_Mar%C3%ADa_del_Monte" class="mw-redirect" title="Santa María del Monte">Santa María del Monte</a> and <a href="/w/index.php?title=Zapotitl%C3%A1n_Salinas&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Zapotitlán Salinas (page does not exist)">Zapotitlán Salinas</a>. The Paleontology Route includes <a href="/w/index.php?title=Atoyatempan_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Atoyatempan (municipality) (page does not exist)">Atoyatempan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Huitziltepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Huitziltepec (municipality)">Santa Clara Huitziltepec</a>, <a href="/wiki/Molcaxac_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Molcaxac (municipality)">Molcaxac</a>, <a href="/wiki/Huatlatlauca_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Huatlatlauca (municipality)">Huatlatlauca</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chigmecatitlan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chigmecatitlan (municipality)">Chigmecatitlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tepexi_de_Rodr%C3%ADguez_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tepexi de Rodríguez (municipality)">Tepexi de Rodríguez</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ixcaquixtla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ixcaquixtla (municipality)">San Juan Ixcaquixtla</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-smixteca&#95;65-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-smixteca-65"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Sierra Norte contains a number of pre-Hispanic archeological sites and colonial architecture. Crafts to be found here include wool clothing, <a href="/wiki/Amatl" class="mw-redirect" title="Amatl">amate paper</a>, clay figures, wood carvings, and embroidered blouses. This area of the state contains the Ruta de la Flor (Flower Route), Ruta Interserrana (Inter-Mountain Route), Ruta del Huipil y Café (Huipil and Coffee Route) and the Ruta Perla Norte (North Pearl Route). The Flower Route includes the municipalities of <a href="/wiki/Chignahuapan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chignahuapan (municipality)">Chignahuapan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Zacatl%C3%A1n_(municipality)" title="Zacatlán (municipality)">Zacatlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Huauchinango_(municipality)" title="Huauchinango (municipality)">Huauchinango</a>, <a href="/wiki/Juan_Galindo_(municipality)" title="Juan Galindo (municipality)">Juan Galindo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pahuatl%C3%A1n_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Pahuatlán (municipality)">Pahuatlán</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tenango,_Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tenango, Puebla (page does not exist)">Tenango</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tetela_de_Ocampo" title="Tetela de Ocampo">Tetela de Ocampo</a> and <a href="/wiki/Xicotepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Xicotepec (municipality)">Xicotepec</a>. The Inter-Mountain Route includes <a href="/wiki/Ahuacatl%C3%A1n,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Ahuacatlán, Puebla">Ahuacatlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Zapotitl%C3%A1n_Municipality,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Zapotitlán Municipality, Puebla">Zapotitlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Xochitl%C3%A1n_de_Vicente_Su%C3%A1rez_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Xochitlán de Vicente Suárez (municipality)">Xochitlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tepango_de_Rodr%C3%ADguez_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tepango de Rodríguez (municipality)">Tepango</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nauzontla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nauzontla (municipality)">Nauzontla</a>. The Huipil and Coffee Route include <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tenextatiloyan&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tenextatiloyan (page does not exist)">Tenextatiloyan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Acajete_Municipality,_Puebla" title="Acajete Municipality, Puebla">Acajete</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cuetzalan" title="Cuetzalan">Cuetzalan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jonotla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jonotla (municipality)">Jonotla</a>, <a href="/wiki/Libres_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Libres (municipality)">Libres</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nopalucan_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nopalucan (municipality)">Nopalucan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oriental_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Oriental (municipality)">Oriental</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Oriental_(municipality)_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Oriental (municipality) (municipality) (page does not exist)">San José Chiapa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tepeyahualco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tepeyahualco (municipality)">Tepeyahualco</a> and <a href="/wiki/Zacapoaxtla_(municipality)" title="Zacapoaxtla (municipality)">Zacapoaxtla</a>. The North Pearl Route includes <a href="/w/index.php?title=Atempan_(municipality)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Atempan (municipality) (page does not exist)">Atempa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chignautla_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Chignautla (municipality)">Chignautla</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hueyapan_(municipality)" title="Hueyapan (municipality)">Hueyapan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Xiutetelco_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Xiutetelco (municipality)">San Juan Xiultetelco</a>, <a href="/wiki/Teziutl%C3%A1n_(municipality)" title="Teziutlán (municipality)">Teziutlán</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tlatlauquitepec_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tlatlauquitepec (municipality)">Tlatlauquitepec</a> and <a href="/wiki/Yaon%C3%A1huac_(municipality)" title="Yaonáhuac (municipality)">Yaonahuac</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-smagica&#95;66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-smagica-66"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>There are a number of former haciendas in the state, many of which have been converted into hotels, spas and other kinds of attractions. Some have also been used as movie and television sets for projects such as <a href="/wiki/Alondra_(telenovela)" class="mw-redirect" title="Alondra (telenovela)">Alondra</a>, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Amor_es_Querer&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Amor es Querer (page does not exist)">Amor es Querer</a>, <a href="/wiki/Man_on_Fire_(2004_film)" title="Man on Fire (2004 film)">Man on Fire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Vantage_Point_(film)" title="Vantage Point (film)">Vantage Point</a> and <a href="/wiki/Frida_(2002_film)" title="Frida (2002 film)">Frida</a>. These include the <a href="/wiki/Chautla_Hacienda" title="Chautla Hacienda">Chautla Hacienda</a> in San Salvador el Verde, Las Calandrias in Atlixco, Micuautla in Puebla, Netxalpa in Atlixco, San Pedro de Ovando in Acatzingo, Ozumba in San José Chiapa, Rancho Jesús in Cuautinchan, San Agustín in Atlixco, San Mateo in Amalucan, San Roque in Atlixco, Santiago Texmelucan in Tepeyahualco de Hidalgo and Oriental Tenextepec in Atlixco.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-filmhaciendas&#95;67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-filmhaciendas-67"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-filmproyectos&#95;68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-filmproyectos-68"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Natural attractions in the state include Amacas in Cuetzalan, Bosque Chignahuapan Forest, the Quetzalapa Chignahuapan Waterfall, Zacatlán Waterfall, La Gloria Cuetzalán Waterfall, Las Brisas Cuetzalan Waterfall, Las Golondrinas Cuetzalan Waterfall, Nexcapa Hauachinango, Ocpaco Zacatlán Waterfall, the arid landscapes of Zapotitlan de Salinas, the Iztalcihual and Popocatepetl volcanos, the basalt columns of Huauchinango, the Valle de Piedras Encimadas in Zacatlán and the Nexcaxa Dam in Huauchinango, el Aguacate Waterfall in Huehuetlán el Grande, and los Ahuehuetes in Atlixco.(scenarios)\n</p><p>Puebla is working with neighboring Veracruz to promote the area\'s tourist attractions and develop them in an ecologically sustainable way. Both state governments are working with organizations of tour operators, hotels and restaurants to pool a fund for activities such as advertising campaigns, especially to Mexico City and the <a href="/wiki/State_of_Mexico" title="State of Mexico">State of Mexico</a>, which account for 80% of all the state\'s visitors. Another is the reimbursement of tolls for those who travel to certain attractions such as the Africam Safari park and two-for-one specials. Efforts have succeeded in raising hotel occupancy rates from 40% to 56% in a number of areas.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-reactivar&#95;69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-reactivar-69"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Archeological_sites">Archeological sites</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=22" title="Edit section: Archeological sites"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mexico.Pue.Cholula.Pyramid.01.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Mexico.Pue.Cholula.Pyramid.01.jpg/250px-Mexico.Pue.Cholula.Pyramid.01.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8b/Mexico.Pue.Cholula.Pyramid.01.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="450" data-file-height="279" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Cholula" title="Great Pyramid of Cholula">Great Pyramid of Cholula</a></figcaption></figure>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cantona12.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Cantona12.jpg/250px-Cantona12.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Cantona12.jpg/500px-Cantona12.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3118" data-file-height="1803" /></a><figcaption>Cantona</figcaption></figure>\n<p><a href="/wiki/Cantona_(Mesoamerican_site)" class="mw-redirect" title="Cantona (Mesoamerican site)">Cantona</a> is a 12 square kilometres (5&#160;sq&#160;mi) archeological site, located in the north of the state between the municipalities of <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tepehualco&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tepehualco (page does not exist)">Tepehualco</a> and <a href="/w/index.php?title=Coyoaco&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Coyoaco (page does not exist)">Coyoaco</a>. It is divided into three units, with work only done on the south unit, which is the best preserved. Here is found the "Acropolis," an area with temples, palaces and other seats of authority. The site was occupied between the 7th and 11th centuries CE and reached its height at the time many other Classic era urban centers were falling. It is thought that this city interrupted the flow of goods from the coast of Veracruz to <a href="/wiki/Teotihuacan" title="Teotihuacan">Teotihuacan</a>, one of the many causes of that city\'s downfall. The site is filled with a large number of patios which measure 50 x 40 meters or larger. Total number of patios found is 620, and 997 mounds have been found as well. In some areas, remains of obsidian and sandstone workshops have been found.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cantonagob&#95;70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cantonagob-70"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Cholula was once a major Mesoamerican city with a multicultural population that was bound by a common religion based on the worship of <a href="/wiki/Quetzalcoatl" class="mw-redirect" title="Quetzalcoatl">Quetzalcoatl</a>. The city was a pilgrimage site for the worship of this deity. Its architecture was complex and shows various foreign influences. Its height was reached during the Classic period between 100 and 900 CE along with <a href="/wiki/Tula_(Mesoamerican_site)" title="Tula (Mesoamerican site)">Tula</a> and Teotihuacan. It was regionally influential for much of the Mesoamerican period, and its polychromic pottery has been found in a large number of sites, indicating trade. By the time the Spanish arrived, it was still a very large city, second only to Tenochtitlan, to which it was subject. Today, the site is known for its Great Pyramid.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cholulagob&#95;71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cholulagob-71"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TepejiViejo.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/TepejiViejo.jpg/250px-TepejiViejo.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="151" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/TepejiViejo.jpg/500px-TepejiViejo.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3114" data-file-height="1881" /></a><figcaption>Tepexi el Viejo</figcaption></figure>\n<p><a href="/wiki/Tepexi_el_Viejo" title="Tepexi el Viejo">Tepexi el Viejo</a> is located southeast of the city of Puebla. It was founded as the seat of one of the most important <a href="/wiki/Popoloca" class="mw-redirect" title="Popoloca">Popoloca</a> dominions and control much of what is now the south of the state from 1200 to 1500 CE. This area\'s light orange colored pottery has been found as far away as Teotihuacan. The site is naturally protected by mountains and canyons and is divided into five areas. Each has platforms, pyramidal mounds, residential areas and tombs. The most important pyramidal mound is located in the center of the site and other, smaller one is located to the extreme west. Residences are located in the northwest, many of which are L-shaped. There is only one natural opening to the area, which is in the south about 6&#160;km (4&#160;mi) outside the city\'s walls.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tepexigob&#95;72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tepexigob-72"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Unlike other sites in the state, <a href="/wiki/Yohualichan" title="Yohualichan">Yohualichan</a> was dominated by coastal groups, which eventually abandoned it in the face of incursions from peoples from the central highlands. The site was a ceremonial center which was probably dominant over other similar sites. Containing niched pyramids as well, it is related to the <a href="/wiki/El_Taj%C3%ADn" title="El Tajín">El Tajín</a> site in Veracruz. There is also a residential area, but it has not been studied.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-yohualichangob&#95;73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-yohualichangob-73"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tepatlaxco_(Mesoamerican_site)&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tepatlaxco (Mesoamerican site) (page does not exist)">Tepatlaxco</a> is located on the south side of the Totlqueme mountain. It is centered on a ceremonial center which has more than eight structures, surrounded by numerous smaller mounds. Much of the site was constructed into the mountain itself, causing it to blend in. In addition to the mountain, there are two large ravines to give the site added protection. The most important structure is named Mound A, which also shows the longest occupation. It measures nine meters high and 36 meters at its base.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tepatlaxcogob&#95;74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tepatlaxcogob-74"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Food">Food</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=23" title="Edit section: Food"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:CemitaSandwich2.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/CemitaSandwich2.JPG/250px-CemitaSandwich2.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/CemitaSandwich2.JPG/500px-CemitaSandwich2.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="3872" data-file-height="2592" /></a><figcaption>Cemita sandwich</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Other foods common to the state include <a href="/wiki/Atole" title="Atole">atole</a> with <a href="/wiki/Chili_pepper" title="Chili pepper">chili pepper</a> (<a href="/wiki/Chileatole" title="Chileatole">chileatole</a>), spicy <a href="/wiki/Mole_(sauce)" title="Mole (sauce)">mole verde</a>, <a href="/wiki/Barbacoa" title="Barbacoa">barbacoa</a>, chilate with chopped onion, cemitas, <a href="/wiki/Cecina_(meat)" title="Cecina (meat)">cecina</a>, guacamole with lime, and mole de caderas or mole espinazo. Many of these are found in the Sierra Mixteca region.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-smixteca&#95;65-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-smixteca-65"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> However, the state is best known for <a href="/wiki/Cemita" title="Cemita">cemitas</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mole_poblano" class="mw-redirect" title="Mole poblano">mole poblano</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chiles_en_nogada" title="Chiles en nogada">chiles en nogada</a> and <a href="/wiki/Chalupa" title="Chalupa">chalupas</a>.\n</p><p>The cemita is a kind of sandwich on a roll, related to the <a href="/wiki/Torta" title="Torta">torta</a>, particularly popular in Mexico City and the <a href="/wiki/Pambazo" title="Pambazo">pambazo</a>, which is of French origin and common in several areas in central Mexico. The sandwich has its origin with two kinds of bread which were brought over from Spain during the colonial period: one called "bizcocho de sal", which was long and hard and a kind of hollow cracker. Both breads were developed for long storage and eventually were made in Puebla with grain from the Atlixco area. These two breads eventually fused into a unique type that became softer by the mid-19th century.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cemitasgob&#95;75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cemitasgob-75"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The name is derived from a Jewish unleavened bread called "semita", which was brought over by <a href="/wiki/Sephardi_Jews" class="mw-redirect" title="Sephardi Jews">Sephardi Jews</a> to <a href="/wiki/New_Spain" title="New Spain">New Spain</a>. These were also produced in Puebla state. The cemitas were prepared at home and filled with potatoes, beans and nopal cactus and eaten by the lower classes. Later, an establishment in the Mercado Victoria market began to sell them to the public filled with meat from bull\'s feet with a <a href="/wiki/Vinaigrette" title="Vinaigrette">vinaigrette</a>, herbs, onions and chili peppers. This new filling was a hit and eventually this and other variations became a staple in many markets and popular eateries. Today, many varieties exist but all are prepared using the same type of bread.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cemitasgob&#95;75-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cemitasgob-75"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mole_Poblano.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Mole_Poblano.jpg/250px-Mole_Poblano.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Mole_Poblano.jpg/500px-Mole_Poblano.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3072" data-file-height="2304" /></a><figcaption>Mole poblano</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The best-known mole is named after the city of Puebla, <a href="/wiki/Mole_poblano" class="mw-redirect" title="Mole poblano">mole poblano</a>. The origin of this sauce is disputed and there are two versions of the legend that are most often cited. The first states that 16th-century nuns from the Convent of Santa Rosa were worried because they had just found out that the archbishop was going to visit them and they had nothing to cook for him except an old turkey in the yard. Supposedly due to divine inspiration, they began to mix together many of the spices and flavorings they had on hand in the kitchen, including different types of chili peppers, other spices, day-old bread, chocolate and approximately twenty other ingredients. They let the sauce simmer for hours and poured it over the turkey meat. Fortunately, the archbishop was very pleased with the meal and the nuns were able to save face.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-national&#95;76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-national-76"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The other story states that the sauce is of pre-Hispanic times and this was served to <a href="/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s" title="Hernán Cortés">Hernán Cortés</a> and the other conquistadors by <a href="/wiki/Moctezuma_II" title="Moctezuma II">Moctezuma II</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-national&#95;76-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-national-76"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The Aztecs did have a preparation called <i>chilmulli</i>, which in <a href="/wiki/Nahuatl" title="Nahuatl">Nahuatl</a> means \'chili pepper sauce\'.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-92percent&#95;77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92percent-77"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> However, there is no evidence that chocolate was ever used to flavor prepared foods or used in chilmulli.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-national&#95;76-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-national-76"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The sauce instead gained ingredients as it was reinterpreted over the colonial period.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-92percent&#95;77-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92percent-77"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Many food writers and gourmets nowadays consider one dish, the legendary turkey in mole poblano, which contains chocolate, to represent the pinnacle of the Mexican cooking tradition.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-national&#95;76-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-national-76"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Chile_en_nogada.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Chile_en_nogada.jpg/250px-Chile_en_nogada.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Chile_en_nogada.jpg/500px-Chile_en_nogada.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="768" /></a><figcaption>Chile en nogada</figcaption></figure>\n<p>According to the legend of chiles en nogada, there were three sisters from the city of Puebla who were in Mexico City. When the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Three_Guarantees" title="Army of the Three Guarantees">Army of the Three Guarantees</a> entered the capital at the end of the <a href="/wiki/Mexican_War_of_Independence" title="Mexican War of Independence">Mexican War of Independence</a>, they were feted by many. At one of these parties, the three sisters fell in love with three of the army\'s officers. Soon after, <a href="/wiki/Agust%C3%ADn_de_Iturbide" title="Agustín de Iturbide">Agustín de Iturbide</a> himself was set to visit the city of Puebla. Remembering the sisters, the soon-to-be emperor wanted to visit them. Wanting to impress Iturbide but not knowing how to cook, the sisters turned to the nuns of the Santa Monica convent who were famous for their food. The nuns decided to invent a dish for the sisters, which would represent the three colors of the <a href="/wiki/Flag_of_Mexico" title="Flag of Mexico">new Mexican flag</a>. On the appointed day, the banquet was prepared with the dish now called chiles en nogada, which pleased Iturbide.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-chilesnogada&#95;78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-chilesnogada-78"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The dish contains poblano chile, walnuts, cream and pomegranate seeds, and is offered seasonally (August–September) in local restaurants.\n</p><p>Chalupas are thick corn tortillas fried in lard, then covered in red or green chili pepper sauce, followed by shredded meat and other toppings. According to legend, they were named after the barges that the <a href="/wiki/Aztec" class="mw-redirect" title="Aztec">Aztecs</a> used to travel in areas such as <a href="/wiki/Tenochtitlan" title="Tenochtitlan">Tenochtitlan</a> (today Mexico City). Chalupas are common in other areas of central Mexico but are considered a specialty of Puebla, where they are served in venues from humble street carts to upscale restaurants.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-chalupasgob&#95;79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-chalupasgob-79"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Myths_and_legends">Myths and legends</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=24" title="Edit section: Myths and legends"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fundacion_Puebla.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Fundacion_Puebla.jpg/250px-Fundacion_Puebla.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="253" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Fundacion_Puebla.jpg/330px-Fundacion_Puebla.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Fundacion_Puebla.jpg/500px-Fundacion_Puebla.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1536" data-file-height="2048" /></a><figcaption>Mural of the founding of Puebla by Roberto Cueva Del Río</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The legend of the founding of the city of Puebla attributes to the act of the vision of a friar <a href="/wiki/Juli%C3%A1n_Garc%C3%A9s" title="Julián Garcés">Julián Garcés</a>, who became the first bishop of Puebla. The legend states that while praying, the friar fell asleep, when he dreamed of a festival in honor the <a href="/wiki/Archangel_Michael" class="mw-redirect" title="Archangel Michael">Archangel Michael</a> happening in a place with leafy trees and a crystal clear river, flowing from springs. As they contemplated the scenery, angels descended from heaven and traced the outlines of the city to be built. When he awoke, he drew what he had seen, deciding he had had a divine vision. He communicated the dream to other <a href="/wiki/Franciscans" title="Franciscans">Franciscans</a> and found the place he saw five days later.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-fundacion&#95;80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fundacion-80"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The story of the <a href="/wiki/Catarina_de_San_Juan" title="Catarina de San Juan">China Poblana</a> is one of the most popular in the state. The girl was taken on the <a href="/wiki/Manila_Galleon" class="mw-redirect" title="Manila Galleon">Manila Galleon</a>, but she was sold to Puebla resident Miguel de Sosa for a price ten times what the <a href="/wiki/Viceroy" title="Viceroy">viceroy</a> offered. She was taken to the city and baptized with the name of Catarina de San Juan in 1620. She maintained her oriental dress which made her conspicuous and it became a fad to imitate some aspects of this dress.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones37&#95;81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones37-81"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>When de Sosa and his wife died, Catherine entered a convent and began to see visions of the Virgin Mary and the <a href="/wiki/Child_Jesus" class="mw-redirect" title="Child Jesus">Child Jesus</a>. Some say that a number of miracles occurred while Catherine lived at the convent and this provoked a kind of veneration of her. When the China Poblana died in 1882, veneration of her as a saint began in earnest, but the practice was put to an end by the <a href="/wiki/Mexican_Inquisition" title="Mexican Inquisition">Mexican Inquisition</a>. Today her remains are in a crypt in the Temple de La Compañia in the city of Puebla.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones38&#95;82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones38-82"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Aztec myth of <a href="/wiki/Popocat%C3%A9petl" title="Popocatépetl">Popocatépetl</a> and <a href="/wiki/Iztacc%C3%ADhuatl" class="mw-redirect" title="Iztaccíhuatl">Iztaccíhuatl</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet" title="Romeo and Juliet">Romeo and Juliet</a> type story, has equal significance in this state as it does in the <a href="/wiki/Valley_of_Mexico" title="Valley of Mexico">Valley of Mexico</a> as the two are equally visible from the city of Puebla, but only in reverse (with Popocatépetl on the left).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones39&#95;83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones39-83"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>There is a popular saying "todo terminó como el Rosario de Amozoc, a golpes y farolazos" (it all ended like the Amozoc Rosary, with blows and drinks). The saying is derived from a legend from the community of <a href="/wiki/Amozoc_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Amozoc (municipality)">Amozoc de Mota</a> in the state. A silversmith apprentice by the name of Alberto was in love with a beautiful girl named Catalina, nicknamed La Culata. However, another apprentice from another shop named Enrique, was also in love with her. Alberto was accepted by la Culata and this made Enrique jealous. Festivities for the beginning of the year were supposed to be organized by the different silver workshops together but the rivalry caused a split in which ecclesiastical authorities needed to intervene. On the first day of the event, at Mass, Enrique saw Alberto and Catherine kiss briefly, which enraged him. During the rosary, while the choir sang "Mater Inmaculata," Enrique heard "mata a la Culata" (kill La Culata), took a knife from his clothing and attacked the couple, killing Catarina. Alberto took a machete from his belt and killed Enrique. A fight ensued which left many dead and wounded. It is said that one can still hear the cries of Catalina as she died.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones3940&#95;84-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones3940-84"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The house at Avenida 3 Ote 201 in the city of Puebla belonged to Pedro de Carvajal, who was a wealthy and respected man. However, he lost his young wife as she gave birth to their second child, a boy. When his daughter turned 15, there were many interested suitors but she was not interested in them. One day a monster appeared at a party in the city provoking terror. The monster went to the Carvajal house and ate the younger son, who was playing out front of the house. Pedro offered a large reward for the capture of the beast. One young man, who wanted the hand of Pedro\'s daughter, appeared at another festival, bearing the head of the beast. It is said that this young man gained noble title and the hand of the daughter as a reward.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-matoanimal&#95;85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-matoanimal-85"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Culture">Culture</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=25" title="Edit section: Culture"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="The_two_volcanos">The two volcanos</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=26" title="Edit section: The two volcanos"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>The state of Puebla is located on the east side of the volcanoes of Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl, opposite of the Valley of Mexico and Mexico City. The two volcanoes have as much significance here as they do on the west side, with many communities nearby maintaining ritual specific to honoring the two. These arose as fertility rituals but today are called "birthdays" with 12 March reserved for Popocatepetl and 30 August for Iztaccíhuatl. On these events, special foods and gifts are prepared as offerings and left in certain places. These traditions have survived despite the evangelization efforts of the colonial period.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones24&#95;86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones24-86"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Festivals_and_holiday">Festivals and holiday</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=27" title="Edit section: Festivals and holiday"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>The state is home to a number of festivals and traditions, from those with a purely pre-Hispanic background, to the far more numerous saints’ days to modern fairs located to regional economies.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-fiestastrad&#95;87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fiestastrad-87"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The largest important events include the <a href="/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead" title="Day of the Dead">Day of the Dead</a> in Huaquechula, the Carnival of Huijotzingo, <a href="/wiki/Spring_equinox_(Northern_Hemisphere)" class="mw-redirect" title="Spring equinox (Northern Hemisphere)">Spring Equinox</a> in Cantona, Fiesta de Santo Entierro y Feria de las Flores, the Fería del Café y el Huipil, the Huey Atlixcáyotl Festival, the Quetzalcoatl Ritual and <a href="/wiki/Cinco_de_Mayo" title="Cinco de Mayo">Cinco de Mayo</a>, celebrated in the entire state.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-fiestastrad&#95;87-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fiestastrad-87"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-cincoschmal&#95;89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cincoschmal-89"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Cinco de Mayo—or the fifth of May—is a holiday that celebrates the date of the Mexican army\'s 1862 victory over France at the Battle of Puebla during the Franco-Mexican War (1861-1867). A relatively minor holiday in Mexico, in the United States Cinco de Mayo has evolved into a commemoration of Mexican culture and heritage, particularly in areas with large Mexican-American populations.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-auto1&#95;90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto1-90"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\nMany Americans mistakenly believe that Cinco de Mayo ("May 5th") is the Mexican equivalent of the United States’ Fourth of July holiday — a date marking the official casting off of colonial rule via the announcement of a new independent country. However, the Mexican version of Independence Day is celebrated on September 16, for it was on that date in 1810 that the commencement of the war for Mexican independence from Spanish rule was pronounced in the small town of Dolores by Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla (an event now referred to as the "Grito de Dolores" — "Cry of Dolores" — or "El Grito de la Independencia").<sup id="cite&#95;ref-auto1&#95;90-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto1-90"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Cinco de Mayo is an important celebration in a number of places the United States, but it is a minor holiday or even unknown in much of Mexico proper. The only place where the holiday, which commemorates the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Puebla" title="Battle of Puebla">Battle of Puebla</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Second_French_intervention_in_Mexico" title="Second French intervention in Mexico">French Intervention in Mexico</a>, is important is in the state of Puebla. The French army invaded the country in 1862 and marched from Veracruz towards the city of Puebla. Just outside the city, inexperienced Mexican troops attacked the French who were camped. This resulted in victory, but the French were ultimately able to move on and take Mexico City, dominating the country until 1867. The annual celebration of the battle began in the state in areas of the country not occupied by the French as a symbol of Mexican pride.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cincoschmal&#95;89-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cincoschmal-89"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Today it is the most important state political commemoration. The most important observances take place at the Loreto and Guadalupe forts in the city of Puebla, where the battle occurred in 1862. The highlight is a reenactment of the event at the site.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg/250px-Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="282" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg/330px-Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg/500px-Ofrenda_mixteca_poblana.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1159" data-file-height="1722" /></a><figcaption>Day of the Dead altar in the Sierra Mixteca</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Like the rest of Mexico, Day of the Dead is celebrated in the state. Two aspects which feature prominently on altars in this state are <a href="/wiki/Mole_(sauce)" title="Mole (sauce)">mole</a> with turkey and large wax candles. Other items can include black <a href="/wiki/Candelabra" title="Candelabra">candelabras</a>, incense burners, candy skulls, decorative paper cutouts, oranges and other fruits in season. Leading to these altars often are a line of small candles to guide the returning spirits. One municipality which is particularly known for its events is <a href="/wiki/Huaquechula_(municipality)" title="Huaquechula (municipality)">Huaquechula</a>. Here, altars constructed in homes can be of multiple levels and are usually covered in white paper. On the first level, food and drink are usually placed, with religious objects and objects related to the deceased on the second level.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-huaquechula&#95;93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-huaquechula-93"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In a number of communities in the state, Carnival is celebrated. The best known of these carnivals takes place in <a href="/wiki/Huejotzingo_(municipality)" class="mw-redirect" title="Huejotzingo (municipality)">Huejotzingo</a>, as it began as a synthesis of a celebration honoring <a href="/wiki/Tlaloc" class="mw-redirect" title="Tlaloc">Tlaloc</a> and the Catholic tradition related to the days before <a href="/wiki/Ash_Wednesday" title="Ash Wednesday">Ash Wednesday</a>.
