Today, this carnival includes many traditional activities such as music, masks and parades, but this one also includes a reenactment of the Battle of Puebla and local legends such as the kidnapping of a governor\'s daughter and<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> the legend of Agustìn Lorenzo (called the Robin Hood of the 18th century).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-huejotzingocarn&#95;94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-huejotzingocarn-94"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Locals attend in colorful costumes and masks representing the <a href="/wiki/Conquistador" title="Conquistador">Conquistadors</a>, demons or animals, adorned with palm fronds or feathers.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-huejotzingocarn&#95;94-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-huejotzingocarn-94"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The capital of Puebla also celebrates Carnival with its signature tradition of the Las Marias, where men disguise themselves as women and mischievous devils.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Another major time for religious observance is <a href="/wiki/Holy_Week" title="Holy Week">Holy Week</a> or Semana Santa. In Puebla, there is the Procession del Silencio or Procession of Silence which occurs on <a href="/wiki/Maundy_Thursday" title="Maundy Thursday">Maundy Thursday</a>, when the city observes a period of silence to mark the death of Jesus.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The spring equinox is the setting for rituals at some of Puebla\'s archeological sites such as Cantona and Cholula. Cantona is an archeological site located near the city of Puebla and was one of the largest cities in early Mesoamerica. Today, the site is popular gathering place on the spring equinox (<a href="/wiki/Spring_equinox_(Northern_Hemisphere)" class="mw-redirect" title="Spring equinox (Northern Hemisphere)">much like Teotihuacan</a>), where people sing, dance and greet the sunrise on this date.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-equinoxcan&#95;95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-equinoxcan-95"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Another site where similar observances are held is the Great Pyramid of Cholula. Here indigenous dances and rituals are performed. The event culminates with the Ritual of Quetzalcoatl, which was an important part of the ancient Cholula culture.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This event draws attendees from various parts of Mexico.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ritquet&#95;96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ritquet-96"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The <a href="/w/index.php?title=Huey_Atlixc%C3%A1yotl_Festival&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Huey Atlixcáyotl Festival (page does not exist)">Huey Atlixcáyotl Festival</a><span class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;">&#160;&#91;<a href="https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huey_Atlixc%C3%A1yotl" class="extiw" title="es:Huey Atlixcáyotl">es</a>&#93;</span> is celebrated in the town of <a href="/wiki/Atlixco" title="Atlixco">Atlixco</a> to celebrate the area\'s local culture and identity. The name means "Atlixco tradition" in <a href="/wiki/Nahuatl" title="Nahuatl">Nahuatl</a> and is centered on the San Miguel Hill (called Popocatica in ancient times) located in the center of the town. It was locally sacred in the pre-Hispanic era, and in colonial times, a hermitage was built there. The event was named a Cultural Heritage of the State of Puebla in 1996.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-festhuey&#95;97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-festhuey-97"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The purpose of the event is to celebrate the survival of indigenous culture after the <a href="/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire" title="Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire">Conquest</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In July, the <a href="/wiki/Pueblo_M%C3%A1gico" class="mw-redirect" title="Pueblo Mágico">Pueblo Mágico</a> of <a href="/wiki/Cuetzalan" title="Cuetzalan">Cuetzalan</a> has the cultural festival of Festival Tradicional, which features traditional dancers who come from various parts of the state. <a href="/wiki/Tetela_de_Ocampo" title="Tetela de Ocampo">Tetela de Ocampo</a> celebrates its Peach Festival in August. On the last day of August, the Procession de los Faroles (Procession of the Lanterns) takes place in <a href="/wiki/Cholula,_Puebla" title="Cholula, Puebla">Cholula</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Puebla has a number of annual fairs meant to highlights the various regions’ products. In <a href="/wiki/Huauchinango_(municipality)" title="Huauchinango (municipality)">Huauchinango</a>, an economic fair and a religious observance are conducted at the same time. The Feria de las Flores (Flower Festival) and the Santo Entierro (Holy Burial) occur in the second half of March. It consists of religious events such as processions and masses. Many cut flower and ornamental plant growers come to display their products and there is the coronation of the Queen of Flowers. Other events include agricultural displays, parades with floats, dances, crafts, <a href="/wiki/Cockfighting" title="Cockfighting">cockfights</a>, sporting events and more.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-huachinango&#95;98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-huachinango-98"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Feria del Café y el Huipil (Coffee and <a href="/wiki/Huipil" title="Huipil">Huipil</a> Festival) takes place in Cuetzalan. The event promotes the area\'s locally grown coffee as well as traditionally made huipil dresses. There are also displays of pre-Hispanic dance, popular music, fireworks and more. The event began in 1949 as the National Festival of Coffee, which is economically important here. The event centered on the choosing of a Coffee Queen, much like other similar kinds of festivals. In 1962, the National Festival of the Huipil was established. Eventually, the two merged to the current event.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-cafehuipil&#95;99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cafehuipil-99"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Other events to promote Puebla\'s products include the Feria de Café in Xicotpec in March and the Feria Nacional de Puebla. The latter is held in the state capital and brings together many of the state\'s agricultural, livestock, craft and industrial producers in an event very analogous to a state fair. The regional fair called the Piloto de Cholula occurs in September.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones2529&#95;88-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones2529-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="China_Poblana">China Poblana</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=28" title="Edit section: China Poblana"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:China_poblana.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b1/China_poblana.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="296" class="mw-file-element" data-file-width="199" data-file-height="310" /></a><figcaption>Woman in <i>china poblana</i> dress</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The China Poblana was a real person who lived during the colonial period. Her real name was Mirra. She was an <a href="/wiki/Indians_in_the_Philippines" class="mw-redirect" title="Indians in the Philippines">Indian</a> who was brought over from <a href="/wiki/Manila" title="Manila">Manila</a> in the 1620s on the <a href="/wiki/Manila_Galleon" class="mw-redirect" title="Manila Galleon">Manila Galleon</a> as a child to work as a slave for the <a href="/wiki/Viceroy" title="Viceroy">viceroy</a> Marques de Gélves. She was soon sold to ship captain Miguel de Sosa who lived in Puebla. According to legend, Mirra was originally a princess in her home country but her family was displaced by the <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_people" title="Portuguese people">Portuguese</a> and she was kidnapped by pirates who sold her. Mirra was considered to be beautiful and exotic. She had been converted to the Catholic faith. Later in her life, she began to have visions of the child Jesus and angels. Her fame grew and she was eventually considered to be something of a prophet. When she died in 1688, people began to venerate her as a saint and many women copied her Asian/Mexican inspired dress.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-chinpob&#95;100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-chinpob-100"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>This fashion led to the now-traditional <i>china poblana</i> dress. It consists of a red skirt heavily decorated with colored sequins that in one part form the image of the eagle found on the Mexican flag and a blouse embroidered with colored thread and beads around the bust area. It is often worn with a <a href="/wiki/Charro" title="Charro">charro</a>-type hat. The outfit is the amalgam of several cultures such as Spanish, especially in the skirt; Chinese, with its use of sequins and beads; and indigenous, with colorful embroidery.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones23&#95;35-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones23-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Dance">Dance</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=29" title="Edit section: Dance"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Folk dance of both indigenous and mixed European and indigenous origin are most often seen at religious and cultural events in many parts of the state. Some of the most popular dances include "Moors and Christians," Dance of the Santiagos" and "Danza de los Arcos." The last is usually performed only by men who dress in white and with a scarf-like garment across the chest, dance in pairs which carry large arch portals covered in flowers and paper decorations. The dance has a number of variations which can include leaps into the air and complicated twirls.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones23&#95;35-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones23-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Dances of the Quetzales is most popular in the Sierra Norte, especially in Cuetzalan. It is a highly symbolic dance and usually performed in conjunction with rituals that relate to good harvests. The dancers form crosses, which signify the four cardinal directions and move in circles, which symbolize the rotation of time. The dancers wear large circular headdresses of quetzal feathers, which give the dance its name, and red suits. The <a href="/wiki/Danza_de_los_Voladores_de_Papantla" class="mw-redirect" title="Danza de los Voladores de Papantla">Dance of the Voladores</a>, which more common in <a href="/wiki/Papantla,_Veracruz" class="mw-redirect" title="Papantla, Veracruz">Papantla, Veracruz</a>, is also performed in a number of communities in the north of Puebla. This consists of five men who climb a tall pole and then four fall and spin from the pole while attached by ropes. The fifth dancer stays on top and plays music and dances as the other men fall. Another important dance in Puebla is the Doce pares de Francia, which recalls the events of the Battle of Puebla.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones24&#95;86-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones24-86"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Architecture">Architecture</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=30" title="Edit section: Architecture"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Biblioteca_Palafoxiana,_exterior.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Biblioteca_Palafoxiana%2C_exterior.JPG/250px-Biblioteca_Palafoxiana%2C_exterior.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Biblioteca_Palafoxiana%2C_exterior.JPG/500px-Biblioteca_Palafoxiana%2C_exterior.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="2560" data-file-height="1920" /></a><figcaption>The exterior of the <a href="/wiki/Biblioteca_Palafoxiana" title="Biblioteca Palafoxiana">Biblioteca Palafoxiana</a> in <a href="/wiki/Puebla_(city)" title="Puebla (city)">Puebla City</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mexico" title="Mexico">Mexico</a>, is recognized by the UNESCO for being the first public library in the <a href="/wiki/Americas" title="Americas">Americas</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Founded in 1646 by <a href="/wiki/Juan_de_Palafox_y_Mendoza" title="Juan de Palafox y Mendoza">Juan de Palafox y Mendoza</a>.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The colonial architecture of the state is defined by its heavy use of ornamental tiles called <a href="/wiki/Talavera_(pottery)" class="mw-redirect" title="Talavera (pottery)">Talavera</a>. This is particularly true in the capital. This makes these buildings more colorful than most of their contemporaries in other parts of Mexico and was one of the reasons that the historic center of the capital was selected as a <a href="/wiki/World_Heritage_Site" title="World Heritage Site">World Heritage Site</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones13&#95;104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones13-104"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>A number of churches and other buildings in rural parts of the state are noted for their "folk baroque" architecture and decoration, especially in Atlixco and the southwest. Folk baroque consists of the use of tile and painted raised stucco based on more traditional <a href="/wiki/Baroque_architecture" title="Baroque architecture">Baroque designs</a>, which was most popular in the 18th century. One well known church of this type is the church of <a href="/w/index.php?title=Jolapan&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Jolapan (page does not exist)">Jolapan</a>, which is modeled after the <a href="/wiki/Tepalcingo" title="Tepalcingo">Tepalcingo</a> Sanctuary in neighboring <a href="/wiki/Morelos" title="Morelos">Morelos</a>. The church of Jolalpan contains richly decorated <a href="/wiki/Pilaster" title="Pilaster">pilasters</a>, <a href="/wiki/Solomonic_column" title="Solomonic column">Solomonic columns</a> and other elements in a design very similar to that of Tepalcingo. Between these there are a number of small churches which also show folk baroque influence such as those in <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tlancualpican&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tlancualpican (page does not exist)">Tlancualpican</a> and <a href="/w/index.php?title=Tzicatl%C3%A1n&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Tzicatlán (page does not exist)">Tzicatlán</a>. The church in Tlancualpican is painted in bright blues, greens and red, with an ornate <a href="/wiki/Fa%C3%A7ade" title="Façade">façade</a> with sculpted leaves, tendrils and niches divided by spiral half-columns all done in stucco. Even more ornate is the church in Tzicatlán, which is a small rural farming village, with the entire surface of the main façade decorated with brightly colored images and sculptures.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-folkbaroque&#95;105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-folkbaroque-105"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In the modern era, architectural styles have evolved into new and sometimes eclectic forms. Skyscrapers, almost all of which are in the city of Puebla, include Edificio Vacas at 42 meters high, Torre Géminis at 50 meters high, Torre Nora at 69 meters high to the tallest, Torre Ejecutiva JVI and Torre Ejecutiva JVI at 100 meters high each. These last two have a triangular shape and are covered in blue tinged glass.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones13&#95;104-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones13-104"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Literature">Literature</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=31" title="Edit section: Literature"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Literature is one of the better-developed arts in the state and includes works such as novels, essays, poetry and theatrical plays. One prominent name from the colonial period is that of José Mariano Beristáin de Souza who was a priest and writers in the 18th century. He is also known for amassing a large library of writings in Spanish over twenty years of his life, which resulted in the Biblioteca Hispanoamericana Septentrional.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones13&#95;104-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones13-104"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> However, literature would not be a major cultural force in the state until the 20th century. One early prominent writer was poet <a href="/w/index.php?title=Gregorio_de_Gante&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Gregorio de Gante (page does not exist)">Gregorio de Gante</a>. In his early career, he was a professor but after the <a href="/wiki/Mexican_Revolution" title="Mexican Revolution">Mexican Revolution</a> broke out the joined revolutionary forces under Antonio Medina. After the war, he began his career as a poet, eventually writing regularly for a newspaper called "El Nacional" and become one of Mexico\'s most popular writers by the 1930s.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones14&#95;106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones14-106"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Many modern works with themes of social injustice and sometimes about the culture and scenery of the state itself. Modern Puebla literature can be traced back to the work of poet <a href="/w/index.php?title=Arturo_Trejo&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Arturo Trejo (page does not exist)">Arturo Trejo</a>, one of the "Generacion de los 50" or Generation of the 1950s.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones13&#95;104-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones13-104"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Elena_Garro" title="Elena Garro">Elena Garro</a> was active during the mid and latter 20th century, whose writings were said to "grab" the reader. Most of her work was autobiographical in one sense or another. She was married to another Mexican writer <a href="/wiki/Octavio_Paz" title="Octavio Paz">Octavio Paz</a>, from whom she divorced in 1959.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones14&#95;106-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones14-106"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Born in Atlixco in 1930, <a href="/w/index.php?title=Hector_Azar&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Hector Azar (page does not exist)">Hector Azar</a> is one of Mexico\'s most noted playwrights in the 20th century. Some of his works include Revista de Revistas, Revista de la Universidad and Jueves de Excelsior. He has also directed and produced plays in Mexico and Europe.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones16&#95;107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones16-107"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Sergio_Pitol_Demeneghi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sergio Pitol Demeneghi">Sergio Pitol Demeneghi</a> is a writer, translator and diplomat who was born in the city of Puebla in 1933. Most of his works relate to the theme of human rights. Much of his writing and translating work relates to his diplomatic functions. His best known works include No hay tal lugar, Infierno de todos and Los climas.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones16&#95;107-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones16-107"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\nBorn in Puebla in 1949, <a href="/wiki/%C3%81ngeles_Mastretta" title="Ángeles Mastretta">Ángeles Mastretta</a>\'s writings are known for their female characters which are prominent. She has found most of her popularity in Spain and Mexico publishing stories in magazines such as Ovaciones and La Jornada. Her books include El Mundo Ilumninado, Arrancame la vida and Mujeres de ojos grandes.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones17&#95;108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones17-108"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n<a href="/w/index.php?title=Jos%C3%A9_Francisco_Conde_Ortega&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="José Francisco Conde Ortega (page does not exist)">José Francisco Conde Ortega</a>, also known simply as Paco Conde, was born in Atlixco in 1951. His writings include chronicles, essays and poetry. His works mostly reflect on everyday urban life with book titles such as Estudios para un cuerpo, Los lobos viven del viento and Práctica de lobo.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones18&#95;109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones18-109"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Jos%C3%A9_Luis_Z%C3%A1rate&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="José Luis Zárate (page does not exist)">José Luis Zárate</a> was born in Puebla in 1966. He is best known for novels such as <a href="/wiki/Xanto:_Novelucha_libre" title="Xanto: Novelucha libre">Xanto: Novelucha libre</a>, La ruta del hielo y la sal and Del cielo oscuro y del abismo, but he has published numerous short stories, essays and poems. He is known in the fantasy genre and has established organizations dedicated to this such as the Asociacion Mexicana de Cienca Ficcion y Fantasia and Circulo Puebla de Ciencia Ficcion y Divulgacion.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones18&#95;109-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones18-109"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Other notable writers from the state include, Fritz Glockner, Pedro Ángel Palou Garcia, Miguel Maldonado, Eduardo Montagner Anguiano, Gabriel Wolfson Reyes, Jaime Mesa and Gabriela Puente.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones19&#95;110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones19-110"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Painting">Painting</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=32" title="Edit section: Painting"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<style style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta,_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG/250px-Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG" decoding="async" width="200" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG/330px-Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG/500px-Still-life_by_Jos%C3%A9_Agust%C3%ADn_Arrieta%2C_San_Diego_Museum_of_Art.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2431" data-file-height="1770" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><i>Still-life</i>, José Agustín Arrieta, c. 1870</div></div></div></div></div>\n<p>Much of the historical painting in the state is found in its colonial churches and reflect the artistic styles of the 16 to 19th centuries. These consist of murals, portraits and biblical scenes done on canvas, wood and other mediums. José Joaquín Magón was born in Puebla in the 18th century is known for his portrait paintings but his other works have mostly religious and mythological themes. He also did a number of works related to <a href="/wiki/New_Spain" title="New Spain">New Spain</a>\'s <a href="/wiki/Casta" title="Casta">caste system</a>. <a href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Berrueco&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Luis Berrueco (page does not exist)">Luis Berrueco</a> is one of the major Pueblan painters from the 18th century. He was also prolific, painting images of religious martyrs and saints which can still be found today in many churches in the state. His style is considered to be unique, marked by delicate faces and profuse ornamentation. Some of his best work can be found at the Santa Clara Church in Atlixco.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones19&#95;110-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones19-110"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Gonzalo Carrasco was born in Otumba, Puebla in 1859. He was both and artist and a Jesuit who produced over 500 religious paintings that can be found all over Mexico and some murals including those in the Basilica de Guadalupe in Puebla and Fordham University in the U.S.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones20&#95;111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones20-111"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Much of Puebla\'s art scene had disappeared before the 20th century but in the 1920s, a group of young artists from the Escuela de Bellas Artes de Puebla (School of Fine Arts of Puebla) began to band together for mutual support. These artists eventually caught the attention and patronage of artists such as <a href="/wiki/Diego_Rivera" title="Diego Rivera">Diego Rivera</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dr._Atl" title="Dr. Atl">Dr. Atl</a> and received visitors such as <a href="/wiki/David_Alfaro_Siquieros" class="mw-redirect" title="David Alfaro Siquieros">David Alfaro Siquieros</a>, <a href="/wiki/Frida_Kahlo" title="Frida Kahlo">Frida Kahlo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Francisco_Cornejo" title="Francisco Cornejo">Francisco Cornejo</a> and <a href="/wiki/Alfredo_Guati_Rojo" title="Alfredo Guati Rojo">Alfredo Guati Rojo</a>. This effort would become the Barrio del Artista.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artefluye&#95;112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artefluye-112"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Barrio del Artista is a neighborhood in the city of Puebla which is home to artists from a number of disciplines. It contains 46 small workshops which permit visitors to observe the work and even chat with the artists. These workshops mostly surround a large plaza with a fountain near a building known as the Café del Artista, managed the Union de Artes Plasticas, A.C. "Barrio del Artista," which was founded in 1941.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-artefluye&#95;112-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-artefluye-112"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ignacio_D%C3%A1vila_Tagle&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Ignacio Dávila Tagle (page does not exist)">Ignacio Dávila Tagle</a> was born in the city of Puebla in 1898 into an artistic family, learning to paint from his father, Daniel Dávila Domínguez. One of his best-known works is his dreamlike mural called "El sueno de fray Julián Garcés" which depicts the legendary founding of the city.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones20&#95;111-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones20-111"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Faustino_Salazar_Garcia&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Faustino Salazar Garcia (page does not exist)">Faustino Salazar Garcia</a> was born in Puebla in 1912. He turned to painting as a child after he lost his mother. His works are known for their emotional qualityAs an established painter, he was one of the founding members of the Unión de Artes Plásticas.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones20&#95;111-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones20-111"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Alejandro_Honda&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Alejandro Honda (page does not exist)">Alejandro Honda</a> was born in San Martin Texmelucan in 1952. This painter\'s works show his fascination for Mesoamerica, which began when he was young. They can also have a sensual edge to them, even his religious paintings such as the María de Magdalena.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones21&#95;113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones21-113"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Gustavo_Cadena&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Gustavo Cadena (page does not exist)">Gustavo Cadena</a> was born in Puebla in 1974 has been a noticed painter since he was a young child. Many of his works reflect daily life, customs and traditions of the state. Some of his better known works include Niño indígena mexicano, Catedral de Puebla, and Pensando en Puebla.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones21&#95;113-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones21-113"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Music">Music</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=33" title="Edit section: Music"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Traditional music in Puebla has been influenced by the waltz, zarzuela and the Mexican version of trova. Although it waned in the 20th century, it has since experienced a revival.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones21&#95;113-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones21-113"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Pelagio_C._Manjarrez&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Pelagio C. Manjarrez (page does not exist)">Pelagio C. Manjarrez</a> (1886–1952) was from Tochimilco. He is not only known for his musical ability but also as a fighter in the Mexican Revolution, professor, journalist and poet. Most of his musical composition relate to dance such as waltzes, marches, foxtrots and tangos. Best known titles include "Porque me has besado tu," "La mañana está de fiesta" and "Alma herida."<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones21&#95;113-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones21-113"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Vicente_T._Mendoza" title="Vicente T. Mendoza">Vicente T. Mendoza</a> (1894–1964) was from Cholula who dedicated himself to researching the folk music of the area, especially those traditions that told the history of many of the state\'s communities. He founded the Folclorología Musical Mexicana. He also composed a number of pieces including the polka "La hora del crepúsculo," the waltz "La molinera," and religious pieces such as "Villancicos alegres para la Navidad" and "Cánticos para Navidad."<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones22&#95;114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones22-114"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/w/index.php?title=Gerardo_Pablo&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Gerardo Pablo (page does not exist)">Gerardo Pablo</a> is one of the main Pueblan composers of modern trova Mexicana who was born in Puebla in 1977. Many of his lyrics deal with social problems in Mexico and his work has been compared to that of <a href="/w/index.php?title=Guty_C%C3%A0rdenas&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Guty Càrdenas (page does not exist)">Guty Càrdenas</a>. Some of his best known works include "Tres noches por semana," "Càntaro", "Reflejos acústicos", "Trago de Ron", "Delirio", "Los Numerosos Nadies" which is based on the work of Uruguayan writer Eduardo Galeano,"Escucha a Gerardo Pablo" and "Quesoy" his most recent work with a Jazz Trio. Other notable musicians include Carlos Espinosa de los Monteros (waltz composer), pianist Celia Valderrábano Andrew who has also composed waltzes. Zarzuela composers include Félix Maria Alcerreca who is a lawyer by profession and Ignacio León who is a priest.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rincones22&#95;114-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rincones22-114"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Rockercoatl" title="Rockercoatl">Rockercoatl</a>, a contemporary musical group based in Puebla, gained notice for performing exclusively in <a href="/wiki/Nahuatl" title="Nahuatl">Nahuatl</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Media">Media</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=34" title="Edit section: Media"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p><a href="/wiki/List_of_newspapers_in_Mexico" title="List of newspapers in Mexico">Newspapers</a> of Puebla include: <i>El Heraldo de Puebla</i>, <i>El Mundo de Tehuacán</i>, <i>El Sol de Puebla</i>, <i>Esto de Puebla</i>, <i>La Jornada de Oriente</i>, <i>La Opinión Universitaria</i>, <i>La Opinión, Diario de la Mañana</i>, <i>Metro de Puebla</i>, <i>Momento Diario</i>, <i>Puebla sin Fronteras</i>, <i>Síntesis de Bolsillo Puebla</i>, and <i>Síntesis, El Periódico de Puebla.</i><sup id="cite&#95;ref-SIC&#95;116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SIC-116"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>115<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Education">Education</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=35" title="Edit section: Education"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BibliotecaUDLAP.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/BibliotecaUDLAP.JPG/250px-BibliotecaUDLAP.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/BibliotecaUDLAP.JPG/500px-BibliotecaUDLAP.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1536" /></a><figcaption>UDLAP library</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Puebla is ranked second in higher education in Mexico with 57 technological colleges and 110 research centers. It ranks fourth in the number of universities and colleges in the nation.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-prometedor&#95;45-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prometedor-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It is home to very prestigious institutions such as <a href="/wiki/Benem%C3%A9rita_Universidad_Aut%C3%B3noma_de_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla">Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla</a> (BUAP) is the oldest and largest university in Puebla founded on 15 April 1587, <a href="/wiki/Tecnol%C3%B3gico_de_Monterrey,_Campus_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Tecnológico de Monterrey, Campus Puebla">Tecnológico de Monterrey, Campus Puebla</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Universidad_de_las_Americas-Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Universidad de las Americas-Puebla">Universidad de las Americas-Puebla</a>, which has substantial ties to the United States, such as being accredited by the <a href="/wiki/Southern_Association_of_Colleges_and_Schools" title="Southern Association of Colleges and Schools">Southern Association of Colleges and Schools</a> and numerous student exchange programs. It has also received substantial economic assistance from the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Agency_for_International_Development" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Agency for International Development">U.S. Agency for International Development</a>. Much of the school\'s setup mimics that of U.S. universities, including student dormitories.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-chronicle&#95;118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-chronicle-118"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>116<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Instituto_Tecnol%C3%B3gico_de_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Instituto Tecnológico de Puebla">Instituto Tecnológico de Puebla</a> was founded in 1972, <a href="/wiki/Universidad_Popular_Aut%C3%B3noma_del_Estado_de_Puebla" title="Universidad Popular Autónoma del Estado de Puebla">Universidad Popular Autónoma del Estado de Puebla</a> (UPAEP) was founded in 1973, and <a href="/wiki/Universidad_Iberoamericana_Puebla" title="Universidad Iberoamericana Puebla">Universidad Iberoamericana Puebla</a> founded in 1983. They were also created to fill a need for higher education of a growing local economy.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-UPAEP&#95;47-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UPAEP-47"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Puebla City has the highest education in the State, but the average of the rest of the population of the state over the age of 15 has finished the first year of middle school with an average number of years in school at 7.4. This is under the national average of 8.1. Of every 100 over age 15, 12 have not gone to school at all, 17 have left school before the end of primary, 21 finish primary, 3 start, but do not finish middle school, 19 finish middle school, 5 begin but do not finish high school, 8 obtain a bachelor\'s degree and 1 has an advanced degree. There are 441, 699 illiterate people, or 13%, according to INEGI, above the national average of eight percent.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-eduinegi&#95;119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-eduinegi-119"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>117<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Government">Government</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=36" title="Edit section: Government"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg/250px-Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg/330px-Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg/500px-Government_Building_In_Puebla.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2272" data-file-height="1704" /></a><figcaption>Hall of protocols of the State Government of Puebla City.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The current division of the territory was created in 1895, which is a system of 21 districts and 217 municipalities. This is down from a high of 222 because the municipalities of San Jerónimo Caleras, San Felipe Hueyotlipan, San Miguel Canoa, La Resurrección, and Totimehuacan were incorporated into the city of Puebla in 1962.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-gobierno&#95;120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-gobierno-120"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The state is headed by a <a href="/wiki/Governor_of_Puebla" title="Governor of Puebla">governor</a> who is <a href="/wiki/Directly_elected" class="mw-redirect" title="Directly elected">directly elected</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Executive_branch" class="mw-redirect" title="Executive branch">executive branch</a> of the government contains the following departments: Governing (Gobernación), Finance, Development, Evaluation and Control of the Public Administration, Economic Development, Tourism, Rural Development, Urban and Ecological Development, Communications and Transportation, Health, Public Education, Culture and Public Defender (Procuraduia General de Justicia). The legislative branch is unicameral with deputies or representatives elected from the various districts of the state. It also consists of a number of commissions dedicated to issues such as state heritage sites, education, agriculture and more. The judicial branch is headed by the Tribunal Superior de Justicia.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-gobierno&#95;120-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-gobierno-120"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Major_communities">Major communities</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Puebla&amp;action=edit&amp;section=37" title="Edit section: Major communities"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<ul><li><a href="/wiki/Acatl%C3%A1n_de_Osorio" title="Acatlán de Osorio">Acatlán de Osorio</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Amozoc_de_Mota" title="Amozoc de Mota">Amozoc de Mota</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Atlixco" title="Atlixco">Atlixco</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Cholula,_Puebla" title="Cholula, Puebla">Cholula</a> (Cholula de Rivadabia)</li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Cuetzal%C3%A1n" class="mw-redirect" title="Cuetzalán">Cuetzalán</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Huauchinango" title="Teziutlán">Teziutlán</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/Zacatlan,_Puebla" class="mw-redirect" title="Zacatlan, Puebla">Zacatlan</a></li></ul>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 <a href="/wiki/President_of_Mexico" title="President of Mexico">President of Mexico</a> 1964–1970</li>\n<li>Vicente Suárez – one of the Niños Héroes of the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Chapultepec" 2026-02-26 13:09:58 | DEBUG    | Scraped content: ScrapedContent(url='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Bullrich', title='Patricia Bullrich - Wikipedia', text='From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Argentine politician (born 1956) Patricia Bullrich Official portrait, 2024. National Senator Incumbent Assumed office 10 December 2025 Constituency City of Buenos Aires Minister of National Security In office 10 December 2023\xa0– 10 December 2025 President Javier Milei Preceded by Aníbal Fernández Succeeded by Alejandra Monteoliva In office 10 December 2015\xa0– 10 December 2019 President Mauricio Macri Preceded by María Cecilia Rodríguez Succeeded by Sabina Frederic National Deputy In office 10 December 2007\xa0– 10 December 2015 Constituency City of Buenos Aires In office 10 December 1993\xa0– 10 December 1997 Constituency City of Buenos Aires Minister of Social Security In office 31 October 2001\xa0– 13 November 2001 President Fernando de la Rúa Preceded by Jorge Antonio San Martino (Secretary of State) Succeeded by José Gabriel Dumón Minister of Labour, Employment and Human Resources In office 6 October 2000\xa0– 29 October 2001 President Fernando de la Rúa Preceded by Alberto Flamarique Succeeded by José Gabriel Dumón Secretary of Criminal Policy and Penitentiary Affairs In office 15 December 1999\xa0– 5 October 2000 President Fernando de la Rúa Preceded by Julio Enrique Aparicio Succeeded by Mariano Ciafardini Personal details Born ( 1956-06-11 ) 11 June 1956 (age\xa069) Buenos Aires , Argentina Party LLA (since 2025) Other political affiliations PJ (1972–1996) New Leadership (1996–1997) Union for Freedom (1997–2018) PRO (2018–2025) Spouses Marcelo Langieri \u200b \u200b ( m. 1975; div. 1982) \u200b Guillermo Yanco \u200b ( m. 1997) \u200b Children 1 Relatives Esteban Bullrich (second cousin) [ 1 ] Alma mater University of Palermo ( BA ) FLACSO ( MA ) National University of General San Martín ( PhD ) [ 2 ] Signature Patricia Bullrich ( Latin American Spanish: [paˈtɾisja ˈβulritʃ] ⓘ ; born 11 June 1956) is an Argentine politician. She currently serves as a National Senator for the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires since December 2025, representing La Libertad Avanza . [ 3 ] She previously served as the Minister of National Security from 2023 to 2025 under president Javier Milei and from 2015 to 2019 under president Mauricio Macri . She was the chairwoman of the Republican Proposal until 2025. [ 4 ] She was born in Buenos Aires, part of the Pueyrredón family . Bullrich graduated from the University of Palermo , and as a young woman she was involved with the Peronist Youth . She married Marcelo Langieri, secretary of Rodolfo Galimberti; Galimberti was a leader of the Montoneros guerrilla and her brother-in-law. They went into exile in 1977, during the Dirty War , and she returned in 1982, after the Falklands War . She was elected deputy for the Justicialist Party in 1993. She left the party and started her own, but could not secure a re-election. She joined the cabinet of president Fernando De la Rúa in 2001. Following the election of Mauricio Macri to the presidency in the 2015 Argentine general election , she became the Minister of Security. She placed regulations against roadblocks from piqueteros , and opposed the secessionist organization Resistencia Ancestral Mapuche . Leading the "hawk" sector of the Juntos por el Cambio coalition, she was appointed its president in 2020. She ran for the 2023 Argentine primary and general elections. She won the primaries against Horacio Rodríguez Larreta , but ended third in the general elections behind Sergio Massa and Javier Milei . She supported Milei on the ballotage with Massa. After Milei was elected President, he chose Bullrich to serve again as Minister of Security. On November 30, 2025, Bullrich resigned from her post as Minister of National Security after she was sworn in as a Senator in the Argentine Senate . [ 5 ] Early life [ edit ] Bullrich was born on 11 June 1956 in Buenos Aires , daughter of Alejandro Bullrich, a cardiologist, and Julieta Luro Pueyrredon. She belongs to two wealthy families on each of her parents\' sides. On her mother\'s side, she belongs to the Pueyrredón family , a traditional lineage of Spanish, French, and Irish descent whose members featured prominently in the early years of Argentine Independence (such as Juan Martín de Pueyrredón and Honorio Pueyrredon ). [ 6 ] On her father\'s side, she descends from Adolfo Bullrich , a businessman and politician of German ancestry, who served as Mayor of Buenos Aires from 1898 to 1902. [ 7 ] Although it was a wealthy family, Alejandro and Julieta divorced, and Patricia adjusted to a simpler lifestyle when her mother got a job as publicist. [ 8 ] She became politically engaged from an early age, abandoning a potential career in field hockey to dedicate herself fully to political activism. [ 9 ] She also worked at the Cheburger fast food joint and became a member of the food workers\' union, encouraging coworkers to unionise as well. [ 10 ] She is the cousin of the singer-songwriter Fabiana Cantilo , and introduced her to Argentine rock . In the TV program " Almorzando con Mirtha Legrand " Cantilo explained that their mothers were close as siblings, and that Bullrich invited her to a concert of the band Pescado Rabioso , led by Luis Alberto Spinetta . This was the first concert that Fabiana Cantilo had attended, years before becoming a rock singer herself. [ 11 ] Patricia skipped school classes one day to attend the music competition TV program "Si lo sabe cante", where she sang the song "El extraño de pelo largo" of La Joven Guardia. She was defeated in the competition. [ 8 ] Peronist Youth years [ edit ] Patricia\'s grandmother, daughter of Honorio Pueyrredon, took her to meet Ricardo Balbín , leader of the Radical Civic Union (UCR). The meeting had the opposite effect than expected, as there was a huge generation gap between them. Rather than make her embrace the ideas of the UCR, supportive of liberal democracy , she rejected Balbín and chose Peronism instead, which proposed far-left politics at the time. [ 11 ] She joined the Peronist Youth (JP), the youth wing of the Peronist movement, aged 17. On 20 June 1973, she joined the procession to Ezeiza to bear witness to Juan Perón \'s return to Argentina following his 18-year exile, but left before the Ezeiza Massacre took place that same day. [ 12 ] She was also present at the Plaza de Mayo on the International Workers\' Day of 1974, when Perón, who had once again become president of Argentina, expelled the Montoneros and the left-wing youth groups from the celebrations. Although both the Peronist unions and guerrillas such as Montoneros had worked together against the Argentine Revolution dictatorship, they had begun a dispute over their political clout on the new democratic government; with the aforementioned expulsion Perón openly sided with the unions. Bullrich herself was a member of the Montoneros under the nom-de-guerre of "Cali", and active in the Columna Norte subgroup commanded by Rodolfo Galimberti . [ 13 ] Galimberti was Bullrich\'s brother-in-law, as he was married to Bullrich\'s sister, Julieta. [ 14 ] Bullrich has denied being a Montoneros member, and maintains that she was just a member of the JP. [ 15 ] [ 16 ] Perón died in 1974 and the Dirty War , an armed conflict between the Montoneros and the military, worsened: the guerrillas resumed the tactics used years before to attempt to remove the current authorities from power. In 1975, Bullrich was arrested for spray-painting political messages on the entrance of the University of Buenos Aires Faculty of Philosophy and Letters , and spent six months in prison. Upon being released, she dropped out of her sociology degree at the University of Buenos Aires and enrolled at the Universidad de Belgrano to study law. [ 10 ] She also rejoined the Columna Norte . By the end of 1975, she started dating Marcelo Langieri, secretary of Galimberti. [ 17 ] The 1976 coup d\'état established a military dictatorship, the National Reorganization Process , that continued the armed conflict against the Montoneros. Montoneros organized an attack on 4 September 1976, that intended to kill a manager of the Sudamtex textile firm. On her way to participate, Bullrich felt that she was being followed and fled. The military had abducted one of the masterminds of the plan and learned about the attack, which allowed them to surprise the Montoneros and kill the whole unit. [ 13 ] In January 1977, Galimberti and Bullrich attached an improvised explosive device to the car of Pepe Noguer, mayor of San Isidro . The device exploded, injuring the daughter and the daughter-in-law of the mayor, Ana María Noguer and Hortensia M. de Noguer. [ 13 ] Patricia Bullrich went into exile in 1977 with her partner Marcelo Langieri, first settling in Brazil, and later in Mexico, Spain and France. [ 8 ] She was still a member of Montoneros living abroad, until Galimberti cut ties with the organization in 1979. [ 13 ] She returned briefly to Argentina in that year, to give birth to her son Francisco. [ 8 ] Political career [ edit ] Bullrich returned to the country after the 1982 Falklands War . [ 12 ] She had conflicts with Dante Gullo over the reorganization of the JP, thinking that it should have its own political leaders rather than follow the older ones. [ 18 ] Peronism lost the 1983 Argentine general election , so she joined the internal faction of Antonio Cafiero that sought to renew the party. Peronism returned to power in 1989 when Carlos Menem won the 1989 Argentine general election . She was elected deputy for the Justicialist Party (PJ) in 1993, alongside Erman González . [ 8 ] She proposed over two hundred bills, including the Art University law, the Cinema law, and the Leasing Contract law. [ 19 ] In 1995, she was named the Legislator of the Year. [ 19 ] Patricia Bullrich left the PJ in 1996 and started New Leadership alongside Gustavo Béliz . She had disagreements with him because she thought that he managed the party unilaterally, without making her part of the decisions. [ 20 ] She left the party as a result and, after briefly considering joining the Frepaso , she started another party. Initially named Cambio 97, it was soon renamed "Unión por Todos" (UPT) as the Cambio 97 name had already been registered. The new party did not get enough votes to allow her to be reelected as deputy in the 1997 Argentine legislative election . She then worked for the Buenos Aires Province on security matters, assisting the municipality of Hurlingham . She resigned in 1998, because of conflicts with León Arslanián , minister of justice of the province. [ 21 ] Patricia Bullrich at the time she served as deputy. In 1999, the UPT became part of the Alliance for Work, Justice and Education , which took Fernando de la Rúa to the Presidency. Bullrich was appointed to office in the Department of Criminal Policy and Penitentiary Matters. In 2001, she was made a cabinet minister, as Secretary of Labour, Employment and Human Resources and, later that year, as Secretary of Social Security. [ 19 ] In 2001 she announced a cut of 13% on retirement wages above $574, 16% of all retirees, which would reduce the deficit by 68.6 millions of pesos. [ 22 ] De la Rúa resigned, and eventually the governor of Buenos Aires Eduardo Duhalde was appointed president by the Congress. Bullrich relaunched the UPT in 2002, aiming for the 2003 presidential elections . The party platform announced reforms on labor and education. [ 23 ] The UPT did not take part in the elections, supporting instead Ricardo López Murphy of the Recreate for Growth party, [ 24 ] who ended in the third place. Both parties united in the alliance "Unión para Recrear Buenos Aires", proposing Bullrich for mayor of Buenos Aires. She ended in the fourth place, with 9.76% of the vote. [ 25 ] The UPT joined forces with the Support for an Egalitarian Republic (ARI) and created the Civic Coalition to run for the 2007 Argentine general election , with Elisa Carrió as a candidate for president. Bullrich ran instead for deputy for Buenos Aires. [ 26 ] Her centrist politics and polemical history as a government minister, however, contributed to the disenchantment of a group of left-wing members of ARI who left the Civic Coalition. [ 27 ] Minister of Security (2015–2019) [ edit ] Patricia Bullrich presents a report about the Resistencia Ancestral Mapuche organization. Mauricio Macri was elected president in 2015 and Patricia Bullrich was appointed Minister of Security. [ 28 ] Within the first days, three criminals convicted for torturing and killing three pharmaceutical businessmen escaped from a high-security prison, leading to a nation-wide operation to recapture them. Bullrich announced on 9 January that the three criminals had been captured, but, in reality, only one had been captured. She tendered her resignation to Macri because of the mistake, but Macri rejected it. The other two criminals were captured a few days later. [ 29 ] Bullrich proposed a protocol to remove roadblocks caused by piqueteros . Such blocks should be announced in advance, restrict only part of the roads, and last for a short time. They should cease if ordered so by the police, and those who commit violent actions shall be detained. This protocol was approved by a meeting of the ministers of security of all provinces of Argentina. [ 30 ] Horacio Rodríguez Larreta , chief of government of the Buenos Aires city, and María Eugenia Vidal , governor of the Buenos Aires province, refused to endorse it, as they thought that doing so could prove controversial. Instead, they preferred to negotiate and stay on good terms with organizations of piqueteros such as the Evita Movement . [ 31 ] Larreta also explained that the city does not need to endorse the protocols because it already has regulations for roadblocks. [ 32 ] Resistencia Ancestral Mapuche (RAM) and the Coordinadora Arauco-Malleco (CAM), two Mapuche organizations that normally operate in Patagonia , expanded their attacks to the city of Buenos Aires. Their goal is to create a Mapuche nation, seceding from Argentina and Chile. Bullrich said that "We won\'t allow an autonomous mapuche republic inside Argentina; that\'s the logic of their request, the denial of the Argentine state, the anarchist logic. Our resolution is total and absolute in not allowing a group that uses violence as a way of action in Argentina." [ 33 ] Facundo Jones Huala, leader of RAM, claimed to be a political prisoner, and that the RAM only acts in self-defense on lands that used to belong to them. [ 34 ] Bullrich organized a joint command with the ministers of security of the Neuquén , Río Negro and Chubut provinces against the RAM, and delivered a report of the actions taken against the organization, including 96 lawsuits, 2 of them for murder. [ 35 ] The Argentine National Gendarmerie forced a group of Mapuche demonstrators to cease a roadblock next to the Chubut River , and the demonstrator Santiago Maldonado went missing after that. The case became a national scandal, with the Gendarmerie (by extension their political authorities, Bullrich and Macri) being accused of an enforced disappearance . Bullrich gave her full support to the Gendarmerie. Maldonado was found dead some months later, drowned in the Chubut river. Bullrich said "The whole world saw what happened with Maldonado. He stayed in the same place where he drowned, without being seen or touched by anyone. Neither the Gendarmerie nor our government would have made a person disappear". [ 12 ] A tourist was stabbed ten times by thieves, who then ran away. The policeman Luis Chocobar shot one of the thieves, claiming that the thief made a movement suggesting he was about to fire a gun. However, a video released by Telefe Noticias showed that the criminal had his back to him. Bullrich, however, pointed out that the video was edited and did not show the exact moment of the gunshot. [ 36 ] Bullrich and Macri supported the actions of Chocobar, on the grounds that it would be a right of self-defense , [ 36 ] while human rights organizations considered it a case of police brutality . [ 12 ] Chocobar was sentenced for homicide four years later. [ 12 ] In November 2018, Bullrich said that "those who wanted to be armed should be allowed to do so", prompting strong criticism and opposition. [ 37 ] [ 38 ] Adrián Marcenac, father of Alfredo Marcenac, a student from Necochea who was murdered by serial shooter Martín Ríos in July 2006 in Belgrano, Buenos Aires , labelled Bullrich\'s comments as "enormously grave" for Argentine society. [ 39 ] Presidential candidate [ edit ] AI image posted by Javier Milei to announce his alliance with Bullrich. Milei associates himself with imagery of lions, and "pato" ("duck") is a common nickname in Spanish for people named "Patricia". [ 40 ] The 2021 Argentine legislative election resulted in a victory for Juntos por el Cambio (JXC), with the libertarian party La Libertad Avanza (LLA) led by Javier Milei , emerging as a significant third party . [ 41 ] Bullrich, who was appointed president of the PRO in 2020, [ 42 ] maintained a positive relationship with Milei, and at one point considered forming an alliance for the 2023 Argentine general election . However, Milei ultimately decided to run independently with his own party. [ 43 ] There was an expectation that Mauricio Macri would run for president once again, as even in defeat he had gotten 41% of the vote in 2019 and his image had improved since then. However, he declined to do so, so the party had primary elections between Bullrich and Horacio Rodríguez Larreta. They represented the "hawks" and "doves" of the party. Macri did not openly side with any of them. [ 44 ] Bullrich chose the former legislator Luis Petri , from the UCR, as the candidate for vice-president. Petri had lost the primary elections for governor of Mendoza to Alfredo Cornejo a short time before. She chose him because he was young, sided with the "hawks", and was not from Buenos Aires; and also because he worked with her during her time as minister of security. As Petri was from the UCR, Bullrich would secure the support of the radicals that were not pleased with the leadership of Gerardo Morales (who supported Larreta), and with the whole party if Larreta was defeated in the primaries. Other politicians briefly considered to run for vice-president under her were Carlos Melconian , Maximiliano Abad , Luis Naidenoff , and Ricardo López Murphy . [ 45 ] Carlos Melconian was proposed instead as Bullrich\'s potential minister of economy. In contrast with Milei, who proposed a full dollarization of the economy, Melconian proposed instead a bimonetary economy, where both the Argentine peso and the United States dollar would be legal tender. Before implementing it, the fiscal deficit would be eliminated, the by-laws of the Central Bank would be amended to prohibit money creation , and the restrictions on the use of US dollars would be removed. [ 46 ] She also proposed the creation of a maximum security prison named after former president Cristina Kirchner. [ 47 ] The primary elections ended with a decisive victory of Bullrich over Larreta. [ 48 ] Once the primaries were concluded, the candidates took part in the presidential debates , explaining their positions and proposals over several topics. [ 49 ] Bullrich promised to end inflation, and to end the roadblocks caused by piqueteros. [ 50 ] Although the primary elections ended with the three main candidates, Bullrich, Milei and Peronist Sergio Massa in a close tie, Massa got ahead in the general election and won with 36% of the vote, followed by Milei with 30%. As a result, both candidates went to a third ballotage election. Bullrich did not take part in it, as JXC ended in third place, but both candidates sought to get the support of her voters. Massa made a speech about institutional stability and public security, usual topics of the UCR and PRO respectively, and Milei focused on the need to join forces against Kirchnerism. [ 51 ] On 25 October 2023, Bullrich officially endorsed Javier Milei for the runoff election. [ 52 ] She did not ask the other parties within JXC, the UCR and the CC, for their opinion, as they have conflicting views over Milei. Both of them met the Wednesday after the elections to negotiate this support, alongside Macri. Milei announced the alliance on his X account, with an AI image of an embrace between a lion and a duck. Milei associates himself with imagery of lions, and "pato" ("duck") is a common nickname in Spanish for people named "Patricia". [ 40 ] Minister of Security (2023–2025) [ edit ] Patricia Bullrich announced a decrease in homicides in Rosario . In December 2023, Patricia Bullrich returned to government as security minister in  president Javier Milei\'s Cabinet. [ 53 ] Bullrich immediately issued a protocol to deal with demonstrations and roadblocks made by piqueteros . The Workers\' Party made an habeas corpus request to prevent the protocol from coming into force, which judge Gustavo Pierretti rejected. Several groups of Piqueteros called for a massive demonstration on 20 December, a week after the inauguration of Javier Milei . The government announced that demonstrators who committed crimes during demonstrations, such as roadblocks or vandalism, would lose their welfare payments, and provided a phone number to denounce piquetero leaders who would be coercing people to take part in such demonstrations. The demonstration had very little attendance, and the phone calls were used to start 660 criminal complaints. [ 54 ] The policies were kept for all later protests. The welfare aid that was outsourced to piquetero organizations returned to the direct state control, and social leaders that worked at the ministry of Social Development despite the conflict of interest were fired. Several audits also revealed that several social organizations that used to control the outsourced welfare aid only used a fraction of it for such a purpose. All this decreased the power of piqueteros, and protests and demonstrations rapidly decreased in size. [ 55 ] The city of Rosario had ongoing problems with narcotics trafficking cartels, who had moved beyond the illegal drug trade into other illicit activities, such as extortion and contract killing . Bullrich announced the "Plan Bandera" ("Flag plan") with governor of Santa Fe Province Maximiliano Pullaro to deal with the problem. One of the initial actions was to enforce stricter conditions at the local prisons, as several crime bosses were already jailed but managed to control the criminal operations nonetheless. The national government installed mobile phone jammers at those prisons, which led to death threats against Pullaro and his family. [ 56 ] Bullrich provided a report of the results of the operation six months later: homicides decreased by 73%, they detained 400 people linked to drug trade, 118 kilograms of cocaine and dope, 50,000 parts of synthetic drugs , 900 kilograms of ammonia, 57,005,062 pesos , 18,050 US dollars and 70 weapons. [ 57 ] Bullrich stayed president of PRO despite being a minister of a government for another party. Initially, both PRO and LLA were allies, but as both parties began to drift apart she sided with Milei\'s party instead of PRO. Both parties ran for the 2025 legislative elections on their own after the failure of the negotiations to create an electoral alliance. Bullrich took part in electoral parades of LLA, and encouraged politicians close to her move to the party. In May 2025 she formally left the PRO and joined LLA. [ 58 ] [ 59 ] Following her election as senator in the 2025 legislative election, on 22 November 2025 President Javier Milei confirmed that Alejandra Monteoliva would be her successor. [ 60 ] Bullrich resigned on 1 December 2025 and Monteoliva took office the following day. [ 61 ] [ 62 ] Political positions [ edit ] Patricia Bullrich announces new policies against traffic obstructions by piqueteros . Patricia Bullrich was a member of Peronist guerrillas in her youth, but grew critical of them as an adult. She described the ideas held by those organizations as an improvised blend of nationalism , Christianity and socialism . She explained that back then she thought that she was taking part in a revolution and that the people would eventually get used to it, but eventually realized that revolutions rarely have a positive outcome. She also thinks that she deluded herself by thinking that Peronism had goals that were not its actual goals. She started to have doubts over her allegiance to the guerrillas when she found out that Montoneros had killed the priest Carlos Mugica , and the aide of Perón José Ignacio Rucci . She realized that Montoneros and the People\'s Revolutionary Army killed people, even if they had not said so openly, and that she was helping that even if from a passive role. [ 16 ] In her book Yo Propongo , written during the presidency of Cristina Kirchner, Bullrich talks about populism and authoritarianism . She considers that democracy in Argentina has been weakened by a dominant-party system coupled with the dismantling of the lead party, which led to a system where only the president has authority, the party is an extension of the president\'s will, and government and state lost any meaningful difference. She considers that political polarization grew beyond only politics and engulfed other areas as well, such as academics and unions. She also pointed out that the Kirchners may want to organize a set of controlled media to advance a "narrative" that is positive towards their policies and hostile against the opposition. She also considers that this style of government was used by the Kirchners to advance policies that are long outdated in the rest of the world, and to conceal its negative results. [ 63 ] In contrast, she proposes to dismantle in politics the dominant-party system, and in economics to advance a sustainable capitalist model. [ 64 ] In relation to the severity of law enforcement , she supports a hardline policy against crime, rejecting the policies of Kirchnerism that grant too many rights to criminals and place rigid controls and obstacles on police work. Although those policies are largely a reaction against the policies of the military dictatorship, Bullrich says that "Argentina must leave the past and look to the future". [ 16 ] In particular, she had conflicting views with Sabina Frederic , minister of security of Alberto Fernández, over the use of taser guns, as Frederic restricted the police of the Argentine Federal Police from using either those or regular guns. [ 65 ] When she was appointed minister of security by Javier Milei, she said "True change is possible if the law is applied in every corner of the country, equally for everyone and without privileges. Argentina needs order. We will be relentless against crime and we will wage a relentless fight against drug trafficking. It\'s simple: whoever does something, pays for it". [ 12 ] Patricia Bullrich supported abortion during the debate in 2018 for a bill that would make it legal. She said that it did not make sense that only the woman could go to jail for it. [ 66 ] However, she also supported a clause for conscientious objection to abortion from medics that may refuse to do it, and to set a minimum age higher than in the proposed bill. [ 67 ] The bill was not approved, and was proposed again in 2020. That time, Bullrich refused to comment her personal opinion on abortion, and considered instead that the country had more pressing economic and societal priorities. [ 68 ] For similar reasons, she did not agree with the proposal of Javier Milei to celebrate a referendum to abolish the bill approved in 2020: she said that it would halt the whole country for a couple of months, and that the priority was to solve the economic crisis. /></a></span></td></tr><tr><td colspan="2" class="infobox-below" style="border-top: 1px solid right;"><div></div></td></tr></tbody></table>\n<p><b>Patricia Bullrich</b> (<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1177148991">.mw-parser-output .IPA-label-small{font-size:85%}.mw-parser-output .references .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .infobox lang="es-Latn-419-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish" title="Help:IPA/Spanish">&#91;paˈtɾisja<span class="wrap"> </span>ˈβulritʃ&#93;</a></span> <span class="ext-phonos"><span data-nosnippet="" id="ooui-php-1" class="noexcerpt ext-phonos-PhonosButton ext-phonos-PhonosButton-emptylabel oo-ui-widget oo-ui-widget-enabled oo-ui-buttonElement oo-ui-buttonElement-frameless oo-ui-iconElement oo-ui-buttonWidget" data-ooui="{&quot;_&quot;:&quot;mw.Phonos.PhonosButton&quot;,&quot;href&quot;:&quot;\\/\\/upload.wikimedia.org\\/wikipedia\\/commons\\/transcoded\\/2\\/2d\\/Patricia_Bullrich_-_nombre_%28ES-ar%29.ogg\\/Patricia_Bullrich_-_nombre_%28ES-ar%29.ogg.mp3&quot;,&quot;rel&quot;:[&quot;nofollow&quot;],&quot;framed&quot;:false,&quot;icon&quot;:&quot;volumeUp&quot;,&quot;data&quot;:{&quot;ipa&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;text&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;lang&quot;:&quot;en&quot;,&quot;wikibase&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;file&quot;:&quot;Patricia
