class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Inauguration_and_the_1889_exposition">Inauguration and the 1889 exposition</h3></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Exposition_Universelle_de_Paris_1889_-_Universit%C3%A4ts-_und_Landesbibliothek_Darmstadt.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Exposition_Universelle_de_Paris_1889_-_Universit%C3%A4ts-_und_Landesbibliothek_Darmstadt.jpg/250px-Exposition_Universelle_de_Paris_1889_-_Universit%C3%A4ts-_und_Landesbibliothek_Darmstadt.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="176" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Exposition_Universelle_de_Paris_1889_-_Universit%C3%A4ts-_und_Landesbibliothek_Darmstadt.jpg/500px-Exposition_Universelle_de_Paris_1889_-_Universit%C3%A4ts-_und_Landesbibliothek_Darmstadt.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="6288" data-file-height="4432" /></a><figcaption>View of the 1889 World\'s Fair</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The main structural work was completed at the end of March 1889 and, on 31 March, Eiffel celebrated by leading a group of government officials, accompanied by representatives of the press, to the top of the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-times1&#95;4&#95;89&#95;20-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-times1_4_89-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Because the lifts were not yet in operation, the ascent was made by foot, and took over an hour, with Eiffel stopping frequently to explain various features. Most of the party chose to stop at the lower levels, but a few, including the structural engineer, Émile Nouguier, the head of construction, Jean Compagnon, the President of the City Council, and reporters from <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Figaro" title="Le Figaro">Le Figaro</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Monde_Illustr%C3%A9" class="mw-redirect" title="Le Monde Illustré">Le Monde Illustré</a></i>, completed the ascent. At 2:35&#160;pm, Eiffel hoisted a large <a href="/wiki/Flag_of_France" title="Flag of France">Tricolour</a> to the accompaniment of a 25-gun salute fired at the first level.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>There was still work to be done, particularly on the lifts and facilities, and the tower was not opened to the public until nine days after the opening of the exposition on 6 May; even then, the lifts had not been completed. The tower was an instant success with the public, and nearly 30,000 visitors made the 1,710-step climb to the top before the lifts entered service on 26 May.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Exposition&#95;31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Exposition-31"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Tickets cost 2 francs for the first level, 3 for the second, and 5 for the top, with half-price admission on Sundays,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and by the end of the exhibition there had been 1,896,987 visitors.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Key&#95;figures&#95;5-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Key_figures-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>After dark, the tower was lit by hundreds of gas lamps, and a beacon sent out three beams of red, white and blue light. Two searchlights mounted on a circular rail were used to illuminate various buildings of the exposition. The daily opening and closing of the exposition were announced by a cannon at the top.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg/250px-Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="298" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg/330px-Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg/500px-Georges_Garen_embrasement_tour_Eiffel.jpg 2x" data-file-width="894" data-file-height="1400" /></a><figcaption>Illumination of the tower at night during the exposition; painted by <a href="/w/index.php?title=Georges_Garen&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Georges Garen (page does not exist)">Georges Garen</a><span class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;">&#160;&#91;<a href="https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Garen" class="extiw" title="fr:Georges Garen">fr</a>&#93;</span>, 1889</figcaption></figure>\n<p>On the second level, the French newspaper <i>Le Figaro</i> had an office and a printing press, where a special souvenir edition, <i>Le Figaro de la Tour</i>, was made.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>At the top, there was a post office where visitors could send letters and postcards as a memento of their visit. <a href="/wiki/Graffiti" title="Graffiti">Graffitists</a> were also catered for: sheets of paper were mounted on the walls each day for visitors to record their impressions of the tower. Gustave Eiffel described the collection of responses as "truly curious".<sup id="cite&#95;ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>\nFamous visitors to the tower included the <a href="/wiki/Edward_VII" title="Edward VII">Prince of Wales</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt" title="Sarah Bernhardt">Sarah Bernhardt</a>, <a href="/wiki/William_Cody" class="mw-redirect" title="William Cody">"Buffalo Bill" Cody</a> (his Wild West show was an attraction at the exposition) and <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Edison" title="Thomas Edison">Thomas Edison</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Exposition&#95;31-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Exposition-31"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Eiffel invited Edison to his private apartment at the top of the tower, where Edison presented him with one of his <a href="/wiki/Phonograph" title="Phonograph">phonographs</a>, a new invention and one of the many highlights of the exposition.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Edison signed the <a href="/wiki/Guestbook" title="Guestbook">guestbook</a> with this message on September 10, 1889: <link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1244412712" /></p><blockquote class="templatequote" style="text-align:justify"><p>To M Eiffel the Engineer the brave builder of so gigantic and original specimen of modern Engineering from one who has the greatest respect and admiration for all Engineers including the Great Engineer the Bon Dieu, Thomas Edison.</p></blockquote>\n<p>Eiffel made use of his apartment at the top of the tower to carry out <a href="/wiki/Meteorology" title="Meteorology">meteorological observations</a>, and also used the tower to perform experiments on the action of air resistance on falling bodies.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Subsequent_events">Subsequent events</h3></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_0" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv/250px--Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv.jpg" controls="" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" class="mw-file-element" width="250" height="188" data-durationhint="43" data-mwtitle="Vue_Lumière_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l&#39;ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_(1898).ogv" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_(1898).ogv"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/6e/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv.360p.webm" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6e/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv" type="video/ogg; codecs=&quot;theora&quot;" data-width="400" data-height="300" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/6e/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv/Vue_Lumi%C3%A8re_No_992_-_Panorama_pendant_l%27ascension_de_la_Tour_Eiffel_%281898%29.ogv.240p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="240p.vp9.webm" data-width="320" data-height="240" /></video></span><figcaption>Panoramic view during ascent of the Eiffel Tower by the <a href="/wiki/Auguste_and_Louis_Lumi%C3%A8re" title="Auguste and Louis Lumière">Lumière brothers</a>, 1898</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Eiffel had a permit for the tower to stand for 20 years. It was to be dismantled in 1909, when its ownership would revert to the <a href="/wiki/Paris" title="Paris">City of Paris</a>. The city had planned to tear it down (part of the original contest rules for designing a tower was that it should be easy to dismantle) but as the tower proved to be valuable for many innovations in the early 20th century, particularly <a href="/wiki/Radio_telegraphy" class="mw-redirect" title="Radio telegraphy">radio telegraphy</a>, it was allowed to remain after the expiry of the permit, and from 1910 it also became part of the International Time Service.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>For the <a href="/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1900)" title="Exposition Universelle (1900)">1900 <i>Exposition Universelle</i></a>, the lifts in the east and west legs were replaced by lifts running as far as the second level constructed by the French firm Fives-Lille. These had a compensating mechanism to keep the floor level as the angle of ascent changed at the first level, and were driven by a similar hydraulic mechanism as the Otis lifts, although this was situated at the base of the tower. Hydraulic pressure was provided by pressurised accumulators located near this mechanism.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-vogel&#95;23-4&#95;39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vogel_23-4-39"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> At the same time the lift in the north pillar was removed and replaced by a staircase to the first level. The layout of both first and second levels was modified. The original lift in the south pillar was removed 13 years later.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg/250px-Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="271" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg/330px-Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg/500px-Santos-Dumont_flight_around_the_Eiffel_Tower.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1802" data-file-height="2569" /></a><figcaption>Santos-Dumont No. 5; 13 July 1901</figcaption></figure>\n<p>On 19 October 1901, <a href="/wiki/Alberto_Santos-Dumont" title="Alberto Santos-Dumont">Alberto Santos-Dumont</a>, flying his <a href="/wiki/Santos-Dumont_number_6" title="Santos-Dumont number 6">No.6</a> <a href="/wiki/Airship" title="Airship">airship</a>, won a 100,000-franc prize offered by <a href="/wiki/Henri_Deutsch_de_la_Meurthe" title="Henri Deutsch de la Meurthe">Henri Deutsch de la Meurthe</a> for the first person to make a flight from <a href="/wiki/Saint-Cloud" title="Saint-Cloud">St. Cloud</a> to the Eiffel Tower and back in less than half an hour.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>From 1910, the <a href="/wiki/Astronomical_clock" title="Astronomical clock">astronomical clocks</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Paris_Observatory" title="Paris Observatory">Paris Observatory</a> sent the time to sea daily through the Eiffel Tower within a radius of 5 000&#160;km.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:110&#95;41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:110-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The development of <a href="/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy" title="Wireless telegraphy">wireless telegraphy</a> allowed unifying <a href="/wiki/Universal_Time" title="Universal Time">Universal Time</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:110&#95;41-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:110-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On 9 March 1911, France adopted <a href="/wiki/Greenwich_Mean_Time" title="Greenwich Mean Time">Greenwich Mean Time</a> by law. However, the law did not refer to <a href="/wiki/Prime_meridian_(Greenwich)" title="Prime meridian (Greenwich)">Greenwich Prime Meridian</a>, but to the <a href="/wiki/Local_mean_time" title="Local mean time">local mean time</a> of Paris delayed by 9 <a href="/wiki/Minute" title="Minute">minutes</a> and 21 <a href="/wiki/Second" title="Second">seconds</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1912, following a report by <a href="/wiki/Gustave-Auguste_Ferri%C3%A9" title="Gustave-Auguste Ferrié">Gustave Ferrié</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_des_Longitudes" title="Bureau des Longitudes">Bureau des Longitudes</a> organized at the Paris Observatory a <i>Conférence internationale de l\'heure radiotélégraphique</i> (International Radiotelegraph Time Conference). The <a href="/wiki/International_Time_Bureau" title="International Time Bureau">International Time Bureau</a> was created and installed in the premises of the Paris Observatory. However, due to <a href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</a>, the International Convention was never ratified.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:272&#95;43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:272-43"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1919, the existence of the International Time Bureau was formalized under the authority of an International Time Commission, under the aegis of the <a href="/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union" title="International Astronomical Union">International Astronomical Union</a>, created by <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Baillaud" title="Benjamin Baillaud">Benjamin Baillaud</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:110&#95;41-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:110-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In 1910, <a href="/wiki/Priest" title="Priest">Father</a> <a href="/wiki/Theodor_Wulf" title="Theodor Wulf">Theodor Wulf</a> measured <a href="/wiki/Radiant_energy" title="Radiant energy">radiant energy</a> at the top and bottom of the tower. He found more at the top than expected, incidentally discovering what are known today as <a href="/wiki/Cosmic_ray" title="Cosmic ray">cosmic rays</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Wulf&#95;44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wulf-44"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Two years later, on 4 February 1912, Austrian tailor <a href="/wiki/Franz_Reichelt" title="Franz Reichelt">Franz Reichelt</a> died after jumping from the first level of the tower (a height of 57 m) to demonstrate his <a href="/wiki/Parachute" title="Parachute">parachute</a> design.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1914, at the outbreak of <a href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War&#160;I</a>, a radio transmitter located in the tower <a href="/wiki/Radio_jamming" title="Radio jamming">jammed</a> German radio communications, seriously hindering their advance on Paris and contributing to the Allied victory at the <a href="/wiki/First_Battle_of_the_Marne" title="First Battle of the Marne">First Battle of the Marne</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Tuchman1994&#95;46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Tuchman1994-46"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>During <a href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</a>, the Eiffel Tower\'s wireless station played a crucial role in intercepting enemy communications from Berlin. In 1914, French forces successfully launched a counter-attack during the Battle of the Marne after gaining critical intelligence on the German Army\'s movements. In 1917, the station intercepted a coded message between Germany and Spain that referenced \'Operative H-21.\' This information contributed to the arrest, conviction, and execution of <a href="/wiki/Mata_Hari" title="Mata Hari">Mata Hari</a>, the famous spy accused of working for Germany.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>From 1925 to 1934, illuminated signs for <a href="/wiki/Citro%C3%ABn" title="Citroën">Citroën</a> adorned three of the tower\'s sides, making it the tallest advertising space in the world at the time.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In April 1935, the tower was used to make experimental low-resolution television transmissions, using a <a href="/wiki/Shortwave" class="mw-redirect" title="Shortwave">shortwave</a> transmitter of 200 watts power. On 17 November, an improved 180-line transmitter was installed.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Herbert2004&#95;49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Herbert2004-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg/250px-Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg" decoding="async" width="200" height="251" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg/330px-Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg/500px-Delaunay_-_Tour_Eiffel.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="1256" /></a><figcaption>The Eiffel Tower has been a subject of art, as in <i><a href="/wiki/Champs_de_Mars:_The_Red_Tower" title="Champs de Mars: The Red Tower">Champs de Mars: The Red Tower</a></i>, a 1911 <a href="/wiki/Cubism" title="Cubism">cubist</a> painting by <a href="/wiki/Robert_Delaunay" title="Robert Delaunay">Robert Delaunay</a>.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>On two separate but related occasions in 1925, the con artist <a href="/wiki/Victor_Lustig" title="Victor Lustig">Victor Lustig</a> "sold" the tower for scrap metal.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Letcher2003&#95;50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Letcher2003-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> A year later, in February 1926, pilot Leon Collet was killed trying to fly under the tower. His aircraft became entangled in an aerial belonging to a wireless station.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/Bust_(sculpture)" title="Bust (sculpture)">bust</a> of Gustave Eiffel by <a href="/wiki/Antoine_Bourdelle" title="Antoine Bourdelle">Antoine Bourdelle</a> was unveiled at the base of the north leg on 2 May 1929.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1930, the tower lost the title of the <a href="/wiki/List_of_tallest_freestanding_structures_in_the_world#Timeline_of_world&#39;s_tallest_freestanding_structures" class="mw-redirect" title="List of tallest freestanding structures in the world">world\'s tallest structure</a> when the <a href="/wiki/Chrysler_Building" title="Chrysler Building">Chrysler Building</a> in New York City was completed.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1938, the decorative arcade around the first level was removed.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Upon the <a href="/wiki/Military_Administration_in_France_(Nazi_Germany)" class="mw-redirect" title="Military Administration in France (Nazi Germany)">German occupation</a> of Paris in 1940, the lift cables were <a href="/wiki/Sabotage" title="Sabotage">cut</a> by the French. The tower was  restricted to German visitors during the occupation and the lifts were not repaired until 1946.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Harriss&#95;80&#95;4&#95;55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Harriss_80_4-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1940, German soldiers had to climb the tower to hoist a swastika-centred <a href="/wiki/Reichskriegsflagge" title="Reichskriegsflagge">Reichskriegsflagge</a>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> but the flag was so large it blew away just a few hours later, and was replaced by a smaller one.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> When visiting Paris, Hitler chose to stay on the ground. When the <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allies</a> were nearing Paris in August 1944, Hitler ordered General <a href="/wiki/Dietrich_von_Choltitz" title="Dietrich von Choltitz">Dietrich von Choltitz</a>, the military governor of Paris, to demolish the tower along with the rest of the city. Von Choltitz disobeyed the order.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-D&#39;Este2003&#95;58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-D&#39;Este2003-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On 25 August, before the Germans had been <a href="/wiki/Liberation_of_Paris" title="Liberation of Paris">driven out of Paris</a>, the German flag was replaced with a Tricolour by two men from the <a href="/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_national_de_la_Marine" title="Musée national de la Marine">French Naval Museum</a>, who narrowly beat three men led by Lucien Sarniguet, who had lowered the Tricolour on 13 June 1940 when Paris fell to the Germans.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Harriss&#95;80&#95;4&#95;55-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Harriss_80_4-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>A fire started in the television transmitter on 3 January 1956, damaging the top of the tower. Repairs took a year, and in 1957, the present radio aerial was added to the top.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-events&#95;59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-events-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1964, the Eiffel Tower was officially declared to be a historical monument by the Minister of Cultural Affairs, <a href="/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Malraux" title="André Malraux">André Malraux</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> A year later, an additional lift system was installed in the north pillar.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official-website-lifts&#95;61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official-website-lifts-61"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>According to interviews, in 1967, <a href="/wiki/Montreal" title="Montreal">Montreal</a> Mayor <a href="/wiki/Jean_Drapeau" title="Jean Drapeau">Jean Drapeau</a> negotiated a secret agreement with <a href="/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle" title="Charles de Gaulle">Charles de Gaulle</a> for the tower to be dismantled and temporarily relocated to Montreal to serve as a landmark and tourist attraction during <a href="/wiki/Expo_67" title="Expo 67">Expo 67</a>. The plan was allegedly vetoed by the company operating the tower out of fear that the French government could refuse permission for the tower to be restored in its original location.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In 1982, the original lifts between the second and third levels were replaced after 97 years in service. These had been closed to the public between November and March because the water in the hydraulic drive tended to freeze. The new cars operate in pairs, with one counterbalancing the other, and perform the journey in one stage, reducing the journey time from eight minutes to less than two minutes. At the same time, two new emergency staircases were installed, replacing the original spiral staircases. In 1983, the south pillar was fitted with an electrically driven Otis lift to serve the <a href="/wiki/Le_Jules_Verne" title="Le Jules Verne">Jules Verne</a> restaurant.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The Fives-Lille lifts in the east and west legs, fitted in 1899, were extensively refurbished in 1986. The cars were replaced, and a computer system was installed to completely automate the lifts. The <a href="/wiki/Power_(physics)" title="Power (physics)">motive power</a> was moved from the water hydraulic system to a new electrically driven oil-filled hydraulic system, and the original water hydraulics were retained solely as a counterbalance system.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official-website-lifts&#95;61-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official-website-lifts-61"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> A service lift was added to the south pillar for moving small loads and maintenance personnel three years later.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Robert_Moriarty" class="mw-redirect" title="Robert Moriarty">Robert Moriarty</a> flew a <a href="/wiki/Beechcraft_Bonanza" title="Beechcraft Bonanza">Beechcraft Bonanza</a> under the tower on 31 March 1984.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 1987, <a href="/wiki/A._J._Hackett" title="A. J. Hackett">A. J. Hackett</a> made one of his first <a href="/wiki/Bungee_jumping" title="Bungee jumping">bungee jumps</a> from the top of the Eiffel Tower, using a special cord he had helped develop. Hackett was arrested by the police.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On 27 October 1991, Thierry Devaux, along with mountain guide Hervé Calvayrac, performed a series of acrobatic figures while bungee jumping from the second floor of the tower. Facing the Champ de Mars, Devaux used an electric winch between figures to go back up to the second floor. When firemen arrived, he stopped after the sixth jump.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:2013_Fireworks_on_Eiffel_Tower_11.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/2013_Fireworks_on_Eiffel_Tower_11.jpg/250px-2013_Fireworks_on_Eiffel_Tower_11.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/2013_Fireworks_on_Eiffel_Tower_11.jpg/500px-2013_Fireworks_on_Eiffel_Tower_11.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3931" data-file-height="2948" /></a><figcaption>The tower is a focal point for New Year\'s Eve and <a href="/wiki/Bastille_Day" title="Bastille Day">Bastille Day</a> celebrations.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>For its "Countdown to the Year 2000" celebration on 31 December 1999, flashing lights and high-powered <a href="/wiki/Searchlight" title="Searchlight">searchlights</a> were installed on the tower. During the last three minutes of the year, the lights were turned on starting from the base of the tower and continuing to the top to welcome 2000 with a huge fireworks show. An exhibition above a cafeteria on the first floor commemorates this event. The searchlights on top of the tower made it a beacon in Paris\'s night sky, and 20,000 flashing bulbs gave the tower a sparkly appearance for five minutes every hour on the hour.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The lights sparkled blue for several nights to herald the new millennium on 31 December 1999. The sparkly lighting continued for 18 months until July 2001. The sparkling lights were turned on again on 21 June 2003, and the display was planned to last for 10 years before they needed replacing.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-allyouneed&#95;68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-allyouneed-68"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>\nThe tower received its 200,000,000th guest on 28 November 2002.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The tower has operated at its maximum capacity of about 7&#160;million visitors per year since 2003.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 2004, the Eiffel Tower began hosting a seasonal ice rink on the first level.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PorterPrince2006&#95;71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PorterPrince2006-71"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/Glass_floor" title="Glass floor">glass floor</a> was installed on the first level during the 2014 refurbishment.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></p><div style="clear:both;" class=""></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Design">Design</h2></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Material">Material</h3></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Sous_la_Tour_Eiffel_1.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Sous_la_Tour_Eiffel_1.jpg/250px-Sous_la_Tour_Eiffel_1.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="171" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Sous_la_Tour_Eiffel_1.jpg/500px-Sous_la_Tour_Eiffel_1.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2935" data-file-height="2013" /></a><figcaption>The Eiffel Tower from below</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The <a href="/wiki/Puddling_(metallurgy)" title="Puddling (metallurgy)">puddle iron</a> (wrought iron) of the Eiffel Tower weighs 7,300 <a href="/wiki/Tonne" title="Tonne">tonnes</a>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Hanser2006&#95;73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hanser2006-73"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and the addition of lifts, shops and antennae have brought the total weight to approximately 10,100&#160;tonnes.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> As a demonstration of the economy of design, if the 7,300&#160;tonnes of metal in the structure were melted down, it would fill the square base, 125 metres (410&#160;ft) on each side, to a depth of only 6.25&#160;cm (2.46&#160;in) assuming the density of the metal to be 7.8&#160;tonnes per cubic metre.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Additionally, a cubic box surrounding the tower (324&#160;m&#160;×&#160;125&#160;m&#160;×&#160;125&#160;m) would contain 6,200&#160;tonnes of air, weighing almost as much as the iron itself. Depending on the <a href="/wiki/Room_temperature" title="Room temperature">ambient temperature</a>, the top of the tower may shift away from the sun by up to 18&#160;cm (7&#160;in) due to <a href="/wiki/Thermal_expansion" title="Thermal expansion">thermal expansion</a> of the metal on the side facing the sun.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Wind_and_weather_considerations">Wind and weather considerations</h3></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg/250px-Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="303" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg/330px-Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg/500px-Lightning_striking_the_Eiffel_Tower_-_NOAA.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1072" data-file-height="1624" /></a><figcaption>Lightning striking the Eiffel Tower in 1902</figcaption></figure>\n<p>When it was built, Eiffel was accused of trying to create something artistic with no regard to the principles of engineering. However, Eiffel and his team were experienced bridge builders. In an interview with the newspaper <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Temps_(Paris)" title="Le Temps (Paris)">Le Temps</a></i> published on 14 February 1887, Eiffel said:\n</p>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1244412712" /><blockquote class="templatequote" style="text-align:justify"><p>Is it not true that the very conditions which give strength also conform to the hidden rules of harmony?<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>... Now to what phenomenon did I have to give primary concern in designing the Tower? It was wind resistance. Well then! I hold that the curvature of the monument\'s four outer edges, which is as mathematical calculation dictated it should be<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>... will give a great impression of strength and beauty, for it will reveal to the eyes of the observer the boldness of the design as a whole.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-debate&#95;77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-debate-77"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></p></blockquote>\n<p>He used graphical methods to determine the strength of the tower and <a href="/wiki/Empirical_evidence" title="Empirical evidence">empirical evidence</a> to account for the effects of wind, rather than a mathematical formula. Close examination of the tower reveals a basically <a href="/wiki/Exponential_function" title="Exponential function">exponential</a> shape.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-sciencedaily2005&#95;78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sciencedaily2005-78"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> All parts of the tower were overdesigned to ensure maximum resistance to wind forces. The top half was assumed to have no gaps in the latticework.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-79" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-79"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> After it was completed, some have put forward various mathematical hypotheses in an attempt to explain the success of the design. A one devised in 2004 after letters sent by Eiffel to the French Society of Civil Engineers in 1885 were translated into English described it as a non-linear integral equation based on counteracting the wind pressure on any point of the tower with the tension between the construction elements at that point.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-sciencedaily2005&#95;78-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sciencedaily2005-78"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The Eiffel Tower sways by up to <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1154941027">.mw-parser-output .frac{white-space:nowrap}.mw-parser-output .frac .num,.mw-parser-output .frac .den{font-size:80%;line-height:0;vertical-align:super}.mw-parser-output .frac .den{vertical-align:sub}.mw-parser-output .sr-only{border:0;clip:rect(0,0,0,0);clip-path:polygon(0px 0px,0px 0px,0px 0px);height:1px;margin:-1px;overflow:hidden;padding:0;position:absolute;width:1px}</style>9&#160;cm (<span class="frac">3<span class="sr-only">+</span><span class="num">1</span>&#8260;<span class="den">2</span></span>&#160;in) in the wind.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div style="clear:left;" class=""></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Floors">Floors</h3></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Ground_floor">Ground floor</h4></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Paris_Eiffel_092.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Paris_Eiffel_092.JPG/250px-Paris_Eiffel_092.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Paris_Eiffel_092.JPG/500px-Paris_Eiffel_092.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448" /></a><figcaption>Base of the Eiffel Tower</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The four columns of the tower each house access stairs and lifts to the first two floors, while at the south column only the lift to the second floor restaurant is publicly accessible.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="Sentence appears to be internally contradictory about whether access is available to first floor from south column (June 2025)">clarification needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="1st_floor">1st floor</h4></div>\n<p>The first floor is publicly accessible by lift or stairs. When originally built, the first level contained three restaurants—one French, one Russian and one <a href="/wiki/Flemish_Region" title="Flemish Region">Flemish</a>—and an "Anglo-American Bar". After the exposition closed, the Flemish restaurant was converted to a 250-seat theatre. Today there is the <span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr">Le 58 Tour Eiffel</i></span> restaurant and other facilities.\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:La_Tour_Eiffel_-_terrasse_de_la_premi%C3%A8re_plate-forme.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/La_Tour_Eiffel_-_terrasse_de_la_premi%C3%A8re_plate-forme.jpg/250px-La_Tour_Eiffel_-_terrasse_de_la_premi%C3%A8re_plate-forme.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="175" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/La_Tour_Eiffel_-_terrasse_de_la_premi%C3%A8re_plate-forme.jpg/500px-La_Tour_Eiffel_-_terrasse_de_la_premi%C3%A8re_plate-forme.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="4114" data-file-height="2881" /></a><figcaption>A promenade 2.6-metre (8&#160;ft 6&#160;in) wide ran around the outside of the first level</figcaption></figure>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="2nd_floor">2nd floor</h4></div>\n<p>The second floor is publicly accessible by lift or stairs and has a restaurant called <span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr"><a href="/wiki/Le_Jules_Verne" title="Le Jules Verne">Le Jules Verne</a></i></span>, a <a href="/wiki/Gourmet" title="Gourmet">gourmet</a> restaurant with its own lift going up from the south column to the second level. This restaurant has one star in the <a href="/wiki/Michelin_Guide" title="Michelin Guide">Michelin Red Guide</a>. It was run by the multi-<a href="/wiki/Michelin_star" class="mw-redirect" title="Michelin star">Michelin star</a> chef <a href="/wiki/Alain_Ducasse" title="Alain Ducasse">Alain Ducasse</a> from 2007 to 2017.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> As of May 2019, it is managed by three-star chef <a href="/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Anton" title="Frédéric Anton">Frédéric Anton</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ParisDigest&#95;82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ParisDigest-82"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It owes its name to the famous science-fiction writer <a href="/wiki/Jules_Verne" title="Jules Verne">Jules Verne</a>.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="3rd_floor">3rd floor</h4></div>\n<p>The third floor is the top floor, publicly accessible by lift.\n</p><p>Originally there were laboratories for various experiments, and a small apartment reserved for Gustave Eiffel to entertain guests, which is now open to the public, complete with period decorations and lifelike <a href="/wiki/Mannequin" title="Mannequin">mannequins</a> of Eiffel and some of his notable guests.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Morton&#95;83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Morton-83"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Gustaves_Apartment_-_Eiffel_(3384390462).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Gustaves_Apartment_-_Eiffel_%283384390462%29.jpg/250px-Gustaves_Apartment_-_Eiffel_%283384390462%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Gustaves_Apartment_-_Eiffel_%283384390462%29.jpg/500px-Gustaves_Apartment_-_Eiffel_%283384390462%29.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="4288" data-file-height="2848" /></a><figcaption>Gustave Eiffel\'s apartment at the third floor</figcaption></figure>\n<p>From 1937 until 1981, there was a restaurant near the top of the tower. It was removed due to structural considerations; engineers had determined it was too heavy and was causing the tower to sag.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This restaurant was sold to an American restaurateur and transported to New York and then New Orleans. It was rebuilt on the edge of <a href="/wiki/Garden_District,_New_Orleans" title="Garden District, New Orleans">New Orleans\' Garden District</a> as a restaurant and later event hall.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> \n</p><p>Today there is a champagne bar on the third floor of the Eiffel Tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Lifts">Lifts</h3></div>\n<p>The arrangement of the lifts has been changed several times during the tower\'s history. Given the elasticity of the cables and the time taken to align the cars with the landings, each lift, in normal service, takes an average of 8 minutes and 50 seconds to do the round trip, spending an average of 1 minute and 15 seconds at each level. The average journey time between levels is 1 minute. The original hydraulic mechanism is on public display in a small museum at the base of the east and west legs. Because the mechanism requires frequent lubrication and maintenance, public access is often restricted. The rope mechanism of the north tower can be seen as visitors exit the lift.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2024)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tour_Eiffel_Ascenseur_Roux,_Combaluzier_et_Lepape.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Tour_Eiffel_Ascenseur_Roux%2C_Combaluzier_et_Lepape.jpg/250px-Tour_Eiffel_Ascenseur_Roux%2C_Combaluzier_et_Lepape.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="202" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Tour_Eiffel_Ascenseur_Roux%2C_Combaluzier_et_Lepape.jpg/500px-Tour_Eiffel_Ascenseur_Roux%2C_Combaluzier_et_Lepape.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="600" data-file-height="485" /></a><figcaption>The Roux, Combaluzier &amp; Lepape lifts during construction</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Equipping the tower with adequate and safe passenger lifts was a major concern of the government commission overseeing the Exposition. Although some visitors could be expected to climb to the first level, or even the second, lifts had to be the main means of ascent.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-vogel&#95;20&#95;87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vogel_20-87"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Constructing lifts to reach the first level was done by making the legs wide enough at the bottom and so nearly straight that they could contain a straight track. A contract was given to the French company Roux, Combaluzier &amp; Lepape for two lifts to be fitted in the east and west legs.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-vogel&#95;28&#95;88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vogel_28-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Roux, Combaluzier &amp; Lepape used a pair of endless chains with rigid, articulated links to which the car was attached. Lead weights on some links of the upper or return sections of the chains counterbalanced most of the car\'s weight. The car was pushed up from below, not pulled up from above: to prevent the chain buckling, it was enclosed in a conduit. At the bottom of the run, the chains passed around 3.9&#160;m (12&#160;ft 10&#160;in) diameter <a href="/wiki/Sprocket" title="Sprocket">sprockets</a>. Smaller sprockets at the top guided the chains.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-vogel&#95;28&#95;88-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vogel_28-88"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg/250px-Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="240" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg/330px-Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Eiffel-Otis_lift-poyet.jpg 2x" data-file-width="435" data-file-height="550" /></a><figcaption>The Otis lifts originally fitted in the north and south legs.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Installing lifts to the second level was more of a challenge because a straight track was impossible. No French company wanted to undertake the work. The European branch of <a href="/wiki/Otis_Elevator_Company" class="mw-redirect" title="Otis Elevator Company">Otis Brothers &amp; Company</a> submitted a proposal, but this was rejected: the fair\'s charter ruled out the use of any foreign material in the construction of the tower. The deadline for bids was extended, but still no French companies put themselves forward, and eventually the contract was given to Otis in July 1887.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-vogel&#95;23-4&#95;39-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vogel_23-4-39"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Otis were confident they would eventually be given the contract and had already started creating designs.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The car was divided into two superimposed compartments, each holding 25 passengers, with the lift operator occupying an exterior platform on the first level. <a href="/wiki/Power_(physics)" title="Power (physics)">Motive power</a> was provided by an inclined hydraulic ram 12.67&#160;m (41&#160;ft 7&#160;in) long and 96.5&#160;cm (38.0&#160;in) in diameter in the tower leg with a stroke of 10.83&#160;m (35&#160;ft 6&#160;in): this moved a carriage carrying six sheaves. Five fixed sheaves were mounted higher up the leg, producing an arrangement similar to a <a href="/wiki/Block_and_tackle" title="Block and tackle">block and tackle</a> but acting in reverse, multiplying the stroke of the piston rather than the force generated. The hydraulic pressure in the driving cylinder was produced by a large open reservoir on the second level. After being exhausted from the cylinder, the water was pumped back up to the reservoir by two pumps in the machinery room at the base of the south leg. This reservoir also provided power to the lifts to the first level.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The original lifts for the journey between the second and third levels were supplied by Léon Edoux. A pair of 81&#160;m (266&#160;ft) hydraulic rams were mounted on the second level, reaching nearly halfway up to the third level. One lift car was mounted on top of these rams: cables ran from the top of this car up to sheaves on the third level and back down to a second car. Each car travelled only half the distance between the second and third levels and passengers were required to change lifts halfway by means of a short gangway. The 10-ton cars each held 65 passengers.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Engraved_names">Engraved names</h3></div>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320" /><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_the_72_names_on_the_Eiffel_Tower" title="List of the 72 names on the Eiffel Tower">List of the 72 names on the Eiffel Tower</a></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Les_savants_de_la_Tour_Eiffel.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Les_savants_de_la_Tour_Eiffel.jpg/250px-Les_savants_de_la_Tour_Eiffel.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Les_savants_de_la_Tour_Eiffel.jpg/500px-Les_savants_de_la_Tour_Eiffel.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1362" data-file-height="1021" /></a><figcaption>Names engraved on the tower</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Gustave Eiffel engraved on the building of the tower the names of 72 French scientists, engineers and mathematicians as a recognition of their contributions. Eiffel chose this "invocation of science" because of his concern over the artists\' protest. At the beginning of the 20th century, the engravings were painted over, but they were restored in 1986–87 by the <span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr">Société Nouvelle d\'exploitation de la Tour Eiffel</i></span>, a company operating the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lab&amp;names&#95;92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lab&amp;names-92"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Aesthetics">Aesthetics</h3></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Eiffel_Tower_plans_21.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Eiffel_Tower_plans_21.jpg/250px-Eiffel_Tower_plans_21.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="178" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Eiffel_Tower_plans_21.jpg/500px-Eiffel_Tower_plans_21.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="4586" data-file-height="3261" /></a><figcaption>Some original architectural details</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The tower is painted in three shades: lighter at the top, getting progressively darker towards the bottom to complement the Parisian sky.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-paintingcolor&#95;93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-paintingcolor-93"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It was originally reddish brown; this changed in 1968 to a bronze colour known as "Eiffel Tower Brown".<sup id="cite&#95;ref-painting&#95;94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-painting-94"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In 2010 the tower was re-painted yellow-brown.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Following the 2024 Summer Olympics held in Paris, Mayor <a href="/wiki/Anne_Hidalgo" title="Anne Hidalgo">Anne Hidalgo</a> proposed keeping the <a href="/wiki/Olympic_symbols" title="Olympic symbols">Olympic rings</a> on the tower permanently. The rings, which measure 95 feet (29&#160;m) wide and 43 feet (13&#160;m) high, were initially installed for the Games and were scheduled for removal after the <a href="/wiki/2024_Summer_Paralympics" title="2024 Summer Paralympics">Paralympics</a>. Hidalgo\'s decision faced criticism from the Eiffel family and some residents concerned about altering the protected monument. The original 30-ton rings would be replaced with lighter versions for long-term display.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The only non-structural elements are the four decorative grill-work arches, added in Sauvestre\'s sketches, which served to make the tower look more substantial and to make a more impressive entrance to the exposition.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>A pop-culture movie cliché is that the view from a Parisian window always includes the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In reality, since zoning restrictions limit the height of most buildings in Paris to seven storeys, only a small number of tall buildings have a clear view of the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_1" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm/250px--Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm.jpg" controls="" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" class="mw-file-element" width="250" height="141" data-durationhint="307" data-mwtitle="Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/90/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm.480p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="1080p.vp9.webm" data-width="1920" data-height="1080" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/90/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="240p.vp9.webm" data-width="426" data-height="240" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/90/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm/Eiffel_Tower_Drone_4k-Qx_c1X3zfEc-313-251.webm.360p.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8, vorbis&quot;" data-transcodekey="360p.webm" data-width="640" data-height="360" /></video></span><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Bird%27s-eye_view" title="Bird&#39;s-eye view">Bird\'s-eye view</a> of the Eiffel Tower</figcaption></figure>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Maintenance">Maintenance</h3></div>\n<p>Maintenance of the tower includes applying 60&#160;tons of paint every 7 years to prevent it from <a href="/wiki/Rust" title="Rust">rusting</a>. The tower has been completely repainted at least 19 times since it was built, with the most recent being in 2010. <a href="/wiki/Lead_paint" title="Lead paint">Lead paint</a> was still being used as recently as 2001 when the practice was stopped out of concern for the environment.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-allyouneed&#95;68-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-allyouneed-68"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Communications">Communications</h2></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="286" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Tour_Eiffel_le_sommet_08-2015_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3380" data-file-height="5080" /></a><figcaption>Top of the Eiffel Tower with antennas</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The tower has been used for making radio transmissions since the beginning of the 20th century. Until the 1950s, sets of aerial wires ran from the <a href="/wiki/Cupola" title="Cupola">cupola</a> to anchors on the <a href="/wiki/Avenue_de_Suffren" title="Avenue de Suffren">Avenue de Suffren</a> and Champ de Mars. These were connected to <a href="/wiki/Longwave" title="Longwave">longwave</a> transmitters in small bunkers. In 1909, a permanent underground radio centre was built near the south pillar, which still exists today. On 20 November 1913, the <a href="/wiki/Paris_Observatory" title="Paris Observatory">Paris Observatory</a>, using the Eiffel Tower as an aerial, exchanged wireless signals with the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Naval_Observatory" title="United States Naval Observatory">United States Naval Observatory</a>, which used an aerial in <a href="/wiki/Arlington_County,_Virginia" title="Arlington County, Virginia">Arlington County, Virginia</a>. The object of the transmissions was to measure the difference in longitude between Paris and Washington, D.C.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Today, radio and digital television signals are transmitted from the Eiffel Tower.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="FM_radio">FM radio</h3></div>\n<table class="wikitable sortable">\n<tbody><tr>\n<th>Frequency\n</th>\n<th>kW\n</th>\n<th>Service\n</th></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>87.8&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>10\n</td>\n<td><a href="/wiki/France_Inter" title="France Inter">France Inter</a>\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>89.0&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>10\n</td>\n<td>RFI Paris\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>89.9&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>6\n</td>\n<td><a href="/wiki/TSF_Jazz" title="TSF Jazz">TSF Jazz</a>\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>90.4&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>10\n</td>\n<td><a href="/wiki/Nostalgie" title="Nostalgie">Nostalgie</a>\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>90.9&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>4\n</td>\n<td><a href="/wiki/Chante_France" title="Chante France">Chante France</a>\n</td></tr></tbody></table>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Digital_television">Digital television</h3></div>\n<p>A television antenna was first installed on the tower in 1957, increasing its height by 18.7&#160;m (61&#160;ft). Work carried out in 2000 added a further 5.3&#160;m (17&#160;ft), giving a total height of 324&#160;m (1,063&#160;ft).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-allyouneed&#95;68-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-allyouneed-68"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Analogue television signals from the Eiffel Tower ceased on 8 March 2011.\n</p>\n<table class="wikitable sortable">\n<tbody><tr>\n<th>Frequency\n</th>\n<th>VHF\n</th>\n<th>UHF\n</th>\n<th>kW\n</th>\n<th>Service\n</th></tr>\n<tr>\n<td>182.25&#160;MHz\n</td>\n<td>6\n</td>\n<td data-sort-value="" style="background: var(--background-color-interactive, #ececec); Eiffel Tower</div></div></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Taller_structures">Taller structures</h2></div>\n<p>The Eiffel Tower was the world\'s tallest structure when completed in 1889, a distinction it retained until 1929 when the <a href="/wiki/Chrysler_Building" title="Chrysler Building">Chrysler Building</a> in New York City was topped out.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The tower also lost its standing as the world\'s tallest tower to the <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Tower" title="Tokyo Tower">Tokyo Tower</a> in 1958 but retains its status as the tallest freestanding (non-guyed) structure in France.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Lattice_towers_taller_than_the_Eiffel_Tower">Lattice towers taller than the Eiffel Tower</h3></div>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320" /><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/List_of_tallest_towers_in_the_world" class="mw-redirect" title="List of tallest towers in the world">List of tallest towers in the world</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lattice_tower" title="Lattice tower">Lattice tower</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Observation_deck" title="Observation deck">Observation deck</a></div>\n<table class="wikitable">\n\n<tbody><tr>\n<th>Name\n</th>\n<th>Pinnacle height\n</th>\n<th>Year\n</th>\n<th>Country\n</th>\n<th>Town\n</th>\n<th>Remarks\n</th></tr>\n<tr>\n<td><a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a></td>\n<td>634&#160;m
