accident</li></ul>\n</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label">Deaths</th><td class="infobox-data" style="text-align: left;">1</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label">Non-fatal injuries</th><td class="infobox-data" style="text-align: left;">0</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label">Arrests</th><td class="infobox-data" style="text-align: left;">8</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label">Convictions</th><td class="infobox-data" style="text-align: left;">Three employees convicted of manslaughter; five other employees acquitted</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label">Sentence</th><td class="infobox-data" style="text-align: left;"><b>Three employees:</b>\n<ul><li>32 months of <a href="/wiki/Community_service" title="Community service">community service</a></li></ul>\n</td></tr></tbody></table>\n<p>On 24 February 2012, 14-year-old Gabriela Yukari Nichimura died after falling from the <i>La Tour Eiffel</i> drop tower at the <a href="/wiki/Hopi_Hari" title="Hopi Hari">Hopi Hari</a> <a href="/wiki/Amusement_park" title="Amusement park">amusement park</a> in <a href="/wiki/Vinhedo" title="Vinhedo">Vinhedo</a>, <a href="/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo_(state)" title="São Paulo (state)">São Paulo</a>, Brazil.\n</p>\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Incident">Incident</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Gabriela_Yukari_Nichimura&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Incident"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Nichimura\'s chair lock opened<sup id="cite&#95;ref-uoltestemunhas&#95;1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-uoltestemunhas-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-g1morte&#95;2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-g1morte-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> at about 66 feet (20 meters) in the air.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Acordo&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Acordo-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The chair had been unused for 10 years, due to the seat\'s location where a person could bump into the metal frame of the <a href="/wiki/Drop_tower" title="Drop tower">drop tower</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-igcadeira&#95;5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-igcadeira-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Therefore it was excluded for additional seat belt installation, and the old chair lock could no longer stay locked by itself; it had been opened before or during rides. But there had not been any sign informing not to use, and the parks authorities dismissed workers\' warning. \n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="La_Tour_Eiffel">La Tour Eiffel</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Gabriela_Yukari_Nichimura&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: La Tour Eiffel"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1224211176">.mw-parser-output .quotebox{background-color:#F9F9F9;border:1px solid #aaa;box-sizing:border-box;padding:10px;font-size:88%;max-width:100%}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft{margin:.5em 1.4em .8em 0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright{margin:.5em 0 .8em 1.4em}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.centered{overflow:hidden;position:relative;margin:.5em auto .8em auto}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft span,.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright span{font-style:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox>blockquote{margin:0;padding:0;border-left:0;font-family:inherit;font-size:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-title{text-align:center;font-size:110%;font-weight:bold}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote>:first-child{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote:last-child>:last-child{margin-bottom:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:before{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" “ ";vertical-align:-45%;line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:after{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" ” ";line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .left-aligned{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .right-aligned{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .center-aligned{text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quote-title,.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quotebox-quote{display:block}.mw-parser-output .quotebox cite{display:block;font-style:normal}@media screen and (max-width:640px){.mw-parser-output .quotebox{width:100%!important;margin:0 0 .8em!important;float:none!important}}</style><div class="quotebox pullquote floatleft" style="width:30%; ;">\n<div class="quotebox-title" style="">Clarification note<sup class="plainlinks nourlexpansion citation" id="ref&#95;a"><a class="external autonumber" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Gabriela_Yukari_Nichimura#endnote_a">[1]</a></sup></div>\n<blockquote class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style="">\n<p>Hopi Hari reports that around 10:20&#160;am today there was an accident involving a 14-year-old visitor who was in the La Tour Eiffel tower. The visitor was rescued and taken to Paulo Sacramento Hospital in the city of Jundiaí, where she died. After the accident, the park decided to end its activities for the day. Hopi Hari reopens tomorrow, Saturday, from 10&#160;am to 7&#160;pm. La Tour Eiffel will remain closed until the causes of the accident are clarified. The review of the ride is carried out by the Technical Police, which will investigate the hypotheses of the accident. The park deeply regrets what happened, [and] is providing all assistance to the victim\'s family and supporting the bodies responsible for investigating the causes of the accident.\n</p>\n</blockquote>\n<div style="padding-bottom: 0; padding-top: 0.5em"><cite class="left-aligned" style=""><a href="/wiki/Hopi_Hari" title="Hopi Hari">Hopi Hari</a>,&#32;Facebook post from the day of the accident</cite></div>\n</div>\n<p>The drop tower initially opened, along with the park itself, on 30 November 1999.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Drop_tower" title="Drop tower">tower</a> allows participants enter into free fall from a height of 69.5 meters, or 228 feet (the equivalent of a 23-story building) at a speed of approximately 94&#160;km/h (58.41&#160;mph).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-uoltestemunhas&#95;1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-uoltestemunhas-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-g1morte&#95;2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-g1morte-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Aftermath_and_investigation">Aftermath and investigation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Gabriela_Yukari_Nichimura&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Aftermath and investigation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>The park closed hours after the accident. A full review of all rides began on 2 March of that year.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-igcadeira&#95;5-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-igcadeira-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Upon completion of the review and the signing of a Conduct Adjustment Term (CAT), the park was reopened on 25 March 2012, but the <a href="/wiki/Drop_tower" title="Drop tower">tower</a> remained closed.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>At the time, Nichimura\'s family planned to sue the park for material and emotional damage,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and asked for <a href="/wiki/Brazilian_real" title="Brazilian real">R$</a> 4 million in compensation from Hopi Hari and <a href="/wiki/Brazilian_real" title="Brazilian real">R$</a> 1 million from <a href="/wiki/Vinhedo" title="Vinhedo">Vinhedo</a> City Hall.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>On 9 May 2012, the <a href="/w/index.php?title=Public_Prosecution_Service_of_the_State_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Public Prosecution Service of the State of São Paulo (page does not exist)">Public Prosecution Service</a> indicted 12 people for the accident, including then-president of the park Armando Pereira Filho.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The park attempted to reach a deal with the family.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In 2017, three employees were convicted of manslaughter, and sentenced to two years and eight months of community service and the payment of a minimum wage for a social entity. Another five employees were acquitted. The family and the park came to an undisclosed agreement.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Acordo&#95;4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Acordo-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Arq&#95;13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Arq-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>On 18 May 2017, the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Federal_Court" title="Supreme Federal Court">Supreme Federal Court</a> discontinued a lawsuit against former park President Armando Pereira Filho. The family received <a href="/wiki/Psychological_trauma" title="Psychological trauma">therapy</a> in the aftermath of the incident.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Arq&#95;13-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Arq-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Reopening">Reopening</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Death_of_Gabriela_Yukari_Nichimura&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Reopening"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>After changes in the drop tower,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-g1mudancas&#95;14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-g1mudancas-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> it was estimated to be back in August 2019,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> but in June 2019 the management decided against its reopening, due to the need for US$480,000 to recover the equipment and the realization of marketing.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="References">References</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a 2026-02-26 13:10:20 | INFO     | Scraping: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Reichelt
2026-02-26 13:10:21 | DEBUG    | Scraped content: ScrapedContent(url='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Reichelt', title='Franz Reichelt - Wikipedia', text='From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia French parachuting pioneer (1878–1912) Franz Reichelt Franz Reichelt wearing his parachute suit Born ( 1878-10-16 ) 16 October 1878 Wegstädtl , Kingdom of Bohemia , Austria-Hungary Died 4 February 1912 (1912-02-04) (aged\xa033) Paris , France Cause\xa0of death Parachute failure Occupations Inventor tailor Franz Reichelt (16 October 1878 – 4 February 1912), also known as Frantz Reichelt [ 1 ] or François Reichelt , was an Austro-Hungarian -born [ 2 ] French tailor , inventor and parachuting pioneer, now sometimes referred to as the Flying Tailor . He is remembered for jumping to his death from the Eiffel Tower while testing a wearable parachute of his own design, a device that today might be called a wingsuit . Reichelt had become fixated on developing a suit for aviators that would convert into a parachute and allow them to survive a fall should they be forced to leave their aircraft in mid-air. Initial experiments conducted with dummies dropped from the fifth floor of his apartment building had been successful, but he was unable to replicate those early successes with any of his subsequent designs. Believing that a suitably high test platform would prove his invention\'s efficacy, Reichelt repeatedly petitioned the Parisian Prefecture of Police for permission to conduct a test from the Eiffel Tower. He finally received permission in 1912, but when he arrived at the tower on 4 February he made it clear that he intended to jump personally rather than conduct an experiment with dummies. Despite attempts to dissuade him, he jumped from the first platform of the tower wearing his invention. The parachute failed to deploy and he plummeted 57 metres (187\xa0ft) to his death. The next day, newspapers were full of illustrated stories about the death of the "reckless inventor", and the jump was shown in newsreels. Early life [ edit ] Franz Reichelt was born on 16 October 1878 in Wegstädtl , Kingdom of Bohemia , Austria-Hungary (today Štětí, Czech Republic), and moved to Paris , France , in 1898. [ 3 ] He obtained French nationality in 1909, adopting the first name François (the French equivalent of the Germanic "Franz"). One of his sisters may have also come to France and been married to a jeweller there, [ 1 ] [ 4 ] but newspaper reports differed on the details of his family life, with most reporting that his sisters stayed in Vienna . Reichelt himself was unmarried. He took an apartment on the third floor at 8 rue Gaillon near the Avenue de l\' Opéra from 1907 and opened what was to become a successful dressmaking business, [ 5 ] catering mostly to Austrians on trips to Paris. [ 6 ] Experiments [ edit ] Illustration of the first parachute jump by Louis-Sébastien Lenormand from the tower of the Montpellier observatory in 1783. From July 1910, Reichelt began to develop a " parachute -suit": [ 3 ] a suit that was not much more bulky than one normally worn by an aviator, but with the addition of a few rods, a silk canopy and a small amount of rubber that allowed it to fold out to become what Reichelt hoped would be a practical and efficient parachute. The dawn of the aviation age brought inevitable accidents coupled with a growing interest in safety measures, most notably in the development of an effective parachute. Early parachuting successes, such as those of Louis-Sébastien Lenormand and Jean-Pierre Blanchard , had successfully used fixed-canopy parachutes (already "open" before the jump began), and André-Jacques Garnerin had invented a frameless parachute suitable for use from high altitudes, but by 1910 there was still no parachute suitable for use in jumping from a plane or at low altitude. Reichelt seems to have become interested in parachute design after hearing some of the stories of fatal accidents among the early aeronauts and aviators. His early tests were successful: dummies equipped with foldable silk "wings" touched down lightly when dropped from five floors, [ 4 ] but converting the prototypes into a wearable "suit" proved difficult. His original design used 6 square metres (65\xa0ft 2 ) of material and weighed around 70 kilograms (150\xa0lb). [ 1 ] He presented his design to the leading aeronautic organization, La Ligue Aérienne at the Aéro-Club de France , hoping that they would test it, but they rejected his designs on the grounds that the construction of the canopy was too weak and attempted to dissuade him from spending further time on development. [ 7 ] Reichelt nevertheless persevered and conducted experimental drops with dummies from the courtyard of his building at rue Gaillon. None of his tests proved successful. In 1911, a Colonel Lalance wrote to the Aéro-Club de France, offering a prize of 10,000 francs for a safety parachute for aviators\xa0– double the prize he had offered the year before. [ 8 ] [ note 1 ] The competition was open for three years and stipulated that the parachute must weigh no more than 25 kilograms (55\xa0lb). [ 8 ] Reichelt refined his design, reducing the weight while increasing the surface area of the material until it reached 12 square metres (130\xa0ft 2 ). [ 1 ] But his tests were still unsuccessful and his dummies invariably fell heavily to earth. L\'Ouest-Éclair reported in 1911 that Reichelt had personally jumped from a height of 8 to 10 metres (26 to 33\xa0ft) at Joinville ; the attempt failed but a pile of straw helped him escape injury. [ 10 ] Le Matin reported an attempt at Nogent from a height of 8 metres (26\xa0ft) that resulted in a broken leg. [ 7 ] Le Petit Journal suggested that Reichelt also made at least two apparently inconclusive tests with dummies from the first deck of the Eiffel Tower during 1911, [ 4 ] but an interview with one of his friends in La Presse made it clear that he had been unsuccessfully applying for permission to conduct a test from the tower for over a year before he finally received the authorization for the final jump. [ 5 ] There had been other tests from the tower during 1910 and 1911 though; Gaston Hervieu, who employed a dummy aircraft and mannequins in his experiments, was attempting to perfect a parachute design to ensure the safe landing of a pilot with all or part of a damaged aircraft. [ 11 ] Reichelt attributed the previous failures of his designs at least in part to the short drop distances over which he had conducted his tests, so he was keen to receive permission to experiment from the tower. [ 6 ] Eiffel Tower jump [ edit ] Reichelt showed off the suit at the foot of the Eiffel Tower shortly before his fatal fall. Reichelt announced to the press in early February 1912 that he had finally received permission and would shortly conduct an experiment from the Eiffel Tower to prove the value of his invention. On Sunday, 4 February, at 7:00 a.m., Reichelt arrived at the tower by car with two friends. He was already wearing his parachute suit. [ 5 ] The news footage of his jump shows him modelling his invention in its folded form, which Le Gaulois described as "only a little more voluminous than ordinary clothing." [ 6 ] The suit did not restrict the wearer\'s movements when the parachute was packed, and Le Petit Parisien described the method of deploying the parachute as being as simple as extending the arms out to form a cross with the body. [ 1 ] Once extended, the outfit resembled "a sort of cloak fitted with a vast hood of silk", according to Le Temps . [ 12 ] L\'Action Française reported that Reichelt stated the surface area of the final design to be 30 square metres (320\xa0ft 2 ) with a canopy height of 5 metres (16\xa0ft), [ 13 ] while Le Figaro judged the surface area might have reached 32 square metres (340\xa0ft 2 ). La Croix claimed that the suit may have weighed as little as 9 kilograms (20\xa0lb). [ 14 ] The weather was cold, with temperatures below 0\xa0°C (32\xa0°F), [ note 2 ] and there was a stiff breeze blowing across the Champ de Mars . [ 4 ] Some police officers were present to maintain order, as the Parisian Prefecture of Police had given Reichelt permission to proceed. After his death, Louis Lépine who, as the Prefect of Police, was ultimately responsible for the permission being granted, issued a statement making it clear that while the police routinely gave permission for experiments to be performed from the Eiffel Tower, it was understood in these cases that dummies would be used. They had given permission in Reichelt\'s case only on the basis that he would be conducting dummy drops, and that under no circumstances would they have allowed him to proceed if they had known he would be making the jump himself. [ 12 ] Lépine assured La Croix that he had never signed an order that allowed a live jump. [ 14 ] From his arrival at the tower, however, Reichelt made it clear that he intended to jump himself. According to a later interview with one of the friends who accompanied him up the tower, this was a surprise to everybody, as Reichelt had concealed his intention until the last moment. [ 12 ] His friends tried to persuade him to use dummies in the experiment, assuring him that he would have other opportunities to make the jump himself. When this failed to make an impression on him, they pointed to the strength of the wind and said he should call off the test on safety grounds, or at least delay until the wind dropped. They were unable to shake his resolve; [ 5 ] seemingly undeterred by the failure of his previous tests, he told journalists from Le Petit Journal that he was totally convinced that his apparatus would work, and work well. When questioned as to whether he planned to take any additional precautions, such as using a safety rope, he replied that he would not, since he intended to trust his life entirely to his parachute: I want to try the experiment myself and without trickery, as I intend to prove the worth of my invention. ( Je veux tenter l’expérience moi-même et sans chiqué, car je tiens à bien prouver la valeur de mon invention. ) [ 4 ] Hervieu, who was present to witness the demonstration, also attempted to dissuade Reichelt from making the jump. He was concerned that the parachute needed longer to fully open than the few seconds the drop from the first platform would allow, and he also presented other technical objections to which Reichelt could not provide a satisfactory response. [ 15 ] Reichelt finally replied that: You are going to see how my seventy-two kilos [159 pounds] and my parachute will give your arguments the most decisive of denials. ( Vous allez voir comment mes soixante-douze kilos et mon parachute vont donner à vos arguments le plus décisif des démentis. ) [ 15 ] Reichelt\'s jump and fall, his body being removed, and measurement of the hollow created by the impact were captured on film. Ropes had been suspended between the legs of the tower by the police at Reichelt\'s request to prevent the crowds from spilling onto the landing zone, and he spent some time discussing the arrangements with the marshals and ensuring that there was sufficient space for his landing before going to the stairs to climb to the first platform. [ 6 ] [ 15 ] According to Le Petit Parisien , Reichelt\'s initial attempt to ascend to the first stage of the tower was blocked by a guard named Gassion, who had witnessed previous unsuccessful dummy drops and feared that Reichelt\'s attempt would end in disaster, though Le Figaro reported that he had merely not received a copy of the order and had to wait for telephone confirmation from his superiors. Despite the guard\'s resistance, by 8:00 a.m. the matter had been resolved: Reichelt, who was visibly shaken by his argument with the guard, was allowed to mount the tower with his two friends and a cinematographer (another was stationed near the foot of the tower to record the jump from below). As Reichelt climbed the stairs he paused, turned back to the crowd, raised his hand and wished them a cheery, "See you soon!" [ 15 ] His friends continued to try to talk him out of the jump, but he remained undeterred. [ 5 ] At 8:22 a.m., observed by a crowd of about thirty journalists and curious onlookers, Reichelt readied himself – facing towards the Seine – on a stool placed on a restaurant table next to the interior guardrail of the tower\'s first deck, a little more than 57 metres (187\xa0ft) above the ground. After adjusting his apparatus with the assistance of his friends and checking the wind direction by throwing a piece of paper taken from a small book, [ 13 ] he placed one foot on the guardrail, hesitated for about forty seconds, then leapt outwards. According to Le Figaro , he was calm and smiling just before he jumped. [ 15 ] His parachute, which had seemed to be only half-open, folded around him almost immediately and he fell for a few seconds before striking the frozen soil at the foot of the tower. Le Petit Parisien reported that Reichelt\'s right leg and arm were crushed, his skull and spine broken, and that he was bleeding from his mouth, nose and ears. Le Figaro noted that his eyes were wide open and dilated. He was already dead by the time onlookers rushed to his body, but he was taken to the Necker Hospital where he was officially pronounced dead, and then on to a police station in the rue Amélie before being returned to his home in rue Gaillon. Édouard Launet, writing in the Summer supplement of Libération in 2009, mentioned that an autopsy concluded that Reichelt had died of a heart attack during his fall. [ 3 ] Aftermath [ edit ] The Prefect of Police, Louis Lépine, denied that Reichelt had been authorized to make a "live" jump. The next day\'s newspapers were full of the story of Reichelt\'s "tragic experiment", complete with photographs; [ 3 ] at least four newspapers, Le Petit Parisien , Le Matin , La Croix and L\'Humanité , [ note 3 ] showed images of the fatal jump. Film of the attempt, including footage of Reichelt\'s body being removed and the onlookers measuring the depth of the crater left by his impact (15 centimetres; 5.9 in [ 4 ] ), was distributed by news organizations. Initial reports speculated on Reichelt\'s state of mind: none assumed he had been suicidal, but many called him discombobulated in the brain. A journalist in Le Gaulois suggested that only half the term "mad genius" applied to Reichelt – although the same report included an interview with one of his friends, who claimed that the tailor had felt pressured into giving a dramatic demonstration to attract sponsors, without whom he could not expect to make a profit before any patent expired. [ 3 ] [ 6 ] Reichelt\'s death was the first to result from a parachuting accident since Charles Leroux died giving a demonstration in Tallinn in 1889. [ 16 ] In fact, on 2 February 1912 – two days prior to Reichelt\'s fatal jump – an American steeplejack , Frederick R. Law , had successfully parachuted from the viewing platform of the torch of the Statue of Liberty (223 feet (68\xa0m) above sea level and 151 feet (46\xa0m) from the base of the statue), seemingly on a whim. [ 17 ] On 6 February, La Croix added a footnote to the report on Reichelt\'s death: another parachuting experiment was to take place on 18 or 25 February at Port-Aviation (often called "Juvisy Airfield") in Viry-Châtillon (often misidentified as Juvisy-sur-Orge ), in which the aviator Camille Guillaume planned to leap from his Blériot monoplane at a height of 300 metres (980\xa0ft) to test a parachute design (the plane would be allowed to crash). [ 14 ] Le Petit Parisien and other newspapers carried pictures of Reichelt\'s fatal fall on their front pages the next day. After Reichelt\'s death, authorities became wary of granting permission for any further parachute experiments using the Eiffel Tower . [ 18 ] Though they continued to grant permissions for parachute dummy drops, [ 19 ] [ 20 ] some hopeful inventors – such as a man named Damblanc, who wished to try his "helicopter parachute" from the second platform – were refused permission to conduct tests, [ 18 ] and even applications for aviation experiments not involving the tower came under renewed scrutiny. More recently, the tower has become the scene of a number of illicit base jumps . A Norwegian man died in 2005 after losing his canopy while attempting a promotional jump for a clothing firm – the first parachuting death at the tower since Reichelt. A sanctioned stunt jump for the 1985 James Bond film A View to a Kill was successful. [ 21 ] Reichelt came momentarily to prominence again in the 1940s in the United States, when his likeness was claimed as the model for one of the figures that were "strangely un-American in expression and garb" in the WPA -funded mural at Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn , New York . [ 22 ] In an incident reminiscent of the 1933 controversy over Diego Rivera \'s Man at the Crossroads mural at Rockefeller Center , a furor erupted over an image depicting two minor leftist aviators, supposedly flanking a central portrait of Joseph Stalin . The WPA already had an unwanted reputation as being sympathetic to the left, and despite the artist August Henkel \'s "glib" explanation of the "accidental" inclusion of a Soviet red star and his claim that the image identified as Stalin was actually of Reichelt, the murals were taken down and three of the four panels burned. [ 23 ] The story of Reichelt\'s misadventure was also the subject of a 1993 French short film , Le Tailleur Autrichien , written and directed by Pablo Lopez Paredes and starring Bruce Myers in the title role. Although there were no viable parachuting solutions for use in aeroplanes when Reichelt began developing his suit, a patent for a packable parachute had been applied for by Gleb Kotelnikov . [ note 4 ] In popular culture [ edit ] Reichelt\'s jump is retold in the novel Chasing the Black Eagle by Canadian author Bruce Geddes. ol>li:first-child::before,.mw-parser-output .hlist dt ol>li:first-child::before,.mw-parser-output .hlist li ol>li:first-child::before{content:" ("counter(listitem)"\\a0 "}</style><div class="hlist">\n<ul><li><a href="/wiki/Inventor" class="mw-redirect" title="Inventor">Inventor</a></li>\n<li>tailor</li></ul>\n</div></td></tr></tbody></table>\n<p><b>Franz Reichelt</b> (16 October 1878 – 4 February 1912), also known as <b>Frantz Reichelt</b><sup id="cite&#95;ref-PP&#95;1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PP-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> or <b>François Reichelt</b>, was an <a href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austro-Hungarian</a>-born<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Yahoo&#95;News&#95;UK&#95;2014&#95;2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Yahoo_News_UK_2014-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> French <a href="/wiki/Tailor" title="Tailor">tailor</a>, inventor and <a href="/wiki/Parachuting" title="Parachuting">parachuting</a> pioneer, now sometimes referred to as the <b>Flying Tailor</b>. He is remembered for jumping to his death from the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a> while testing a wearable <a href="/wiki/Parachute" title="Parachute">parachute</a> of his own design, a device that today might be called a <a href="/wiki/Wingsuit_flying" title="Wingsuit flying">wingsuit</a>. Reichelt had become fixated on developing a suit for aviators that would convert into a parachute and allow them to survive a fall should they be forced to leave their aircraft in mid-air. Initial experiments conducted with dummies dropped from the fifth floor of his apartment building had been successful, but he was unable to replicate those early successes with any of his subsequent designs.\n</p><p>Believing that a suitably high test platform would prove his invention\'s efficacy, Reichelt repeatedly petitioned the Parisian <a href="/wiki/Prefecture_of_Police" title="Prefecture of Police">Prefecture of Police</a> for permission to conduct a test from the Eiffel Tower. He finally received permission in 1912, but when he arrived at the tower on 4<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>February he made it clear that he intended to jump personally rather than conduct an experiment with dummies. Despite attempts to dissuade him, he jumped from the first platform of the tower wearing his invention. The parachute failed to deploy and he plummeted 57 metres (187&#160;ft) to his death. The next day, newspapers were full of illustrated stories about the death of the "reckless inventor", and the jump was shown in newsreels.\n</p>\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Early_life">Early life</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Early life"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Franz Reichelt was born on 16 October 1878 in <a href="/wiki/%C5%A0t%C4%9Bt%C3%AD" title="Štětí">Wegstädtl</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bohemia" title="Kingdom of Bohemia">Kingdom of Bohemia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</a> (today Štětí, Czech Republic), and moved to <a href="/wiki/Paris" title="Paris">Paris</a>, <a href="/wiki/French_Third_Republic" title="French Third Republic">France</a>, in 1898.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lib&#95;3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lib-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> He obtained French nationality in 1909, adopting the first name François (the French equivalent of the Germanic "Franz"). One of his sisters may have also come to France and been married to a jeweller there,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PP&#95;1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PP-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> but newspaper reports differed on the details of his family life, with most reporting that his sisters stayed in <a href="/wiki/Vienna" title="Vienna">Vienna</a>. Reichelt himself was unmarried. He took an apartment on the third floor at 8 rue Gaillon near the Avenue de l\'<a href="/wiki/Palais_Garnier" title="Palais Garnier">Opéra</a> from 1907 and opened what was to become a successful <a href="/wiki/Dressmaking" class="mw-redirect" title="Dressmaking">dressmaking</a> business,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LP&#95;5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LP-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> catering mostly to Austrians on trips to Paris.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LG&#95;6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LG-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Experiments">Experiments</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Experiments"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Early_flight_02561u_(3).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A man leaping from a tower." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg/250px-Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="279" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg/330px-Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg/500px-Early_flight_02561u_%283%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2239" data-file-height="3292" /></a><figcaption>Illustration of the first parachute jump by <a href="/wiki/Louis-S%C3%A9bastien_Lenormand" title="Louis-Sébastien Lenormand">Louis-Sébastien Lenormand</a> from the tower of the <a href="/wiki/Montpellier" title="Montpellier">Montpellier</a> observatory in 1783.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>From July 1910, Reichelt began to develop a "<a href="/wiki/Parachute" title="Parachute">parachute</a>-suit":<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lib&#95;3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lib-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> a suit that was not much more bulky than one normally worn by an aviator, but with the addition of a few rods, a silk canopy and a small amount of rubber that allowed it to fold out to become what Reichelt hoped would be a practical and efficient parachute.\n</p><p>The dawn of the aviation age brought inevitable accidents coupled with a growing interest in safety measures, most notably in the development of an effective parachute. Early parachuting successes, such as those of <a href="/wiki/Louis-S%C3%A9bastien_Lenormand" title="Louis-Sébastien Lenormand">Louis-Sébastien Lenormand</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Blanchard" title="Jean-Pierre Blanchard">Jean-Pierre Blanchard</a>, had successfully used fixed-canopy parachutes (already "open" before the jump began), and <a href="/wiki/Andr%C3%A9-Jacques_Garnerin" title="André-Jacques Garnerin">André-Jacques Garnerin</a> had invented a frameless parachute suitable for use from high altitudes, but by 1910 there was still no parachute suitable for use in jumping from a plane or at low altitude. \n</p><p>Reichelt seems to have become interested in parachute design after hearing some of the stories of fatal accidents among the early aeronauts and aviators. His early tests were successful: dummies equipped with foldable silk "wings" touched down lightly when dropped from five floors,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> but converting the <a href="/wiki/Prototype" title="Prototype">prototypes</a> into a wearable "suit" proved difficult. His original design used 6 square metres (65&#160;ft<sup>2</sup>) of material and weighed around 70 kilograms (150&#160;lb).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PP&#95;1-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PP-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> He presented his design to the leading aeronautic organization, <i>La Ligue Aérienne</i> at the <a href="/wiki/A%C3%A9ro-Club_de_France" title="Aéro-Club de France">Aéro-Club de France</a>, hoping that they would test it, but they rejected his designs on the grounds that the construction of the canopy was too weak and attempted to dissuade him from spending further time on development.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LM&#95;7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LM-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Reichelt nevertheless persevered and conducted experimental drops with dummies from the courtyard of his building at rue Gaillon. None of his tests proved successful.\n</p><p>In 1911, a Colonel Lalance wrote to the Aéro-Club de France, offering a prize of 10,000 francs for a safety parachute for aviators&#160;&#8211;&#32;double the prize he had offered the year before.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FM&#95;8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FM-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>note 1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The competition was open for three years and stipulated that the parachute must weigh no more than 25 kilograms (55&#160;lb).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FM&#95;8-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FM-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Reichelt refined his design, reducing the weight while increasing the surface area of the material until it reached 12 square metres (130&#160;ft<sup>2</sup>).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PP&#95;1-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PP-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> But his tests were still unsuccessful and his dummies invariably fell heavily to earth. \n</p><p><i><a href="/wiki/L%27Ouest-%C3%89clair" title="L&#39;Ouest-Éclair">L\'Ouest-Éclair</a></i> reported in 1911 that Reichelt had personally jumped from a height of 8 to 10 metres (26 to 33&#160;ft) at <a href="/wiki/Joinville,_Haute-Marne" title="Joinville, Haute-Marne">Joinville</a>; the attempt failed but a pile of straw helped him escape injury.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-OE&#95;11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-OE-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Matin_(France)" title="Le Matin (France)">Le Matin</a></i> reported an attempt at <a href="/wiki/Nogent,_Haute-Marne" title="Nogent, Haute-Marne">Nogent</a> from a height of 8 metres (26&#160;ft) that resulted in a broken leg.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LM&#95;7-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LM-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Petit_Journal_(newspaper)" title="Le Petit Journal (newspaper)">Le Petit Journal</a></i> suggested that Reichelt also made at least two apparently inconclusive tests with dummies from the first deck of the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a> during 1911,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> but an interview with one of his friends in <i><a href="/wiki/La_Presse_(French_newspaper)" title="La Presse (French newspaper)">La Presse</a></i> made it clear that he had been unsuccessfully applying for permission to conduct a test from the tower for over a year before he finally received the authorization for the final jump.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LP&#95;5-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LP-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>There had been other tests from the tower during 1910 and 1911 though; Gaston Hervieu, who employed a dummy aircraft and <a href="/wiki/Mannequin" title="Mannequin">mannequins</a> in his experiments, was attempting to perfect a parachute design to ensure the safe landing of a pilot with all or part of a damaged aircraft.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-F&#95;12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-F-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Reichelt attributed the previous failures of his designs at least in part to the short drop distances over which he had conducted his tests, so he was keen to receive permission to experiment from the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LG&#95;6-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LG-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div style="clear:both;" class=""></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Eiffel_Tower_jump">Eiffel Tower jump</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Eiffel Tower jump"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Parachutespringen,_SFA022812154.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg/250px-Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="272" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg/330px-Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg/500px-Parachutespringen%2C_SFA022812154.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2481" data-file-height="3555" /></a><figcaption>Reichelt showed off the suit at the foot of the Eiffel Tower shortly before his fatal fall.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Reichelt announced to the press in early February 1912 that he had finally received permission and would shortly conduct an experiment from the Eiffel Tower to prove the value of his invention.\n</p><p>On Sunday, 4 February, at 7:00 a.m., Reichelt arrived at the tower by car with two friends. He was already wearing his parachute suit.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LP&#95;5-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LP-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The news footage of his jump shows him modelling his invention in its folded form, which <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Gaulois" title="Le Gaulois">Le Gaulois</a></i> described as "only a little more voluminous than ordinary clothing."<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LG&#95;6-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LG-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The suit did not restrict the wearer\'s movements when the parachute was packed, and <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Petit_Parisien" title="Le Petit Parisien">Le Petit Parisien</a></i> described the method of deploying the parachute as being as simple as extending the arms out to form a cross with the body.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PP&#95;1-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PP-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Once extended, the outfit resembled "a sort of cloak fitted with a vast hood of silk", according to <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Temps_(Paris)" title="Le Temps (Paris)">Le Temps</a></i>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LT&#95;13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LT-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/L%27Action_Fran%C3%A7aise" class="mw-redirect" title="L&#39;Action Française">L\'Action Française</a></i> reported that Reichelt stated the surface area of the final design to be 30 square metres (320&#160;ft<sup>2</sup>) with a canopy height of 5 metres (16&#160;ft),<sup id="cite&#95;ref-AF&#95;14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AF-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> while <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Figaro" title="Le Figaro">Le Figaro</a></i> judged the surface area might have reached 32 square metres (340&#160;ft<sup>2</sup>). <i><a href="/wiki/La_Croix_(newspaper)" title="La Croix (newspaper)">La Croix</a></i> claimed that the suit may have weighed as little as 9 kilograms (20&#160;lb).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LC&#95;15-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LC-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The weather was cold, with temperatures below 0&#160;°C (32&#160;°F),<sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>note 2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and there was a stiff breeze blowing across the <a href="/wiki/Champ_de_Mars,_Paris" class="mw-redirect" title="Champ de Mars, Paris">Champ de Mars</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Some police officers were present to maintain order, as the Parisian <a href="/wiki/Prefecture_of_Police" title="Prefecture of Police">Prefecture of Police</a> had given Reichelt permission to proceed. After his death, <a href="/wiki/Louis_L%C3%A9pine" title="Louis Lépine">Louis Lépine</a> who, as the Prefect of Police, was ultimately responsible for the permission being granted, issued a statement making it clear that while the police routinely gave permission for experiments to be performed from the Eiffel Tower, it was understood in these cases that dummies would be used. They had given permission in Reichelt\'s case only on the basis that he would be conducting dummy drops, and that under no circumstances would they have allowed him to proceed if they had known he would be making the jump himself.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LT&#95;13-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LT-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Lépine assured <i>La Croix</i> that he had never signed an order that allowed a live jump.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LC&#95;15-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LC-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> \n</p><p>From his arrival at the tower, however, Reichelt made it clear that he intended to jump himself. According to a later interview with one of the friends who accompanied him up the tower, this was a surprise to everybody, as Reichelt had concealed his intention until the last moment.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LT&#95;13-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LT-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> His friends tried to persuade him to use dummies in the experiment, assuring him that he would have other opportunities to make the jump himself. When this failed to make an impression on him, they pointed to the strength of the wind and said he should call off the test on safety grounds, or at least delay until the wind dropped. They were unable to shake his resolve;<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LP&#95;5-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LP-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> seemingly undeterred by the failure of his previous tests, he told journalists from <i>Le Petit Journal</i> that he was totally convinced that his apparatus would work, and work well. When questioned as to whether he planned to take any additional precautions, such as using a safety rope, he replied that he would not, since he intended to trust his life entirely to his parachute:\n</p>\n<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1244412712">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 32px}.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;margin-top:0}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{padding-left:1.6em}}</style><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>I want to try the experiment myself and without trickery, as I intend to prove the worth of my invention. (<span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr">Je veux tenter l’expérience moi-même et sans chiqué, car je tiens à bien prouver la valeur de mon invention.</i></span>)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></p></blockquote>\n<p>Hervieu, who was present to witness the demonstration, also attempted to dissuade Reichelt from making the jump. He was concerned that the parachute needed longer to fully open than the few seconds the drop from the first platform would allow, and he also presented other technical objections to which Reichelt could not provide a satisfactory response.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LF&#95;17-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LF-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Reichelt finally replied that:\n</p>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1244412712" /><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>You are going to see how my seventy-two kilos [159 pounds] and my parachute will give your arguments the most decisive of denials. (<span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr">Vous allez voir comment mes soixante-douze kilos et mon parachute vont donner à vos arguments le plus décisif des démentis.</i></span>)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LF&#95;17-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LF-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></p></blockquote>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_0" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv/250px--Reichelt.ogv.jpg" controls="" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" class="mw-file-element" width="250" height="188" data-durationhint="106" data-mwtitle="Reichelt.ogv" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:Reichelt.ogv"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv" type="video/ogg; codecs=&quot;theora&quot;" data-width="1200" data-height="900" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv/Reichelt.ogv.480p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="480p.vp9.webm" data-width="640" data-height="480" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv/Reichelt.ogv.144p.mjpeg.mov" type="video/quicktime" data-transcodekey="144p.mjpeg.mov" data-width="192" data-height="144" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv/Reichelt.ogv.240p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="240p.vp9.webm" data-width="320" data-height="240" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ea/Reichelt.ogv/Reichelt.ogv.360p.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8, vorbis&quot;" data-transcodekey="360p.webm" data-width="480" data-height="360" /></video></span><figcaption>Reichelt\'s jump and fall, his body being removed, and measurement of the hollow created by the impact were captured on film.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Ropes had been suspended between the legs of the tower by the police at Reichelt\'s request to prevent the crowds from spilling onto the landing zone, and he spent some time discussing the arrangements with the marshals and ensuring that there was sufficient space for his landing before going to the stairs to climb to the first platform.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LG&#95;6-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LG-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-LF&#95;17-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LF-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>According to <i>Le Petit Parisien</i>, Reichelt\'s initial attempt to ascend to the first stage of the tower was blocked by a guard named Gassion, who had witnessed previous unsuccessful dummy drops and feared that Reichelt\'s attempt would end in disaster, though <i>Le Figaro</i> reported that he had merely not received a copy of the order and had to wait for telephone confirmation from his superiors. Despite the guard\'s resistance, by 8:00 a.m. the matter had been resolved: Reichelt, who was visibly shaken by his argument with the guard, was allowed to mount the tower with his two friends and a <a href="/wiki/Cinematographer" title="Cinematographer">cinematographer</a> (another was stationed near the foot of the tower to record the jump from below). As Reichelt climbed the stairs he paused, turned back to the crowd, raised his hand and wished them a cheery, "See you soon!"<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LF&#95;17-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LF-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> His friends continued to try to talk him out of the jump, but he remained undeterred.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LP&#95;5-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LP-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> \n</p><p>At 8:22 a.m., observed by a crowd of about thirty journalists and curious onlookers, Reichelt readied himself – facing towards the <a href="/wiki/Seine" title="Seine">Seine</a> – on a stool placed on a restaurant table next to the interior guardrail of the tower\'s first deck, a little more than 57 metres (187&#160;ft) above the ground. After adjusting his apparatus with the assistance of his friends and checking the wind direction by throwing a piece of paper taken from a small book,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-AF&#95;14-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AF-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> he placed one foot on the guardrail, hesitated for about forty seconds, then leapt outwards. According to <i>Le Figaro</i>, he was calm and smiling just before he jumped.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LF&#95;17-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LF-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> His parachute, which had seemed to be only half-open, folded around him almost immediately and he fell for a few seconds before striking the frozen soil at the foot of the tower.\n</p><p><i>Le Petit Parisien</i> reported that Reichelt\'s right leg and arm were crushed, his skull and spine broken, and that he was bleeding from his mouth, nose and ears. <i>Le Figaro</i> noted that his eyes were wide open and dilated. He was already dead by the time onlookers rushed to his body, but he was taken to the <a href="/wiki/Necker-Enfants_Malades_Hospital" class="mw-redirect" title="Necker-Enfants Malades Hospital">Necker Hospital</a> where he was officially pronounced dead, and then on to a police station in the rue Amélie before being returned to his home in rue Gaillon. Édouard Launet, writing in the Summer supplement of <i><a href="/wiki/Lib%C3%A9ration" title="Libération">Libération</a></i> in 2009, mentioned that an <a href="/wiki/Autopsy" title="Autopsy">autopsy</a> concluded that Reichelt had died of a heart attack during his fall.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lib&#95;3-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lib-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Aftermath">Aftermath</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Aftermath"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Louis Lépine" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg/250px-Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="260" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg/330px-Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg/500px-Louis_L%C3%A9pine.jpg 2x" data-file-width="747" data-file-height="1024" /></a><figcaption> The Prefect of Police, Louis Lépine, denied that Reichelt had been authorized to make a "live" jump.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>The next day\'s newspapers were full of the story of Reichelt\'s "tragic experiment", complete with photographs;<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lib&#95;3-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lib-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> at least four newspapers, <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Petit_Parisien" title="Le Petit Parisien">Le Petit Parisien</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Matin_(France)" title="Le Matin (France)">Le Matin</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/La_Croix_(newspaper)" title="La Croix (newspaper)">La Croix</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/L%27Humanit%C3%A9" title="L&#39;Humanité">L\'Humanité</a></i>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>note 3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> showed images of the fatal jump. Film of the attempt, including footage of Reichelt\'s body being removed and the onlookers measuring the depth of the <a href="/wiki/Impact_crater" title="Impact crater">crater left by his impact</a> (15 centimetres; 5.9 in<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PJ&#95;4-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PJ-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>), was distributed by news organizations. \n</p><p>Initial reports speculated on Reichelt\'s state of mind: none assumed he had been suicidal, but many called him discombobulated in the brain. A journalist in <i><a href="/wiki/Le_Gaulois" title="Le Gaulois">Le Gaulois</a></i> suggested that only half the term "mad genius" applied to Reichelt – although the same report included an interview with one of his friends, who claimed that the tailor had felt pressured into giving a dramatic demonstration to attract sponsors, without whom he could not expect to make a profit before any <a href="/wiki/Patent" title="Patent">patent</a> expired.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-lib&#95;3-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lib-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-LG&#95;6-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LG-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Reichelt\'s death was the first to result from a parachuting accident since <a href="/wiki/Charles_Leroux" title="Charles Leroux">Charles Leroux</a> died giving a demonstration in <a href="/wiki/Tallinn" title="Tallinn">Tallinn</a> in 1889.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FI&#95;19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FI-19"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In fact, on 2 February 1912 – two days prior to Reichelt\'s fatal jump – an American <a href="/wiki/Steeplejack" title="Steeplejack">steeplejack</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rodman_Law" title="Rodman Law">Frederick R. Law</a>, had successfully parachuted from the viewing platform of the torch of the <a href="/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty" title="Statue of Liberty">Statue of Liberty</a> (223 feet (68&#160;m) above sea level and 151 feet (46&#160;m) from the base of the statue), seemingly on a whim.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-NYT&#95;20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On 6 February, <i>La Croix</i> added a footnote to the report on Reichelt\'s death: another parachuting experiment was to take place on 18 or 25 February at <a href="/wiki/Port-Aviation" title="Port-Aviation">Port-Aviation</a> (often called "Juvisy Airfield") in <a href="/wiki/Viry-Ch%C3%A2tillon" title="Viry-Châtillon">Viry-Châtillon</a> (often misidentified as <a href="/wiki/Juvisy-sur-Orge" title="Juvisy-sur-Orge">Juvisy-sur-Orge</a>), in which the aviator Camille Guillaume planned to leap from his <a href="/wiki/Bl%C3%A9riot_A%C3%A9ronautique" title="Blériot Aéronautique">Blériot</a> monoplane at a height of 300 metres (980&#160;ft) to test a parachute design (the plane would be allowed to crash).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-LC&#95;15-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LC-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Franz_Reichelt.png" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Newspaper photo montage" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Franz_Reichelt.png/250px-Franz_Reichelt.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="268" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Franz_Reichelt.png/500px-Franz_Reichelt.png 1.5x" data-file-width="1095" data-file-height="1174" /></a><figcaption><i>Le Petit Parisien</i> and other newspapers carried pictures of Reichelt\'s fatal fall on their front pages the next day.</figcaption></figure>\n<p>After Reichelt\'s death, authorities became wary of granting permission for any further parachute experiments using the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FM2&#95;21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FM2-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Though they continued to grant permissions for parachute dummy drops,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-NYT2&#95;22-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT2-22"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-FM3&#95;23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FM3-23"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> some hopeful inventors – such as a man named Damblanc, who wished to try his "helicopter parachute" from the second platform – were refused permission to conduct tests,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FM2&#95;21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FM2-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and even applications for aviation experiments not involving the tower came under renewed scrutiny. More recently, the tower has become the scene of a number of illicit <a href="/wiki/BASE_jumping" title="BASE jumping">base jumps</a>. A Norwegian man died in 2005 after losing his <a href="/wiki/Canopy_(parachute)" class="mw-redirect" title="Canopy (parachute)">canopy</a> while attempting a promotional jump for a clothing firm – the first parachuting death at the tower since Reichelt. A sanctioned stunt jump for the 1985 James Bond film <i><a href="/wiki/A_View_to_a_Kill" title="A View to a Kill">A View to a Kill</a></i> was successful.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Reichelt came momentarily to prominence again in the 1940s in the United States, when his likeness was claimed as the model for one of the figures that were "strangely un-American in expression and garb" in the <a href="/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration" title="Works Progress Administration">WPA</a>-funded mural at <a href="/wiki/Floyd_Bennett_Field" title="Floyd Bennett Field">Floyd Bennett Field</a> in <a href="/wiki/Brooklyn" title="Brooklyn">Brooklyn</a>, <a href="/wiki/New_York_(state)" title="New York (state)">New York</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In an incident reminiscent of the 1933 controversy over <a href="/wiki/Diego_Rivera" title="Diego Rivera">Diego Rivera</a>\'s <i><a href="/wiki/Man_at_the_Crossroads" title="Man at the Crossroads">Man at the Crossroads</a></i> mural at <a href="/wiki/Rockefeller_Center" title="Rockefeller Center">Rockefeller Center</a>, a furor erupted over an image depicting two minor <a href="/wiki/Left-wing_politics" title="Left-wing politics">leftist</a> aviators, supposedly flanking a central portrait of <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Stalin" title="Joseph Stalin">Joseph Stalin</a>. The WPA already had an unwanted reputation as being sympathetic to the left, and despite the artist <a href="/wiki/August_Henkel" title="August Henkel">August Henkel</a>\'s "glib" explanation of the "accidental" inclusion of a Soviet <a href="/wiki/Red_star" title="Red star">red star</a> and his claim that the image identified as Stalin was actually of Reichelt, the murals were taken down and three of the four panels burned.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Time&#95;26-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Time-26"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The story of Reichelt\'s misadventure was also the subject of a 1993 French <a href="/wiki/Short_film" title="Short film">short film</a>, <span title="French-language text"><i lang="fr">Le Tailleur Autrichien</i></span>, written and directed by Pablo Lopez Paredes and starring <a href="/wiki/Bruce_Myers_(actor)" title="Bruce Myers (actor)">Bruce Myers</a> in the title role.\n</p><p>Although there were no viable parachuting solutions for use in aeroplanes when Reichelt began developing his suit, a patent for a packable parachute had been applied for by <a href="/wiki/Gleb_Kotelnikov" title="Gleb Kotelnikov">Gleb Kotelnikov</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>note 4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_popular_culture">In popular culture</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: In popular culture"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Reichelt\'s jump is retold in the novel <i>Chasing the Black Eagle</i> by Canadian author Bruce Geddes.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (November 2025)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Franz_Reichelt&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: See also"><span>edit</span></a><span by their own inventions">List of inventors killed by their own inventions</a></li>\n<li><a href="/wiki/List_of_unusual_deaths_in_the_20th_century" title="List of unusual deaths in the 20th century">List of unusual deaths in the 20th century</a></li></ul>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Notes">Notes</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span div.reflist-liststyle-lower-roman .references{list-style-type:lower-roman}</style><div>\n<div class="mw-references-wrap"><ol class="references" data-mw-group="note">\n<li id="cite&#95;note-10"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-10">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">The prize was eventually presented to <a href="/w/index.php?title=Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bonnet&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Frédéric Bonnet (page does not exist)">Frédéric Bonnet</a> in 1913.<sup
