[ 3 ] Main contractor Takenaka Corporation [ 1 ] Website en .tokyotower .co .jp Tokyo Tower ( 東京タワー , Tōkyō Tawā ; pronounced [toːkʲoː taꜜɰᵝaː] ⓘ ) , a.k.a. Japan Radio Tower ( 日本電波塔 , Nippon denpatō ) is a communications and observation tower in the district of Shiba-koen in Minato, Tokyo , Japan, completed in 1958. At 332.9 metres (1,092 feet), it was the tallest tower in Japan until the construction of Tokyo Skytree in 2012. It is a lattice tower inspired by the Eiffel Tower , and is painted white and international orange to comply with air safety regulations. The tower\'s main sources of income are antenna leasing and tourism, and its five-story base building FootTown houses a number of restaurants, gift shops, and other attractions. Departing from it, guests can visit two observation decks: the two-story Main Deck at 150\xa0m (490\xa0ft), and the smaller Top Deck at 249.6\xa0m (819\xa0ft). The tower is repainted every five years, the process itself taking a year to complete. In 1961, transmission antennas were added. They are used for radio and television broadcasting and now broadcast signals for media outlets such as NHK , TBS Television , and Fuji Television . The height of the tower was not suitable for Japan\'s planned terrestrial digital broadcasting planned for July 2011, and for the Tokyo area. A taller digital broadcasting tower, known as Tokyo Skytree , was completed on 29 February 2012. Tokyo Tower has become a prominent landmark and frequently appears in media set in Tokyo. Construction [ edit ] Construction underway on 25 February 1958 Tokyo Tower around 1961 A large broadcasting tower was needed in the Kantō region after NHK , Japan\'s public broadcasting station, began television broadcasting in 1953. Private broadcasting companies began operating in the months following the construction of NHK\'s own transmission tower. This communications boom led the Japanese government to believe that transmission towers would soon be built all over Tokyo, eventually overrunning the city. The proposed solution was the construction of one large tower capable of transmitting to the entire region. [ 4 ] Furthermore, because of the country\'s postwar boom in the 1950s, Japan was searching for a monument to symbolize its national recovery from World War II , as one of the countries most ravaged by the war. [ 5 ] [ 6 ] Hisakichi Maeda, founder and president of Nippon Denpatō, the tower\'s owner and operator, originally planned for the tower to be taller than the Empire State Building , which at 381\xa0m (1,250\xa0ft) was the highest structure in the world at the time. However, the plan fell through because of the lack of both funds and materials. The tower\'s height was eventually determined by the distance the TV stations needed to transmit throughout the Kantō region, a distance of about 150 kilometres (93 miles). [ 4 ] Tachū Naitō , designer of tall buildings in Japan, was chosen to design the newly proposed tower. [ 4 ] Looking to the Western world for inspiration, Naitō based his design on the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France. [ 7 ] With the help of engineering company Nikken Sekkei Ltd., Naitō claimed his design could withstand earthquakes with twice the intensity of the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake or typhoons with wind speeds of up to 220\xa0km/h (140\xa0mph). [ 4 ] The new construction project attracted hundreds of tobi ( 鳶 ), traditional Japanese construction workers who specialized in the construction of high-rise structures. The Takenaka Corporation broke ground in June 1957 and each day at least 400\xa0laborers worked on the tower. [ 4 ] It was constructed of steel , a third of which was scrap metal taken from US tanks damaged in the Korean War . [ 8 ] [ 9 ] When the 90-metre (300\xa0ft)-long antenna was bolted into place on 14 October 1958, Tokyo Tower was the tallest freestanding tower in the world, taking the title from the Eiffel Tower by 9\xa0m (30\xa0ft). [ 10 ] [ failed verification ] Though physically taller than the Eiffel Tower, Tokyo Tower weighs about 4,000\xa0tons, 3,300 less than the Eiffel Tower [ 11 ] as it is significantly thinner and simpler in construction. It was opened to the public on 23 December 1958 at a final cost of ¥ 2.8 billion ($8.4 million in 1958). [ 9 ] [ 12 ] Tokyo Tower was mortgaged for ¥10\xa0billion in 2000. [ 13 ] It was the tallest artificial structure in Japan until April 2012, when it was surpassed by the Tokyo Skytree . [ 7 ] Planned as an antenna for telecommunications and brightly colored in accordance with the time\'s Aviation Law, the tower\'s two panoramic observatories are mostly frequented by tourists today. The tower constitutes a clear reference point in the center\'s skyline, forming a strong landmark, both night and day. [ 14 ] The tower is periodically repainted in a process that takes about a year to complete. [ 15 ] [ 16 ] This traditionally occurred every five years, but the latest painting in 2019 utilized a new, more durable coating that extended the official timetable to seven years, projecting the next painting for 2026. [ 17 ] Functions [ edit ] The Top Deck, located directly below the tower\'s digital television broadcasting equipment Tokyo Tower\'s two main revenue sources are antenna leasing and tourism. It functions as a radio and television broadcasting antenna support structure and is a tourist destination that houses a variety of attractions. The tower recorded its 190\xa0millionth visitor in 2024. [ 18 ] Previously, visitor numbers had steadily declined in the 1990s, bottoming out at 2.3\xa0million in 2000 [ 19 ] before rising again. [ 6 ] The first area tourists visit upon reaching the tower is FootTown, a five-story building stationed directly at the base. There, visitors can eat, shop, and enjoy various novelties and attractions. Elevators that depart from the first floor of FootTown can be used to reach the first of two observation decks, the two-story Main Observatory. [ 20 ] For the price of another ticket, visitors can board another set of elevators from the second floor of the Main Observatory to reach the final observation deck—the Special Observatory. [ 21 ] The names were changed following renovation of the top deck in 2018. [ 22 ] Broadcasting [ edit ] Looking down from the glass-flooring at Tokyo Tower Tokyo Tower, a member of the World Federation of Great Towers, has been used by many organizations for broadcasting purposes. The structure was intended for broadcasting television, but radio antennas were installed in 1961 because it could accommodate them. [ 6 ] While analog and digital television broadcasts are no longer conducted from the site, two FM radio stations remain on Tokyo Tower. Stations that use or have used the tower\'s antenna include: [ 11 ] Current [ edit ] Tokyo FM (JOAU-FM): 80.0 MHz InterFM (JODW-FM): 89.7 MHz Former [ edit ] NHK General TV Tokyo (JOAK-TV): VHF Channel 1 ( Analog ) NHK Educational TV Tokyo (JOAB-TV): VHF Channel 3 ( Analog ) Nippon Television Tokyo (JOAX-TV): VHF Channel 4 ( Analog ) Tokyo Broadcasting System Television (JORX-TV): TBS Television/ VHF Channel 6 ( Analog ) Fuji Television Tokyo (JOCX-TV): Fuji Television Analog/ VHF Channel 8 ( Analog ) TV Asahi Tokyo (JOEX-TV): TV Asahi Analog Television/ VHF Channel 10 ( Analog ) TV Tokyo (JOTX-TV): VHF Channel 12 ( Analog ) Tokyo Metropolitan Television (JOMX-TV): UHF Channel 14 ( Analog ) The University of the Air TV (JOUD-TV): UHF Channel 16 ( Analog ) tvk (JOKM-TV): UHF Channel 42 ( Analog ) The University of the Air-FM (JOUD-FM): 77.1 MHz J-Wave (JOAV-FM): 81.3 MHz NHK Radio FM Tokyo (JOAK-FM): 82.5 MHz Tokyo Tower, built in 1958 The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake did slight damage to the antenna of Tokyo Tower. Japan employs both analog and digital broadcasting. In July 2011 all television broadcasting was changed to solely digital. Tokyo Tower is not a reliable broadcasting antenna for completely digital broadcasting because the tower is not tall enough to transmit the higher frequency waves to areas surrounded by forests or high-rise buildings. As an alternative, a new 634-metre-tall (2,100\xa0ft) tower, the Tokyo Skytree , was opened in 2012. [ 6 ] In an attempt to make Tokyo Tower more appealing to NHK and the five other commercial broadcasters who planned to move their transmitting stations to the new tower, Nihon Denpatō officials drafted a plan to extend its digital broadcasting antenna by 80 to 100\xa0m (260 to 330\xa0ft) at a cost of approximately ¥4\xa0billion (US$50 million). [ 23 ] As a result of their move to the Skytree, only one digital television station remained on Tokyo Tower: that of the Open University of Japan , whose JOUD-DTV and JOUD-FM continued on the tower until shutting down in 2018. FM radio stations will continue to use the tower for broadcasting in the Tokyo area. Masahiro Kawada, the tower\'s planning director, raised the possibility of the tower becoming a backup for the Tokyo Skytree, depending on what the TV broadcasters want or need. [ 6 ] [ 24 ] The antenna\'s tip was damaged on 11 March 2011 by the Tōhoku earthquake . [ 25 ] On 19 July 2012, Tokyo Tower\'s height shrank to 315 meters while the top antenna was repaired for damage from the earthquake. [ 2 ] Attractions [ edit ] As tourism was always one of the tower\'s intended purposes, its five-story base building opened with a number of attractions in addition to housing elevators for the tower proper. The building was initially advertised as a "modern science museum," with the lower two floors focused on shops and restaurants, and the third and fourth on showrooms for the latest technologies from various electronics and broadcast companies (the fifth was closed to the public, being used to house heavy transmission equipment). [ 26 ] [ 27 ] With public interests shifting over time, attractions have constantly been renovated or rotated out for new ones, among the more notable: A wax museum on the third floor in 1970, advertised as Japan\'s first, displaying London -made figures of Leonardo and The Last Supper , John F. Kennedy , Chiune Sugihara , The Beatles , and more (closed 2013). [ 28 ] An aquarium on the first floor in 1978, offering many exotic fish for both display and sale (closed 2018). [ 29 ] A "trick art" gallery on the fourth floor in 1994, dedicated to various forms of Trompe-l\'œil and other optical illusion art (closed 2012). The building\'s roof leads to the tower\'s outside stairwell, comprising approximately 660\xa0steps up to the Main Deck; on weekends and holidays only, visitors may use these stairs as an alternative to the tower\'s internal elevators (for the same entry fare) and earn a certificate for completing the climb. [ 30 ] For many years, the roof also held a small playground that offered several simple rides and old-fashioned arcade games , and hosted live performances for children. [ 31 ] FootTown [ edit ] The base of Tokyo Tower with the FootTown building located underneath In 2005, the base building was heavily renovated and renamed FootTown . [ 32 ] While a few historical mainstays such as the Tower Restaurant, [ 33 ] aquarium, [ 34 ] wax museum [ 35 ] and trick art gallery [ 36 ] survived for a time, many new tenants were added, including a FamilyMart convenience store on the first floor [ 20 ] and a Guinness World Records museum [ 37 ] and hologram gallery named Gallery DeLux [ 38 ] on the third floor. The second-floor food court was also heavily reorganized, [ 39 ] [ 40 ] and many of the older souvenir shops consolidated into a single area called Tokyo Omiyage Town . The rooftop playground was also initially retained, albeit incorporated into a larger area known as the "Glass Plaza" meant to better accommodate live performances and FootTown\'s seasonal beer gardens . [ 41 ] In late 2013 the playground was quietly removed; since then, the roof space has continued to host expanded beer (and highball ) [ 42 ] gardens as well as a pickleball court. [ 43 ] As of 2026, FootTown\'s current major tenants include MOS Burger , Baskin-Robbins , Lawson S , and Pizza-La in addition to RED° (see below). Galleries and murals dedicated to the tower\'s history may also be found on the first and third floors. [ 44 ] Tokyo One Piece Tower [ edit ] Main article: Tokyo One Piece Tower In 2015, FootTown launched an indoor amusement park based on Eiichiro Oda \'s hit manga/anime series One Piece . It hosted a range of attractions, shops, and restaurants, offering patrons exclusive games, merchandise, and live performances themed to the fictional world and its characters. [ 45 ] [ 46 ] In 2020, due to concerns over the COVID-19 pandemic , the park was temporarily, then permanently closed down. [ 47 ] However, several of its attendant renovations, including FootTown\'s first escalators and a publicly-open fifth floor (the transmission equipment having been relocated to the Skytree) remained. RED° Tokyo Tower [ edit ] In 2022, One Piece Tower\'s former facilities were renovated into RED° Tokyo Tower, a multi-story arcade dedicated to VR and AR games . [ 48 ] Currently billed as Japan\'s largest esports park, it occupies roughly one-third of FootTown\'s first and third floors, and the entirety of the floors above. Observatories [ edit ] Daijingu Shrine, on the second floor of the Main Deck Separate from FootTown, the tower\'s observatories host their own shops and attractions. In particular, the two-story main deck contains a café, a private lounge, and a small shrine dedicated to Amaterasu , reputed to be the highest shrine in all of central Tokyo . Appearance [ edit ] Tokyo Tower in January 2011 with the Tokyo Skytree under construction in the background Tokyo Tower requires 28,000 litres (7,400 US gallons) of paint to completely paint the structure white and international orange , complying with air safety regulations. [ 11 ] Before the tower\'s 30th anniversary in 1987, the only lighting on the tower were light bulbs located on the corner contours that extended from the base to the antenna. In the spring of 1987, Nihon Denpatō invited lighting designer Motoko Ishii to visit the tower. Since its opening 30\xa0years earlier, the tower\'s annual ticket sales had dropped significantly, and in a bid to revitalize the tower and again establish it as an important tourist attraction and symbol of Tokyo, Ishii was hired to redesign Tokyo Tower\'s lighting arrangement. [ 49 ] Unveiled in 1989, the new lighting arrangement required the removal of the contour-outlining light bulbs and the installation of 176\xa0floodlights in and around the tower\'s frame. [ 49 ] From dusk to midnight, the floodlights illuminate the entire tower. [ 11 ] Sodium vapor lamps are used from 2 October to 6 July to cover the tower in an orange color. From 7 July to 1 October, the lights are changed to metal halide lamps to illuminate the tower with a white color. The reasoning behind the change is a seasonal one. Ishii reasoned that orange is a warmer color and helps to offset the cold winter months. Conversely, white is thought a cool color that helps during the hot summer months. [ 50 ] "Christmas Light Down Story", 2010 "Diamond Veil" lighting Occasionally, Tokyo Tower\'s lighting is changed to specific arrangements for special events. The tower is specially lit for some annual events.\nSince 2000, the entire tower has been illuminated in a pink light on 1 October to highlight the beginning of National Breast Cancer Awareness Month . The tower has also had a variety of special lighting arrangements for Christmas since 1994. During New Year\'s Eve , the tower lights up at midnight with a year number displayed on one side of the observatory to mark the arrival of the new year. [ 50 ] Special Japanese events have been cause to light the tower in several non-traditional ways. In 2002, alternating sections of the tower were lit blue to help celebrate the opening of the FIFA World Cup in Japan. Alternating sections of the tower were lit green on Saint Patrick\'s Day in 2007 to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Japanese–Irish relations. On a few occasions, Tokyo Tower has even been specially lit to correspond with corporate events. For example, the top half of the tower was lit green to correspond with the Japanese premiere of The Matrix Reloaded and different sections of the tower were lit red, white and black to commemorate the first day of sales of Coca-Cola C2 . [ 50 ] In the summer of 2021, the tower was lit up in Olympic colours to celebrate the 2020 Summer Olympics and 2020 Summer Paralympics in Tokyo, both of which had been delayed a year due to the COVID-19 pandemic . [ 51 ] On November 18, 2021, the tower was lit up at 17:17 in the red of Major League Baseball \'s Los Angeles Angels following the awarding of the American League MVP to two-way player Shohei Ohtani . [ 52 ] The tower was lit for the new millennium in 2000 with Motoko Ishii again reprising her role as the designer. [ 53 ] In December 2008, Nihon Denpatō spent $6.5\xa0million to create a new night-time illumination scheme—titled the "Diamond Veil"—to celebrate the tower\'s 50th anniversary. The arrangement featured 276\xa0lights in seven colors equally distributed across the towers four faces. [ 9 ] When employing specialty lighting on the tower, the Main Observatory often plays an important role. During the second international " White Band Day" on 10 September 2005, the tower was completely unlit except for the Main Observatory, which was lit with a bright white light. The resulting white ring represented the White Band referenced in the day\'s name. The two floors of windows that make up the exterior of the Main Observatory are utilized to display words or numbers. When the tower employed lighting to commemorate terrestrial digital broadcasting first being available in the Kantō region on 1 December 2005, each side of the Main Observatory displayed the characters 地デジ ( chi deji , an abbreviation for 地上デジタル放送 chijō dejitaru hōsō terrestrial digital broadcasting). [ 50 ] More recently, the observatory displayed both "TOKYO" and "2016" to stress Tokyo\'s 2016 Olympic bid . [ 54 ] Primitive images, such as hearts, have also been displayed using the observatory\'s windows. [ 50 ] Tokyo Tower seen from the 33rd floor of Azabudai Hills JP Tower Tokyo Tower, with Shiodome in the background The tower\'s original lighting arrangement, used until 1989 Renovation [ edit ] Operations at the Tokyo Tower Top Deck (at the height of 250 m) were suspended in 2016. The Top Deck reopened on 3 March 2018. At that time, Tokyo Tower also announced the renaming of both decks. Renovations on the main deck, which began in September 2016, caused partial closure of the deck. [ 22 ] Mascots [ edit ] Tokyo Tower has two mascots named Noppon ( ノッポン ) . They are two brothers: Older Brother, who wears blue dungarees , and Younger Brother, who wears red dungarees. They were unveiled on 23 December 1998 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Tokyo Tower. [ 55 ] Media representation [ edit ] Motion around Tokyo Tower at night, 2019 Just as the Eiffel Tower is often used in popular culture to immediately locate a scene in Paris, Tokyo Tower is often used in the same way for Tokyo. It is used in anime and manga such as Doraemon , Tokyo Magnitude 8.0 , Magic Knight Rayearth , Please Save My Earth , Cardcaptor Sakura , Digimon , Detective Conan , Sailor Moon , Tenchi Muyo! , Sakamoto Days and Death Note . [ 56 ] The tower is frequently used in the Japanese kaiju (giant monster) film genre. It has been the location of numerous battles and visitations by Godzilla , Mothra , Gamera and King Kong ( King Kong Escapes ) wherein it is frequently destroyed and rebuilt. [ 12 ] [ 57 ] Tokyo Tower is represented in Unicode as an emoji at code point U+1F5FC: 🗼 Tokyo Tower and its construction often appears in Shōwa nostalgia fiction and non-fiction, where it is used as a symbol of the financial prosperity of Shōwa era Japan. [ 58 ] For example, the 2005 film Always Sanchōme no Yūhi , based on the popular manga series by Ryōhei Saigan, was a nostalgic view of life in the neighborhoods beneath the construction of Tokyo Tower. class="mw-file-element" data-file-width="20" data-file-height="20" /></a></span></td></tr></tbody></table>\n<p><b>Tokyo Tower</b><span style="font-weight: normal"> (<span title="Japanese-language text"><span lang="ja">東京タワー</span></span>, <span title="Hepburn transliteration"><i lang="ja-Latn">Tōkyō Tawā</i></span>; <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1177148991">.mw-parser-output .IPA-label-small{font-size:85%}.mw-parser-output .references .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .infobox .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .navbox .IPA-label-small{font-size:100%}</style><span class="IPA-label IPA-label-small">pronounced</span> <span class="IPA nowrap" lang="ja-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Japanese" title="Help:IPA/Japanese">&#91;toːkʲoː<span class="wrap"> </span>taꜜɰᵝaː&#93;</a></span> <span class="ext-phonos"><span data-nosnippet="" id="ooui-php-1" class="noexcerpt ext-phonos-PhonosButton ext-phonos-PhonosButton-emptylabel oo-ui-widget oo-ui-widget-enabled oo-ui-buttonElement oo-ui-buttonElement-frameless oo-ui-iconElement oo-ui-buttonWidget" data-ooui="{&quot;_&quot;:&quot;mw.Phonos.PhonosButton&quot;,&quot;href&quot;:&quot;\\/\\/upload.wikimedia.org\\/wikipedia\\/commons\\/transcoded\\/a\\/a8\\/TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg\\/TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg.mp3&quot;,&quot;rel&quot;:[&quot;nofollow&quot;],&quot;framed&quot;:false,&quot;icon&quot;:&quot;volumeUp&quot;,&quot;data&quot;:{&quot;ipa&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;text&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;lang&quot;:&quot;en&quot;,&quot;wikibase&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;file&quot;:&quot;TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg&quot;},&quot;classes&quot;:[&quot;noexcerpt&quot;,&quot;ext-phonos-PhonosButton&quot;,&quot;ext-phonos-PhonosButton-emptylabel&quot;]}"><a role="button" tabindex="0" href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/a/a8/TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg/TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg.mp3" rel="nofollow" aria-label="Play audio" title="Play audio" class="oo-ui-buttonElement-button"><span class="oo-ui-iconElement-icon oo-ui-icon-volumeUp"></span><span class="oo-ui-labelElement-label"></span><span class="oo-ui-indicatorElement-indicator oo-ui-indicatorElement-noIndicator"></span></a></span><sup class="ext-phonos-attribution noexcerpt navigation-not-searchable"><a href="/wiki/File:TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg" title="File:TomJ-TokyoTower.ogg">ⓘ</a></sup></span>)</span>, a.k.a. <b>Japan Radio Tower</b> (<span title="Japanese-language text"><span lang="ja">日本電波塔</span></span>, <span title="Japanese-language romanization"><i lang="ja-Latn">Nippon denpatō</i></span>) is a <a href="/wiki/Radio_masts_and_towers" title="Radio masts and towers">communications</a> and <a href="/wiki/Observation_tower" title="Observation tower">observation tower</a> in the district of Shiba-koen in <a href="/wiki/Minato,_Tokyo" title="Minato, Tokyo">Minato, Tokyo</a>, Japan, completed in 1958. At 332.9 metres (1,092 feet), it was the <a href="/wiki/List_of_tallest_structures_in_Japan" title="List of tallest structures in Japan">tallest tower in Japan</a> until the construction of <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a> in 2012. It is a <a href="/wiki/Lattice_tower" title="Lattice tower">lattice tower</a> inspired by the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a>, and is painted white and <a href="/wiki/International_orange" title="International orange">international orange</a> to comply with <a href="/wiki/Aviation_safety" title="Aviation safety">air safety</a> regulations.\n</p><p>The tower\'s main sources of income are antenna leasing and tourism, and its five-story base building FootTown houses a number of restaurants, gift shops, and other attractions. Departing from it, guests can visit two observation decks: the two-story Main Deck at 150&#160;m (490&#160;ft), and the smaller Top Deck at 249.6&#160;m (819&#160;ft). The tower is repainted every five years, the process itself taking a year to complete.\n</p><p>In 1961, transmission antennas were added. They are used for radio and television broadcasting and now broadcast signals for media outlets such as <a href="/wiki/NHK" title="NHK">NHK</a>, <a href="/wiki/TBS_Television_(Japan)" title="TBS Television (Japan)">TBS Television</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Fuji_Television" title="Fuji Television">Fuji Television</a>. The height of the tower was not suitable for Japan\'s planned <a href="/wiki/Digital_terrestrial_television" title="Digital terrestrial television">terrestrial digital broadcasting</a> planned for July 2011, and for the Tokyo area. A taller digital broadcasting tower, known as <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a>, was completed on 29 February 2012. Tokyo Tower has become a prominent <a href="/wiki/Landmark" title="Landmark">landmark</a> and frequently appears in media set in Tokyo.\n</p>\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />\n<div .multiimageinner span:not(.skin-invert-image):not(.skin-invert):not(.bg-transparent) img{background-color:white}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tleft"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:292px;max-width:292px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:192px;max-width:192px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:150px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg/250px-Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg/330px-Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/83/Tokyo_tower_construction.jpg 2x" data-file-width="355" data-file-height="281" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Construction underway on 25 February 1958</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:96px;max-width:96px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:150px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_1961.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Tokyo_Tower_1961.jpg/120px-Tokyo_Tower_1961.jpg" decoding="async" width="94" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Tokyo_Tower_1961.jpg/250px-Tokyo_Tower_1961.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1262" data-file-height="2010" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Tokyo Tower around 1961</div></div></div></div></div>\n<p>A large broadcasting tower was needed in the <a href="/wiki/Kant%C5%8D_region" title="Kantō region">Kantō region</a> after <a href="/wiki/NHK" title="NHK">NHK</a>, Japan\'s <a href="/wiki/Public_broadcaster" class="mw-redirect" title="Public broadcaster">public broadcasting</a> station, began television broadcasting in 1953. Private broadcasting companies began operating in the months following the construction of NHK\'s own transmission tower. This communications boom led the Japanese government to believe that transmission towers would soon be built all over Tokyo, eventually overrunning the city. The proposed solution was the construction of one large tower capable of transmitting to the entire region.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-JT&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JT-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Furthermore, because of the country\'s <a href="/wiki/Japanese_post-war_economic_miracle" class="mw-redirect" title="Japanese post-war economic miracle">postwar boom</a> in the 1950s, Japan was searching for a monument to symbolize its national recovery from <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, as one of the countries most ravaged by the war.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-big&#95;in&#95;japan&#95;5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-big_in_japan-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-new&#95;JT&#95;6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-new_JT-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Hisakichi Maeda, founder and president of Nippon Denpatō, the tower\'s owner and operator, originally planned for the tower to be taller than the <a href="/wiki/Empire_State_Building" title="Empire State Building">Empire State Building</a>, which at 381&#160;m (1,250&#160;ft) was the highest structure in the world at the time. However, the plan fell through because of the lack of both funds and materials. The tower\'s height was eventually determined by the distance the TV stations needed to transmit throughout the Kantō region, a distance of about 150 kilometres (93 miles).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-JT&#95;4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JT-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p><a href="/wiki/Tach%C5%AB_Nait%C5%8D" title="Tachū Naitō">Tachū Naitō</a>, designer of tall buildings in Japan, was chosen to design the newly proposed tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-JT&#95;4-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JT-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Looking to the <a href="/wiki/Western_world" title="Western world">Western world</a> for inspiration, Naitō based his design on the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a> in Paris, France.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-sc&#95;7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sc-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> With the help of engineering company Nikken Sekkei Ltd., Naitō claimed his design could withstand earthquakes with twice the intensity of the <a href="/wiki/1923_Great_Kant%C5%8D_earthquake" class="mw-redirect" title="1923 Great Kantō earthquake">1923 Great Kantō earthquake</a> or <a href="/wiki/Typhoon" title="Typhoon">typhoons</a> with wind speeds of up to 220&#160;km/h (140&#160;mph).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-JT&#95;4-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JT-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The new construction project attracted hundreds of <i>tobi</i> (<a href="https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%B3%B6%E8%81%B7" class="extiw" title="ja:鳶職">鳶</a>), traditional Japanese construction workers who specialized in the construction of high-rise structures. The <a href="/wiki/Takenaka_Corporation" title="Takenaka Corporation">Takenaka Corporation</a> broke ground in June 1957 and each day at least 400&#160;laborers worked on the tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-JT&#95;4-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-JT-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It was constructed of <a href="/wiki/Steel" title="Steel">steel</a>, a third of which was scrap metal taken from US tanks damaged in the <a href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korean War</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-herald&#95;9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-herald-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> When the 90-metre (300&#160;ft)-long antenna was bolted into place on 14 October 1958, Tokyo Tower was the <a href="/wiki/List_of_towers" class="mw-redirect" title="List of towers">tallest freestanding tower</a> in the world, taking the title from the Eiffel Tower by 9&#160;m (30&#160;ft).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ET&#95;10-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ET-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="The material near this tag failed verification of its source citation(s). (December 2022)">failed verification</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>\n</p><p>Though physically taller than the Eiffel Tower, Tokyo Tower weighs about 4,000&#160;tons, 3,300 less than the Eiffel Tower<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official&#95;data&#95;11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official_data-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> as it is significantly thinner and simpler in construction. It was opened to the public on 23 December 1958 at a final cost of <a href="/wiki/Japanese_yen" title="Japanese yen">¥</a>2.8 billion ($8.4 million in 1958).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-herald&#95;9-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-herald-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-colliers&#95;12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-colliers-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Tokyo Tower was <a href="/wiki/Mortgage_loan" class="mw-redirect" title="Mortgage loan">mortgaged</a> for ¥10&#160;billion in 2000.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> It was the tallest artificial structure in Japan until April 2012, when it was surpassed by the <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-sc&#95;7-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sc-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Planned as an antenna for telecommunications and brightly colored in accordance with the time\'s Aviation Law, the tower\'s two panoramic observatories are mostly frequented by tourists today. The tower constitutes a clear reference point in the center\'s skyline, forming a strong landmark, both night and day.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Sacchi&#95;14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Sacchi-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The tower is periodically repainted in a process that takes about a year to complete.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> This traditionally occurred every five years, but the latest painting in 2019 utilized a new, more durable coating that extended the official timetable to seven years, projecting the next painting for 2026.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Functions">Functions</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Functions"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Special_observatory.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Special_observatory.jpg/250px-Special_observatory.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="375" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Special_observatory.jpg/500px-Special_observatory.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2336" data-file-height="3504" /></a><figcaption>The Top Deck, located directly below the tower\'s digital television broadcasting equipment</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Tokyo Tower\'s two main revenue sources are antenna leasing and tourism. It functions as a radio and television broadcasting antenna support structure and is a tourist destination that houses a variety of attractions. The tower recorded its 190&#160;millionth visitor in 2024.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Previously, visitor numbers had steadily declined in the 1990s, bottoming out at 2.3&#160;million in 2000<sup id="cite&#95;ref-AP&#95;19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AP-19"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> before rising again.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-new&#95;JT&#95;6-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-new_JT-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The first area tourists visit upon reaching the tower is FootTown, a five-story building stationed directly at the base. There, visitors can eat, shop, and enjoy various novelties and attractions. Elevators that depart from the first floor of FootTown can be used to reach the first of two observation decks, the two-story Main Observatory.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FT&#95;1F&#95;20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FT_1F-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> For the price of another ticket, visitors can board another set of elevators from the second floor of the Main Observatory to reach the final observation deck—the Special Observatory.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-observatory&#95;21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-observatory-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The names were changed following renovation of the top deck in 2018.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tokyotower.co.jp&#95;22-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tokyotower.co.jp-22"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Broadcasting">Broadcasting</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Broadcasting"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_look_down_window.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Tokyo_Tower_look_down_window.JPG/250px-Tokyo_Tower_look_down_window.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Tokyo_Tower_look_down_window.JPG/500px-Tokyo_Tower_look_down_window.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1944" /></a><figcaption>Looking down from the glass-flooring at Tokyo Tower</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Tokyo Tower, a member of the World Federation of Great Towers, has been used by many organizations for broadcasting purposes. The structure was intended for broadcasting television, but radio antennas were installed in 1961 because it could accommodate them.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-new&#95;JT&#95;6-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-new_JT-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> While analog and digital television broadcasts are no longer conducted from the site, two FM radio stations remain on Tokyo Tower. Stations that use or have used the tower\'s antenna include:<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official&#95;data&#95;11-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official_data-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Current">Current</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1273380762/mw-parser-output/.tmulti" /><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:292px;max-width:292px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:105px;max-width:105px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:241px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_during_daytime.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Tokyo_Tower_during_daytime.jpg/120px-Tokyo_Tower_during_daytime.jpg" decoding="async" width="103" height="242" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Tokyo_Tower_during_daytime.jpg/250px-Tokyo_Tower_during_daytime.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3312" data-file-height="7776" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Tokyo Tower, built in 1958</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:183px;max-width:183px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:241px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg/250px-2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg" decoding="async" width="181" height="241" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg/330px-2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/16/2011_Japan_Earthquake_Tokyo_Tower.jpg 2x" data-file-width="450" data-file-height="600" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">The <a href="/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake" class="mw-redirect" title="2011 Tōhoku earthquake">2011 Tōhoku earthquake</a> did slight damage to the antenna of Tokyo Tower.</div></div></div></div></div>\n<p>Japan employs both analog and digital broadcasting. In July 2011 all television broadcasting was changed to solely digital. Tokyo Tower is not a reliable broadcasting antenna for completely digital broadcasting because the tower is not tall enough to transmit the higher frequency waves to areas surrounded by forests or high-rise buildings. As an alternative, a new 634-metre-tall (2,100&#160;ft) tower, the <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a>, was opened in 2012.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-new&#95;JT&#95;6-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-new_JT-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In an attempt to make Tokyo Tower more appealing to <a href="/wiki/NHK" title="NHK">NHK</a> and the five other commercial broadcasters who planned to move their transmitting stations to the new tower, Nihon Denpatō officials drafted a plan to extend its digital broadcasting antenna by 80 to 100&#160;m (260 to 330&#160;ft) at a cost of approximately ¥4&#160;billion (US$50 million).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>As a result of their move to the Skytree, only one digital television station remained on Tokyo Tower: that of the <a href="/wiki/Open_University_of_Japan" title="Open University of Japan">Open University of Japan</a>, whose JOUD-DTV and JOUD-FM continued on the tower until shutting down in 2018. FM radio stations will continue to use the tower for broadcasting in the Tokyo area. Masahiro Kawada, the tower\'s planning director, raised the possibility of the tower becoming a backup for the Tokyo Skytree, depending on what the TV broadcasters want or need.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-new&#95;JT&#95;6-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-new_JT-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The antenna\'s tip was damaged on 11 March 2011 by the <a href="/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami" title="2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami">Tōhoku earthquake</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On 19 July 2012, Tokyo Tower\'s height shrank to 315 meters while the top antenna was repaired for damage from the earthquake.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-english.kyodonews.jp&#95;2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-english.kyodonews.jp-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Attractions">Attractions</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Attractions"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>As tourism was always one of the tower\'s intended purposes, its five-story base building opened with a number of attractions in addition to housing elevators for the tower proper. The building was initially advertised as a "modern science museum," with the lower two floors focused on shops and restaurants, and the third and fourth on showrooms for the latest technologies from various electronics and broadcast companies (the fifth was closed to the public, being used to house heavy transmission equipment).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>With public interests shifting over time, attractions have constantly been renovated or rotated out for new ones, among the more notable:\n</p>\n<ul><li>A <a href="/wiki/Wax_museum" title="Wax museum">wax museum</a> on the third floor in 1970, advertised as Japan\'s first, displaying <a href="/wiki/London" title="London">London</a>-made figures of <a href="/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci" title="Leonardo da Vinci">Leonardo</a> and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Last_Supper_(Leonardo)" title="The Last Supper (Leonardo)">The Last Supper</a></i>, <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy" title="John F. Kennedy">John F. Kennedy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chiune_Sugihara" title="Chiune Sugihara">Chiune Sugihara</a>, <a href="/wiki/The_Beatles" title="The Beatles">The Beatles</a>, and more (closed 2013).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>\n<li>An <a href="/wiki/Public_aquarium" title="Public aquarium">aquarium</a> on the first floor in 1978, offering many exotic fish for both display and sale (closed 2018).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>\n<li>A "trick art" gallery on the fourth floor in 1994, dedicated to various forms of <i><a href="/wiki/Trompe-l%27%C5%93il" title="Trompe-l&#39;œil">Trompe-l\'œil</a></i> and other <a href="/wiki/Optical_illusion" title="Optical illusion">optical illusion</a> art (closed 2012).</li></ul>\n<p>The building\'s roof leads to the tower\'s outside stairwell, comprising approximately 660&#160;steps up to the Main Deck; on weekends and holidays only, visitors may use these stairs as an alternative to the tower\'s internal elevators (for the same entry fare) and earn a certificate for completing the climb.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> For many years, the roof also held a small playground that offered several simple rides and old-fashioned <a href="/wiki/Arcade_game" title="Arcade game">arcade games</a>, and hosted live performances for children.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="FootTown">FootTown</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: FootTown"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BaseofTokyoTower.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/BaseofTokyoTower.JPG/250px-BaseofTokyoTower.JPG" decoding="async" width="190" height="253" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/BaseofTokyoTower.JPG/330px-BaseofTokyoTower.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/BaseofTokyoTower.JPG/500px-BaseofTokyoTower.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1704" data-file-height="2272" /></a><figcaption>The base of Tokyo Tower with the FootTown building located underneath</figcaption></figure><p>In 2005, the base building was heavily renovated and renamed <i>FootTown</i>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> While a few historical mainstays such as the Tower Restaurant,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> aquarium,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> wax museum<sup id="cite&#95;ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and trick art gallery<sup id="cite&#95;ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> survived for a time, many new tenants were added, including a <a href="/wiki/FamilyMart" title="FamilyMart">FamilyMart</a> convenience store on the first floor<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FT&#95;1F&#95;20-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FT_1F-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and a <a href="/wiki/Guinness_Book_of_World_Records" class="mw-redirect" title="Guinness Book of World Records">Guinness World Records</a> museum<sup id="cite&#95;ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Hologram" class="mw-redirect" title="Hologram">hologram</a> gallery named Gallery DeLux<sup id="cite&#95;ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> on the third floor. The second-floor <a href="/wiki/Food_court" title="Food court">food court</a> was also heavily reorganized,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and many of the older souvenir shops consolidated into a single area called <i>Tokyo <a href="/wiki/Omiyage" title="Omiyage">Omiyage</a> Town</i>.\n</p><p>The rooftop playground was also initially retained, albeit incorporated into a larger area known as the "Glass Plaza" meant to better accommodate live performances and FootTown\'s seasonal <a href="/wiki/Beer_garden" title="Beer garden">beer gardens</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In late 2013 the playground was quietly removed; since then, the roof space has continued to host expanded beer (and <a href="/wiki/Highball" title="Highball">highball</a>)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> gardens as well as a <a href="/wiki/Pickleball" title="Pickleball">pickleball</a> court.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>As of 2026, FootTown\'s current major tenants include <a href="/wiki/MOS_Burger" title="MOS Burger">MOS Burger</a>, <a href="/wiki/Baskin-Robbins" title="Baskin-Robbins">Baskin-Robbins</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lawson_(store)" title="Lawson (store)">Lawson S</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pizza-La" title="Pizza-La">Pizza-La</a> in addition to RED° (see below). Galleries and murals dedicated to the tower\'s history may also be found on the first and third floors.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tokyotower.co.jp/foottown&#95;44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tokyotower.co.jp/foottown-44"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading5"><h5 id="Tokyo_One_Piece_Tower">Tokyo One Piece Tower</h5><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: Tokyo One Piece Tower"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320" /><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_One_Piece_Tower" title="Tokyo One Piece Tower">Tokyo One Piece Tower</a></div>\n<p>In 2015, FootTown launched an indoor amusement park based on <a href="/wiki/Eiichiro_Oda" title="Eiichiro Oda">Eiichiro Oda</a>\'s hit manga/anime series <i><a href="/wiki/One_Piece" title="One Piece">One Piece</a></i>. It hosted a range of attractions, shops, and restaurants, offering patrons exclusive games, merchandise, and live performances themed to the fictional world and its characters.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>In 2020, due to concerns over the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a>, the park was temporarily, then permanently closed down.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> However, several of its attendant renovations, including FootTown\'s first <a href="/wiki/Escalator" title="Escalator">escalators</a> and a publicly-open fifth floor (the transmission equipment having been relocated to the Skytree) remained.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading5"><h5 id="RED°_Tokyo_Tower"><span id="RED.C2.B0_Tokyo_Tower"></span>RED° Tokyo Tower</h5><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: RED° Tokyo Tower"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>In 2022, One Piece Tower\'s former facilities were renovated into RED° Tokyo Tower, a multi-story <a href="/wiki/Amusement_arcade" title="Amusement arcade">arcade</a> dedicated to <a href="/wiki/Virtual_reality_game" title="Virtual reality game">VR</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_augmented_reality_video_games" title="List of augmented reality video games">AR games</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Currently billed as Japan\'s largest <a href="/wiki/Esports" title="Esports">esports</a> park, it occupies roughly one-third of FootTown\'s first and third floors, and the entirety of the floors above.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Observatories">Observatories</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=10" title="Edit section: Observatories"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_shinto_shrine.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Tokyo_Tower_shinto_shrine.jpg/250px-Tokyo_Tower_shinto_shrine.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Tokyo_Tower_shinto_shrine.jpg/500px-Tokyo_Tower_shinto_shrine.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1944" /></a><figcaption><i>Daijingu</i> Shrine, on the second floor of the Main Deck</figcaption></figure><p>\nSeparate from FootTown, the tower\'s observatories host their own shops and attractions. In particular, the two-story main deck contains a café, a private lounge, and a small <a href="/wiki/Shinto_shrine" title="Shinto shrine">shrine</a> dedicated to <a href="/wiki/Amaterasu" title="Amaterasu">Amaterasu</a>, reputed to be the highest shrine in all of <a href="/wiki/Special_wards_of_Tokyo" title="Special wards of Tokyo">central Tokyo</a>.</p><div style="clear:both;" class=""></div>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Appearance">Appearance</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=11" title="Edit section: Appearance"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_and_Tokyo_Sky_Tree_2011_January.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Tokyo_Tower_and_Tokyo_Sky_Tree_2011_January.jpg/250px-Tokyo_Tower_and_Tokyo_Sky_Tree_2011_January.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="154" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Tokyo_Tower_and_Tokyo_Sky_Tree_2011_January.jpg/500px-Tokyo_Tower_and_Tokyo_Sky_Tree_2011_January.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3840" data-file-height="2360" /></a><figcaption>Tokyo Tower in January 2011 with the <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree" title="Tokyo Skytree">Tokyo Skytree</a> under construction in the background</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Tokyo Tower requires 28,000 litres (7,400 US gallons) of paint to completely paint the structure white and <a href="/wiki/International_orange" title="International orange">international orange</a>, complying with <a href="/wiki/Air_safety" class="mw-redirect" title="Air safety">air safety</a> regulations.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official&#95;data&#95;11-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official_data-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Before the tower\'s 30th anniversary in 1987, the only lighting on the tower were light bulbs located on the corner contours that extended from the base to the antenna. In the spring of 1987, Nihon Denpatō invited <a href="/wiki/Lighting_designer" class="mw-redirect" title="Lighting designer">lighting designer</a> <a href="/wiki/Motoko_Ishii" title="Motoko Ishii">Motoko Ishii</a> to visit the tower. Since its opening 30&#160;years earlier, the tower\'s annual ticket sales had dropped significantly, and in a bid to revitalize the tower and again establish it as an important tourist attraction and symbol of Tokyo, Ishii was hired to redesign Tokyo Tower\'s lighting arrangement.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ishii&#95;49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ishii-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Unveiled in 1989, the new lighting arrangement required the removal of the contour-outlining light bulbs and the installation of 176&#160;floodlights in and around the tower\'s frame.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ishii&#95;49-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ishii-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> From dusk to midnight, the floodlights illuminate the entire tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-official&#95;data&#95;11-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-official_data-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Sodium_vapor_lamp" class="mw-redirect" title="Sodium vapor lamp">Sodium vapor lamps</a> are used from 2 October to 6 July to cover the tower in an orange color. From 7 July to 1 October, the lights are changed to <a href="/wiki/Metal_halide_lamp" class="mw-redirect" title="Metal halide lamp">metal halide lamps</a> to illuminate the tower with a white color. The reasoning behind the change is a seasonal one. Ishii reasoned that orange is a warmer color and helps to offset the cold winter months. Conversely, white is thought a cool color that helps during the hot summer months.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-japan&#95;lights&#95;50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-japan_lights-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1273380762/mw-parser-output/.tmulti" /><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:292px;max-width:292px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:146px;max-width:146px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:216px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:20101225-tokyotower-tarotokyo.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/20101225-tokyotower-tarotokyo.jpg/250px-20101225-tokyotower-tarotokyo.jpg" decoding="async" width="144" height="217" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/20101225-tokyotower-tarotokyo.jpg/330px-20101225-tokyotower-tarotokyo.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2121" data-file-height="3192" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">"Christmas Light Down Story", 2010</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:142px;max-width:142px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:216px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Tokyo_Tower_at_night_9.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Tokyo_Tower_at_night_9.JPG/250px-Tokyo_Tower_at_night_9.JPG" decoding="async" width="140" height="216" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Tokyo_Tower_at_night_9.JPG/330px-Tokyo_Tower_at_night_9.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1500" data-file-height="2315" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">"Diamond Veil" lighting</div></div></div></div></div>\n<p>Occasionally, Tokyo Tower\'s lighting is changed to specific arrangements for special events. The tower is specially lit for some annual events.\nSince 2000, the entire tower has been illuminated in a pink light on 1 October to highlight the beginning of <a href="/wiki/National_Breast_Cancer_Awareness_Month" class="mw-redirect" title="National Breast Cancer Awareness Month">National Breast Cancer Awareness Month</a>. The tower has also had a variety of special lighting arrangements for <a href="/wiki/Christmas" title="Christmas">Christmas</a> since 1994. During <a href="/wiki/New_Year%27s_Eve" title="New Year&#39;s Eve">New Year\'s Eve</a>, the tower lights up at midnight with a year number displayed on one side of the observatory to mark the arrival of the new year.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-japan&#95;lights&#95;50-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-japan_lights-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Special Japanese events have been cause to light the tower in several non-traditional ways. In 2002, alternating sections of the tower were lit blue to help celebrate the opening of the <a href="/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup" title="2002 FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</a> in Japan. Alternating sections of the tower were lit green on <a href="/wiki/Saint_Patrick%27s_Day" title="Saint Patrick&#39;s Day">Saint Patrick\'s Day</a> in 2007 to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Japanese–Irish relations. On a few occasions, Tokyo Tower has even been specially lit to correspond with corporate events. For example, the top half of the tower was lit green to correspond with the Japanese premiere of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Matrix_Reloaded" title="The Matrix Reloaded">The Matrix Reloaded</a></i> and different sections of the tower were lit red, white and black to commemorate the first day of sales of <a href="/wiki/Coca-Cola_C2" title="Coca-Cola C2">Coca-Cola C2</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-japan&#95;lights&#95;50-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-japan_lights-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In the summer of 2021, the tower was lit up in Olympic colours to celebrate the <a href="/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics" title="2020 Summer Olympics">2020 Summer Olympics</a> and <a href="/wiki/2020_Summer_Paralympics" title="2020 Summer Paralympics">2020 Summer Paralympics</a> in Tokyo, both of which had been delayed a year due to the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> On November 18, 2021, the tower was lit up at 17:17 in the red of <a href="/wiki/Major_League_Baseball" title="Major League Baseball">Major League Baseball</a>\'s <a href="/wiki/Los_Angeles_Angels" title="Los Angeles Angels">Los Angeles Angels</a> following the awarding of the American League MVP to two-way player <a href="/wiki/Shohei_Ohtani" title="Shohei Ohtani">Shohei Ohtani</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>The tower was lit for the new millennium in 2000 with Motoko Ishii again reprising her role as the designer.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In December 2008, Nihon Denpatō spent $6.5&#160;million to create a new night-time illumination scheme—titled the "Diamond Veil"—to celebrate the tower\'s 50th anniversary. The arrangement featured 276&#160;lights in seven colors equally distributed across the towers four faces.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-herald&#95;9-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-herald-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>When employing specialty lighting on the tower, the Main Observatory often plays an important role. During the second international "<a href="/wiki/White_Band" class="mw-redirect" title="White Band">White Band</a> Day" on 10 September 2005, the tower was completely unlit except for the Main Observatory, which was lit with a bright white light. The resulting white ring represented the White Band referenced in the day\'s name. The two floors of windows that make up the exterior of the Main Observatory are utilized to display words or numbers. When the tower employed lighting to commemorate <a href="/wiki/Digital_terrestrial_television" title="Digital terrestrial television">terrestrial digital broadcasting</a> first being available in the <a href="/wiki/Kant%C5%8D_region" title="Kantō region">Kantō region</a> on 1 December 2005, each side of the Main Observatory displayed the characters <span class="t&#95;nihongo&#95;kanji"><span title="Japanese-language text"><span lang="ja">地デジ</span></span></span> (<i>chi deji</i>, an abbreviation for <span class="t&#95;nihongo&#95;kanji"><span title="Japanese-language text"><span lang="ja">地上デジタル放送</span></span></span> <i>chijō dejitaru hōsō</i>  terrestrial digital broadcasting).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-japan&#95;lights&#95;50-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-japan_lights-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> More recently, the observatory displayed both "TOKYO" and "2016" to stress Tokyo\'s <a href="/wiki/Tokyo_2016_Olympic_bid" class="mw-redirect" title="Tokyo 2016 Olympic bid">2016 Olympic bid</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Primitive images, such as hearts, have also been displayed using the observatory\'s windows.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-japan&#95;lights&#95;50-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-japan_lights-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:View_from_33rd_floor_of_Azabudai_Hills_JP_Tower_9.jpg" class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Renovation">Renovation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=12" title="Edit section: Renovation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Operations at the Tokyo Tower Top Deck (at the height of 250 m) were suspended in 2016. The Top Deck reopened on 3 March 2018. At that time, Tokyo Tower also announced the renaming of both decks. Renovations on the main deck, which began in September 2016, caused partial closure of the deck.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-tokyotower.co.jp&#95;22-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tokyotower.co.jp-22"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Mascots">Mascots</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=13" title="Edit section: Mascots"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<p>Tokyo Tower has two mascots named Noppon<span style="font-weight: normal"> (<span title="Japanese-language text"><span lang="ja">ノッポン</span></span>)</span>. They are two brothers: Older Brother, who wears blue <a href="/wiki/Overall" class="mw-redirect" title="Overall">dungarees</a>, and Younger Brother, who wears red dungarees. They were unveiled on 23 December 1998 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Tokyo Tower.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Noppon&#95;55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Noppon-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Media_representation">Media representation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Tokyo_Tower&amp;action=edit&amp;section=14" title="Edit section: Media representation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><video id="mwe_player_0" poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm/250px-seek%3D10-TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm.jpg" controls="" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" class="mw-file-element" width="250" height="444" data-durationhint="15" data-mwtitle="TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm.480p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="480p.vp9.webm" data-width="270" data-height="480" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm.1080p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="1080p.vp9.webm" data-width="608" data-height="1080" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8&quot;" data-width="1080" data-height="1920" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm.240p.vp9.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;" data-transcodekey="240p.vp9.webm" data-width="136" data-height="240" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/2e/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm/TokyoTower-night-2019-10-29.webm.360p.webm" type="video/webm; codecs=&quot;vp8, vorbis&quot;" data-transcodekey="360p.webm" data-width="202" data-height="360" /></video></span><figcaption>Motion around Tokyo Tower at night, 2019</figcaption></figure>\n<p>Just as the <a href="/wiki/Eiffel_Tower" title="Eiffel Tower">Eiffel Tower</a> is often used in popular culture to immediately locate a scene in Paris, Tokyo Tower is often used in the same way for Tokyo. It is used in <a href="/wiki/Anime" title="Anime">anime</a> and <a href="/wiki/Manga" title="Manga">manga</a> such as <i><a href="/wiki/Doraemon" title="Doraemon">Doraemon</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Tokyo_Magnitude_8.0" title="Tokyo Magnitude 8.0">Tokyo Magnitude 8.0</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Magic_Knight_Rayearth" title="Magic Knight Rayearth">Magic Knight Rayearth</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Please_Save_My_Earth" title="Please Save My Earth">Please Save My Earth</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Cardcaptor_Sakura" title="Cardcaptor Sakura">Cardcaptor Sakura</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Digimon" title="Digimon">Digimon</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Detective_Conan" class="mw-redirect" title="Detective Conan">Detective Conan</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Sailor_Moon" title="Sailor Moon">Sailor Moon</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Tenchi_Muyo!" title="Tenchi Muyo!">Tenchi Muyo!</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Sakamoto_Days" title="Sakamoto Days">Sakamoto Days</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Death_Note" title="Death Note">Death Note</a></i>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-anime&#95;56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-anime-56"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The tower is frequently used in the Japanese <i><a href="/wiki/Kaiju" title="Kaiju">kaiju</a></i> (giant monster) film genre. It has been the location of numerous battles and visitations by <a href="/wiki/Godzilla" title="Godzilla">Godzilla</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mothra" title="Mothra">Mothra</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gamera" title="Gamera">Gamera</a> and <a href="/wiki/King_Kong" title="King Kong">King Kong</a> (<i><a href="/wiki/King_Kong_Escapes" title="King Kong Escapes">King Kong Escapes</a></i>) wherein it is frequently destroyed and rebuilt.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-colliers&#95;12-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-colliers-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-AFI&#95;57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AFI-57"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>\n</p><p>Tokyo Tower is represented in <a href="/wiki/Unicode" title="Unicode">Unicode</a> as an <a href="/wiki/Emoji" title="Emoji">emoji</a> at code point U+1F5FC: 🗼\n</p><p>Tokyo Tower and its construction often appears in <a href="/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dwa_nostalgia" title="Shōwa nostalgia">Shōwa nostalgia</a> fiction and non-fiction, where it is used as a symbol of the financial prosperity of Shōwa era Japan.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> For example, the 2005 film <i><a href="/wiki/Always_Sanch%C5%8Dme_no_Y%C5%ABhi" class="mw-redirect" title="Always Sanchōme no Yūhi">Always Sanchōme no Yūhi</a></i>, based on the popular manga series by Ryōhei Saigan, was a nostalgic view of life in the neighborhoods beneath the construction of Tokyo Tower.\n</p>\n<div class="mw-heading 2026-02-26 13:10:23 | DEBUG    | Scraped content: ScrapedContent(url='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Link_(building)', title='The Link (building) - Wikipedia', text='Coordinates : 48°53′16″N 2°14′53″E \ufeff / \ufeff 48.88772°N 2.24798°E \ufeff / 48.88772; 2.24798 From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Office in Paris, France The Link Tour The link ( French ) Interactive map of the The Link area General information Status Completed Type Office Architectural style Neo-futurism Location Puteaux , Paris , France , 6 Cr Michelet, Puteaux, Paris Coordinates 48°53′16″N 2°14′53″E \ufeff / \ufeff 48.88772°N 2.24798°E \ufeff / 48.88772; 2.24798 Construction started 2021 Completed 2025 Owner Groupama Height Roof 242\xa0m (794\xa0ft) [ 1 ] Technical details Structural system Concrete Floor count 52 Floor area 135,000\xa0m 2 (1,450,000\xa0sq\xa0ft) Design and construction Architect Philippe Chiambaretta Developer Redman Main contractor Vinci SA Website thelink-ladefense .com The Link is a mixed-use skyscraper building development under construction in Puteaux , France . It will be part of the La Défense business district. Completed in 2025, the tallest tower stands at 242\xa0m (794\xa0ft) tall with 52 floors, making it the tallest skyscraper in the Paris metropolitan area and in France, and the second tallest structure overall, after the Eiffel Tower . [ 2 ] The tower will house the new headquarters of French energy company TotalEnergies , which is currently located in Tour Total . [ 3 ] History [ edit ] In July 2017, Total has chosen the Link tower to house its next headquarters. Between 5,500 and 6,000 employees, previously located in the Coupole and Michelet towers, will be grouped together in this new skyscraper. [ 4 ] Its construction cost was estimated at one billion euros in October 2021. [ 5 ] On June 11, 2020, Groupama announced the groundbreaking of The Link with the start of the demolition work on the existing building, which would be followed in 2021 by foundation work on the new towers. [ 6 ] Architecture [ edit ] The complex consists of two office towers called Arche and Seine, standing at 242 and 178 meters high respectively, connected by 35 platforms called "links", a term derived from the English "link" and meaning "connection". The tallest tower will house the new headquarters of TotalEnergies , currently located in the Coupole Tower. [ 7 ] The Link project comprises approximately 130,000 m² of office space. It is located near a green space. The building includes duplex floors of approximately 6,000 m² and high ceilings, to allow internal pedestrian movement and limit the use of elevators. [ 8 ] The tower, by its height and position, is designed to visually rebalance the historic Axe historique . The building features a double-skin insulating façade incorporating photovoltaic panels and aims to reduce energy consumption by 50% compared to the towers previously occupied by the company. Accessibility to the district from Puteaux is to be improved through the renovation of Cours Michelet.
